# Do CRA Ratings Reflect Differences in Performance: An Examination Using Federal Reserve Data

## Key Findings

## **Executive Summary**

As a first step for assessing whether reform for the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) is necessary, analysts should ascertain whether CRA ratings correspond to significant differences in performance. If they do not, then either refined or new performance measures need to be developed. This report utilized a new Federal Reserve database of a sample of 6,300 CRA exams conducted during 2005 through 2017. The database contains data for bank performance for assessment areas (AAs), or geographical areas containing bank branches.

This analysis first tested whether retail loan performance measures such as the percent of home loans to low- and moderate-income (LMI) borrowers are higher for better ratings on the lending test, one of the major components of CRA exams. We found that, in general, better outcomes corresponded to higher ratings for retail loan performance measures but that the differences in performance tended to be not as wide as expected. In contrast, measures used to assess community development loans and investments tended to indicate greater differences in bank performance across ratings categories.

The results suggest the need for refinement of performance measures, especially for the retail loan indicators, rather than a complete overhaul. The Federal Reserve data indicates a rating system that is not fundamentally broken or arbitrary but a system that should be sharpened. We suggest a more explicit sorting of bank performance into different ratings categories based on how banks perform against their peers and that more testing should be conducted to assess whether different peer benchmarks should be developed for banks with different business models.

In addition, the findings argue for retention of qualitative factors and allowance for performance in one area to compensate for poorer performance in other areas, but also for more explicit methods for indicating how the qualitative factors and compensation procedures contribute to ratings. Nonetheless, even when accounting for qualitative factors, the quantitative performance measures used on CRA exams should indicate significant median differences in performance across ratings categories.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)’s final rule for changing the CRA regulations does not employ a careful data-based assessment of the nature considered in this report. Although the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) signed on to the proposed rule, they pulled out of the final rulemaking. The OCC should withdraw its final rule and embark on a new one with the Federal Reserve Board and the FDIC.

## **Introduction**

Banks and community groups have advocated for the reform of the CRA regulation in part because of concerns related to the subjectivity of CRA ratings. If CRA ratings do not reflect differences in actual bank performance in lending, investing and providing bank services to LMI communities, CRA will not achieve its fullest potential in increasing lending, investing and services to underserved borrowers and communities.

In order to reduce subjectivity in CRA ratings, must CRA ratings and exams be radically overhauled as executed by the OCC’s final rule? Alternatively, would incremental reforms be more effective? The bottom line is that a ratings system should accurately reflect differences in performance so that the banks with lower ratings would be motivated to increase their lending, investments and services to LMI borrowers and communities.

A substantial body of research has found that CRA has been effective in increasing access to credit and capital for LMI borrowers and neighborhoods. [Economists at the Federal Reserve Bank in Philadelphia](https://www.philadelphiafed.org/-/media/research-and-data/publications/working-papers/2017/wp17-15.pdf) found that CRA increased home lending in LMI neighborhoods by up to 20%. [Bostic and colleagues](https://www.philadelphiafed.org/-/media/research-and-data/publications/working-papers/2018/wp18-27.pdf) revealed that CRA also increased small business lending. [Ding and Reid](https://www.philadelphiafed.org/-/media/research-and-data/publications/working-papers/2019/wp19-36.pdf) showed that CRA prevented the closure of profitable branches in LMI census tracts.

Clearly, CRA has motivated banks to serve LMI communities. While this report was not designed to offer estimates regarding the extent to which CRA has reached its potential to increase access to credit and capital, it did examine whether the rating system can be improved, which in turn would increase access to credit and capital for underserved communities.

NCRC utilized the recently released Federal Reserve database on CRA exams conducted between 2005 and 2017 for this report. [Our recent comment letter to the OCC and FDIC](https://ncrc.org/ncrc-supplemental-cra-comment-using-federal-reserve-cra-data/) described the database in detail.

## **Findings**

***Overall Ratings***

Table 1 below shows that overall CRA ratings could be improved in terms of differentiating bank performance. For example, it is unlikely that upwards of 90% of banks performed in a Satisfactory manner as recorded by CRA ratings over the last several years. On the other end of the ratings distribution, the portion of banks that failed their exams (Needs-to-Improve and Substantial Noncompliance) dropped from a high of 10% in the early years of public disclosure of ratings to 2% or less in recent years.

A shortcoming in the ratings system is that four ratings are the only possible overall ratings. Five ratings would allow for more distinctions in performance. The large bank exam has a lending test, an investment test and a service test. Each of these tests would have five overall ratings: Outstanding, High Satisfactory, Low Satisfactory, Needs-to-Improve and Substantial Noncompliance. If the overall ratings divided the current Satisfactory rating into High and Low-Satisfactory, the 90% of banks that had scored Satisfactory would now be divided into two buckets, which would better reflect their performance.

The OCC  hesitated to establish five overall ratings, citing the CRA statute that lists just four ratings. However, it could establish point scales that would more effectively differentiate the performance of the banks with Satisfactory ratings. On a point scale of 1 to 100, for example, banks with Satisfactory ratings could have points ranging from 60 to 90; those with scores of 60 to 75 would have Low Satisfactory ratings and those scoring 76 to 90 would have High Satisfactory ratings. Alternatively, if Low and High Satisfactory were not assigned to point ranges, it would still be clear that banks scoring lower on the point scale were performing in a manner that is not quite Satisfactory.

![CRA Ratings from 1990 to 2019](https://ncrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Do-CRA-Tables-v2-1.png)

***Ratings on Retail Part of Lending Test and Performance Measures***

The lending test uses various performance measures to assess a bank’s retail lending performance. For home lending, two of these measures are the percent of loans to LMI borrowers and the percent of loans in LMI tracts. For small business lending, the two measures are percent of loans to the smallest businesses (revenues less than $1 million) and percent of loans in LMI tracts.

Table 2 tests the relationship between the five ratings on the lending test and percent of loans to LMI borrowers. At the outset, it is important to remember that there may not be a perfect relationship between ratings and percent of loans. Higher percentages of loans on one performance measure may not always translate into higher ratings since the lending test has several measures. Also, it is possible for a bank to compensate for poor performance on one measure with better performance on another measure. However, the median percentage of loans to LMI borrowers should be generally different for banks with different ratings, particularly over a large sample size.

This examination also split banks into different asset categories to see if different relationships emerge between ratings and performance for the different asset categories. Following the methodology of Calem, Lambie-Hanson and Wachter described in [our comment letter](https://www.ncrc.org/ncrc-supplemental-cra-comment-using-federal-reserve-cra-data/) to the OCC and FDIC, NCRC classified the banks as community banks with assets up to $10 billion, regional banks with assets between $10 billion and $50 billion and large banks with assets over $50 billion. This report did not include findings for banks with Substantial Noncompliance ratings since there are too few observations for these banks.

A highly visible finding in Table 2 was that large banks issued a considerably lower percentage of loans to LMI borrowers from 2005 through 2017 than their smaller counterparts. Some large banks have stated that their higher loan volumes makes it harder for them to perform as well on a performance measure of percent of loans to LMI borrowers. Also, large banks could be performing better on other parts of the lending test. However, this finding suggested that there is room to rate large banks more rigorously on the lending test and on this particular measure.

Another clear finding was that the percentage of loans to LMI borrowers for banks with High Satisfactory ratings was higher than the percentage of loans to LMI borrowers for banks with Outstanding ratings. For banks in all categories, the median percentage of loans on an assessment area (AA) level to LMI borrowers was 11.83% for banks with Outstanding ratings and 12.78% for banks with High Satisfactory ratings. Performance on other performance measures might be compensating in the case of banks with Outstanding ratings. However, the question remains whether at the median, the scoring system could more effectively and logically differentiate banks in these two ratings categories with Outstanding banks achieving higher ratings.

Except for regional banks, banks with High Satisfactory ratings issued a higher median percentage of loans to LMI borrowers at an AA level than banks with Low Satisfactory ratings. The difference was generally two to three percentage points between the two ratings.

The sharpest differences in performance occurred between banks with Low Satisfactory ratings (10.43%) and banks with Needs-to-Improve ratings (2.13%). Banks with Needs-to-Improve ratings were making few loans to LMI borrowers.

![Percent of Home Loans to LMI Borrowers by Bank Category and Lending Test Rating](https://ncrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Do-CRA-Tables-v2-2.png)

Table 3 results were more consistent with expectations. For each bank category and overall, the median percentage of loans in LMI tracts at the AA level was higher by one to two percentage points for banks with Outstanding than High Satisfactory ratings. A similar difference occurred between banks with High Satisfactory and Low Satisfactory ratings. Finally, a stark difference in median percentage of loans in LMI tracts occurred between banks with Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings.

Large banks did not perform worse than their smaller counterparts in percent of loans in LMI tracts in contrast to percent of loans to LMI borrowers. This does not necessarily absolve large banks since it is arguable that LMI tracts is an easier performance measure since a portion of lending in LMI tracts is to middle- and upper-income borrowers.

![Percent of Home Loans in LMI Tracts by Bank Category and Lending Test Rating](https://ncrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Do-CRA-Tables-v2-3-775px.png)

Table 4, examining lending to the smallest businesses with revenues below $1 million, revealed a different result than Table 3 in that the median percentages of loans at the AA level to the target population was not noticeably different across ratings categories. The difference between all banks with Outstanding ratings compared to banks with High Satisfactory ratings was about two percentage points (61.47% vs. 59.2%). However, the regional banks could be responsible for a significant amount of this difference; the performance of regional banks with Outstanding and High Satisfactory ratings differed by four percentage points whereas the difference was narrower for the other two bank categories. Again, except for regional banks, the difference between High and Low Satisfactory ratings in the portion of loans to the smallest businesses was less than one percentage point. Finally, it was only the community bank category that exhibited a sizable difference in the percent of loans to the smallest businesses between banks in Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings.

Another notable finding was that large banks trail their counterparts in lending to the smallest businesses. For example, regional banks with Outstanding ratings issued a median percentage at the AA level of 67.49% of their loans to the smallest businesses compared to large banks’ median of 55.96%. This was consistent with the home lending results. Large banks had the most difficulty relative to their peers in lending to borrowers with the lowest incomes or revenues than in lending to LMI tracts.

![Percent of Loans to Smallest Businesses by Bank Category and Lending Test Rating](https://ncrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Do-CRA-Tables-v2-4.png)

Table 5, revealing the median percent of loans to small businesses in LMI tracts at the AA level, continued the theme of expected differences between the rating categories but differences of small magnitudes and inconsistencies across the various bank asset categories. Overall, the difference between banks with Outstanding and High Satisfactory ratings in the portion of loans in LMI tracts was about one percentage point, with greater differences between regional and community banks than large banks. There were muted differences of less than one percentage point between banks with High Satisfactory and Low Satisfactory ratings. Finally, there were pronounced differences of more than five percentage points between banks with Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings.

![Percent of Small Business Loans in LMI Tracts by Bank Category and Lending Test Rating](https://ncrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Do-CRA-Tables-v2-5.png)

Another measure of performance on the lending test is the amount of community development (CD) loans. CD loans finance larger scale projects than individual homes or loans for small businesses. CD loans support affordable housing (often multi-family, rental housing), larger scale economic development projects or initiatives that revitalize and stabilize LMI communities.

Table 6 displays a ratio of CD loans by deposits, which is similar to ratios used on the lending test. For regional and community banks, it showed that higher ratios corresponded to better ratings as to be expected. Moreover, the differences in the ratios for the rating categories were more pronounced than for the measures used for the retail part of the lending test described above. For example, the median CD loan ratio at the AA level of regional banks with Outstanding ratings was 3.97%; 1.63% for those with High Satisfactory ratings; and .41% for those with Low Satisfactory ratings. Expressed another way, the median ratio for banks with Outstanding ratings was 137% higher than the ratio for High Satisfactory banks, which was in turn 297% higher than the ratio for Low Satisfactory banks.

Another way to consider the significant differences in ratios for banks with different ratings is to remember that they express the percentage of deposits devoted to CD lending. Banks with Outstanding ratings were devoting 137% more of their deposits to CD loans than banks with High Satisfactory rating. This was a much more significant difference than a retail performance measure that differs by one percentage point between banks with different ratings: one percentage point or a difference of 20% vs. 21% of loans is a considerably smaller difference in resources for a LMI population than 100% more deposits devoted to CD financing.

The median ratios for community banks were quite different for Outstanding and High Satisfactory banks (2.15% vs. 1.78% for a 20% difference). The differences for those with High and Low Satisfactory ratings were somewhat narrower.

Large bank ratios had an unusual pattern with median ratios for banks with High Satisfactory ratings being higher than those with Outstanding ratings. However, the differences between the other ratings were in the expected direction and were large. A possible explanation for the unusual position of banks with Outstanding and High Satisfactory ratings is that some very large banks [were downgraded for fair lending violations](https://ncrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/cra_geography_paper_050517.pdf) during the years of the financial crisis.

Overall, the differences were larger for the CD part of the lending test than on the performance measures of the retail test. It is possible that the CD measure is a deciding factor determining ratings on the lending test.

![Median Ratio of CD Loans to Deposits by Bank Category and Lending Test Rating](https://ncrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Do-CRA-Tables-v2-6.png)

***Ratings on investment test and levels of community development investments***

The dollar amount of investments is a significant criterion on the current investment test. CRA exams often measure this activity by reporting overall dollar levels but also comparing investments to assets or Tier One capital. This study used a ratio of community development (CD) investments divided by deposits since assets cannot be apportioned easily at the AA level and since the OCC finalized the use of deposits in the denominator of their CRA evaluation measure.

In contrast to the retail portion of the lending test, differences across rating categories were more pronounced except for the top two ratings in the case of community banks. The median ratio at the AA level for community banks was 1.22% for those that received Outstanding on the investment test and 1.3% for those that received High Satisfactory. The median ratio for community banks rated Low Satisfactory nosedived to .53% and was a mere .01% for community banks rated Needs-to-Improve.

Regional and large banks exhibited wide differences among the ratings categories. Large banks with Outstanding ratings had a median ratio at the AA level of 2.45% while those with High Satisfactory had a significantly smaller ratio of 1.2%. A very similar difference was present for regional banks. The ratios for banks in those two categories with Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings were quite small.

![Median Ratio of CD Investments to Deposits by Bank Category and Investment Test Rating](https://ncrc.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Do-CRA-Tables-v2-7.png)

## **Implications of Findings**

Generally, the analysis found expected differences among banks with various ratings on retail test performance measures but differences were often narrow. The analysis revealed some inconsistencies like higher percentage of loans to LMI borrowers for large banks scoring High Satisfactory rather than Outstanding. The anomalies in the large bank ratings could be explained by some very large banks being downgraded during the financial crisis for violations of fair lending and consumer compliance law as discussed above.

Large banks significantly trailed their smaller peers in percent of loans to LMI borrowers and smallest businesses. This difference in performance did not occur when considering lending in LMI tracts. It seems that ratings could be tougher on these performance measures in order to encourage large banks to increase their percentage of loans to these categories of borrowers.

The other major finding was that the performance measures for CD lending and investment generally revealed larger differences among banks with various ratings than the measures for the retail portion of the lending test. While the median percent of retail loans generally varied by a percentage point among the ratings, the differences in the CD loan and investment ratios were often as high as 100%.

The ratings methodology on the retail portion of the lending test could be improved. NCRC suggests an approach that awards a rating based on how a bank compares to its aggregate peer or peer group of lenders. The percentages below indicate how a bank’s percentage of loans to a borrower group compares to the peer. For example, if the peer group issued 20% of loans to LMI borrowers, the bank would need to issue more than 20% of loans to LMI borrowers in order to score Outstanding on the performance measure. Below are possible ranges relative to the aggregate peer performance:

***Outstanding:*** greater than 100% because the bank would be better than its peers.

***High Satisfactory:***80% to 99% because the bank would be approximately in line with its peers.

***Low Satisfactory:*** 60% to 79% because the bank would be below its peers, but not so far below to be considered not satisfactory.

***Needs to Improve:*** 40% to 60% because the bank would be at approximately half the level of its peers.

***Substantial Noncompliance:*** 39% and lower because the bank would be far below the level of its peers.

Another decision would be what groups of banks would constitute the “aggregate peer.” CRA exams currently consider all lenders reporting HMDA or CRA data at the AA level to be the aggregate peer. [In recent research](https://ncrc.org/proposed-occ-and-fdic-geographic-analysis-of-home-mortgage-and-small-business-lending-permission-to-decrease-lending-for-the-largest-banks/), NCRC found that banks with branches in an AA tend to lend at higher percentages than those without branches in an AA. Banks without branches could be credit card banks in the case of small business lending, internet-based banks or banks using correspondents or brokers in the case of home lending.

A legitimate question is whether banks with different business models should be expected to perform at the same level on a performance measure or whether that is not possible because the different models make them good at some aspects of CRA performance and not as good at others. In the initial years after a change to the CRA regulation and exams, it might make sense to use different peer aggregates for branch-based institutions and non-branch ones. It would not make sense to fail non-branch banks if they are far behind their branch-based peers on the retail loan performance measures. However, their scale above could be adjusted so fewer of them are obtaining Outstanding and High Satisfactory ratings since they are not performing as well on retail loan performance measures as their branch-based peers. Over time, it is hoped that the performance converges to a higher level for banks of various business models. Future rule makings could then adjust peer aggregates and scales.

In addition to the differences in performance between branch-based and non-branch based banks, the agencies should see if there are significant differences revealed by the performance measures among banks with various asset levels. If there are differences, the agencies should make any appropriate adjustments to aggregate peers.

This paper did not analyze demographic measures that include comparing the percent of home loans to LMI borrowers to the percent of households in an AA that are LMI. Empirical testing similar to that presented in this paper should test performance on demographic measures. In a previous report, [NCRC found high rates of failure](https://ncrc.org/proposed-occ-and-fdic-geographic-analysis-of-home-mortgage-and-small-business-lending-permission-to-decrease-lending-for-the-largest-banks/) for a demographic measure proposed by the OCC and FDIC. Perhaps one refinement could be to compare a bank’s performance against aggregate peer performance on a demographic benchmark using a scale similar to that above.

Further complications to ratings in current CRA exams are qualitative factors and allowance of performance in some tests to compensate for lackluster performance in other tests. CRA should not be a strictly quantitative exercise because responsiveness to unique needs and different economic conditions in different AAs cannot be captured in performance measures such as percent of loans to LMI borrowers. NCRC [stated in its comment letter](https://ncrc.org/ncrc-comments-regarding-notice-of-proposed-rulemaking-docket-id-occ-2018-0008-and-rin-3064-af22/) that qualitative measures capturing responsiveness, innovation and flexibility should count for 20% to 30% of the rating on a test. In addition, within reason, a higher score on one component test could compensate for a lower score on another component test. For instance, if internet-based banks are not as successful in retail lending to LMI borrowers, perhaps they should be expected to offer higher levels of CD finance or service. Various weights for each component test builds in compensation.

Even with qualitative and compensating factors as part of component tests, medians of performance measures over a large sample of several years at the AA level should reflect larger differences than observed in the measures of the retail test. The scale suggested above could achieve that. The only way to assess this possibility is for the OCC to have collaborated in designing even more comprehensive databases than the Federal Reserve did and then to test rigorously different approaches with the database. While the Federal Reserve pioneered an effort and created a database that had not ever been collected before, the database did not include variables for all three major component tests. Service test variables such as the percent of branches in LMI tracts were missing. It is possible that three agencies combining resources could have created a more thorough database.

## **Conclusion**

Using Federal Reserve data on a large sample of CRA exams, this analysis found that CRA ratings reflect actual differences in bank performance on the retail lending test and the investment test. The performance measures, particularly those related to the retail lending test, should be sharpened so that they more clearly differentiate performance as reflected in CRA ratings. The overall objective is to reform the present ratings system, in which 90% of banks receive one rating that is Satisfactory, when it is clear that there are more differences in performance than revealed by the current system. An update to CRA, rather than the radical overhaul as finalized by the OCC, would achieve meaningful ratings reform.

In particular, ratings for large banks should be toughened. NCRC found that they considerably lagged their smaller counterparts in the percentage of loans to LMI borrowers and to the smallest businesses. This finding was similar to that in the Calem, Lambie-Hanson and Wachter study mentioned above.

The OCC’s final rule is not evidence-based. The OCC’s  final rule is not based on data analysis nor does it include a publicly available database like the Federal Reserve made available. Stakeholders cannot estimate its impact using data on lending, investing and service provision. It must be withdrawn to allow for a more thoughtful and data driven rulemaking to proceed.

After implementation of a new regulation and examinations, the agencies should produce annual reports that include analyses of performance measures along the lines of this analysis and indicate whether the performance measures are working as desired or whether further changes are needed.

## **Methodology Appendix**

The Federal Reserve used HMDA data for calculating the number of loans to various borrower groups inside AAs and outside AAs. We used the HMDA data for inside AAs since CRA exams measure home lending inside AAs. The small business data collected by the Federal Reserve did not always include separate totals for inside AAs so we used the lending data labeled as “total” when there was no data for inside AAs for a borrower group.

NCRC used all banks up to $10 billion for community banks for the lending test, but stripped out intermediate small and small banks in this category for the investment test and for the community development lending analysis. Small banks are not evaluated for community development financing and intermediate small banks do not have an investment test.

The Federal Reserve database did not contain variables related to the service test such as the percent of branches in LMI tracts. Therefore, we could not assess service test ratings compared to performance measures.

*Josh Silver is NCRC’s Senior Advisor, Policy and Government Affairs.  
Jason Richardson is NCRC’s Director of Research & Evaluation.*

This NCRC (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) report examines whether Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) ratings reflect real differences in bank performance, using a new Federal Reserve database of 6,300 CRA exams conducted from 2005 through 2017. The analysis was authored by Josh Silver (Senior Advisor, Policy and Government Affairs) and Jason Richardson (Director of Research & Evaluation).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Retail loan performance measures generally showed higher ratings corresponding to better outcomes, but the differences were narrower than expected.
- Community development (CD) loan and investment measures showed much larger performance differences across ratings categories (often ~100% differences) compared to retail measures (often just 1 percentage point differences).
- Approximately 90% of banks received a Satisfactory rating, indicating the four-tier rating system fails to adequately differentiate performance. NCRC recommends splitting Satisfactory into High and Low Satisfactory tiers.
- Large banks significantly lagged smaller banks in percent of loans to LMI borrowers and to the smallest businesses, though they did not trail on LMI tract lending.
- Anomalies existed, including banks with High Satisfactory ratings sometimes outperforming banks with Outstanding ratings (e.g., median LMI borrower lending of 12.78% for High Satisfactory vs. 11.83% for Outstanding), potentially explained by large banks being downgraded for fair lending violations during the financial crisis.
- The sharpest performance differences occurred between Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings (e.g., 10.43% vs. 2.13% for LMI borrower lending).

RECOMMENDATIONS:
- NCRC advocates for incremental reform rather than radical overhaul, contrary to the OCC's final rule.
- Proposes a peer-relative rating scale comparing bank performance to aggregate peers (Outstanding: >100% of peer level; High Satisfactory: 80-99%; Low Satisfactory: 60-79%; Needs-to-Improve: 40-60%; Substantial Noncompliance: <39%).
- Suggests different peer benchmarks may be needed for different business models (branch-based vs. non-branch banks) and asset sizes.
- Recommends retaining qualitative factors (20-30% of ratings) and compensation mechanisms where strong performance on one test can offset weaker performance elsewhere.
- Calls for the OCC to withdraw its final rule, which NCRC argues is not evidence-based, and to collaborate with the Federal Reserve Board and FDIC on new rulemaking with a publicly available database.
- Recommends annual agency reports analyzing performance measures after new regulations are implemented.

METHODOLOGY NOTES:
- Banks classified as community (up to $10B assets), regional ($10B-$50B), and large (over $50B).
- The Federal Reserve database lacked service test variables (e.g., percent of branches in LMI tracts), limiting analysis.
- Banks with Substantial Noncompliance ratings were excluded due to insufficient observations.
args.key_excerpts: "The results suggest the need for refinement of performance measures, especially for the retail loan indicators, rather than a complete overhaul. The Federal Reserve data indicates a rating system that is not fundamentally broken or arbitrary but a system that should be sharpened."

args.summary:
This is the Federal Reserve Board's Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) search page, which provides a searchable database of Performance Evaluations & Ratings for Federal Reserve-supervised state member banks. The page is part of the official Federal Reserve System website and covers the CRA framework under the Federal Open Market Committee.

The search tool allows users to filter results by several criteria: institution name or ID, overall CRA rating (All, Outstanding, Satisfactory, Needs to Improve, Substantial Noncompliance), city, county, state (all 50 states plus Puerto Rico and DC), asset size range (from 0-$350K up to $100M+), exam year (1995-2026), public year (1995-2026), and exam method (Intermediate Small Bank, Small Bank, Large Bank, Limited Purpose, Strategic Plan, Wholesale). Users can also filter by component test ratings including Lending Test, Investment Test, Service Test, and Community Development Test ratings.

The results table displays a paginated list (64 pages total) of bank evaluation records, showing for each bank: Bank Name with RSSD ID, Headquarters Location, Overall Rating, Exam Date (Performance Evaluation), Public Date, Exam Method, and Asset Size (in thousands). Each entry includes a link to download the full Performance Evaluation (PE) PDF.

Sample data from the first page shows 30 banks, including examples like:
- 1ST SOURCE BANK (South Bend, IN) - Rated "Outstanding," Large Bank exam method, $8,411,706K assets, exam date Sep 25, 2023
- ALLY BANK (Sandy, UT) - Rated "Outstanding," Strategic Plan exam method, $181,409,000K assets, exam date Apr 21, 2025
- 1NB BANK (Carlyle, IL) - Rated "Satisfactory," Small Bank, $293,354K assets, exam date Sep 02, 2025
- ADIRONDACK TRUST COMPANY (Saratoga Springs, NY) - Rated "Satisfactory," Large Bank, $1,714,346K assets, exam date Jun 30, 2025

The page includes records dating back to 1998 and forward through 2026 exam years, with most banks receiving "Satisfactory" ratings and only a few receiving "Outstanding."

## Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)

### Evaluating a Bank's CRA Performance

The Federal Reserve evaluates how well state member banks have helped meet the needs of their communities using one of five evaluation methods tailored to a bank's size or business strategy. The Board continues to apply the 1995 regulations to banks.

The Federal Reserve makes banks' Performance Evaluations public through an [online database](/apps/CRAPubWeb/CRA/BankRating) that can be searched using institution or exam criteria or [by bank branch location](/apps/CRAPubWeb/Branch/BankRatingByBranch). In addition, each bank is required to maintain a copy of the Performance Evaluation in its public file and make it available to customers upon request.

Each Performance Evaluation includes:

#### CRA Ratings

One of the following overall CRA ratings will be assigned based on the evaluation of a bank's CRA performance:

#### Types of CRA Ratings

**Overall CRA Rating**  
All banks are issued an overall rating. This is the institution's primary CRA rating.

**State Rating or Multistate MSA Rating**   
A *state rating* is generally assigned if a bank has branches in more than one state. A bank that has branches in more than one state is also known as an interstate bank.

A *multistate MSA rating* is assigned if a bank has branches in two or more states within a multistate metropolitan statistical area.

**Infographic: What is a Multistate Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA)?**

![MSA infographic thumbnail](/consumerscommunities/files/CRA-thumb-300px-opt2.jpg)

![MSA infographic thumbnail](/consumerscommunities/files/CRA-thumb-300px-opt2.jpg)

[View infographic (PDF)](/consumerscommunities/files/msa-infographic.pdf)

CRA activity is captured in either a state rating or a multistate MSA rating, but not both.

**Component Ratings**   
Component ratings are assigned to two types of banks:

Note: There are two gradations of satisfactory for the large bank component tests (high-satisfactory and low-satisfactory).

Small banks, wholesale and limited purpose banks, and banks with strategic plans DO NOT receive component ratings.

Important note: Small banks, wholesale and limited purpose banks, and banks with strategic plans DO NOT receive component ratings.

The page also lists the broader scope of Federal Reserve responsibilities, including monetary policy (Federal Open Market Committee), supervision, financial stability, payment policies, research and data resources (including interest rates, exchange rates, bank structure data, financial accounts, etc.), community development, and consumer resources. The Federal Reserve is headquartered at 20th Street and Constitution Avenue N.W., Washington, DC 20551.

# Community Reinvestment Act: When Do Cra Ratings Threaten Mergers?

![MetaIcon](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdaeryun-en.vercel.app%2F_next%2Fstatic%2Fmedia%2Fmeta.21eedc1c.webp&w=96&q=75)

CRA services cover examination response, 2024 CRA Final Rule, fair lending, merger protests, and DOJ redlining defense.

When a regional bank receives a Needs to Improve CRA rating before merger, a community group files CRA protests, or OCC examiners flag fair lending issues, CRA rating impact on approval becomes urgent. Community Reinvestment Act services address CRA examinations, performance evaluation responses, merger application CRA protests, fair lending compliance, and community development investment planning. In the United States, the framework draws on Community Reinvestment Act of 1977, 2024 CRA Final Rule, Fair Housing Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and OCC/FDIC/FRB joint regulations. A CRA compliance attorney represents banks, bank holding companies, savings institutions, and merger applicants across CRA proceedings and parallel fair lending matters. Core services include CRA examination preparation, fair lending audit, merger CRA strategy, and enforcement defense.

## 1. What Cra Obligations Apply to Banks?

Community Reinvestment Act services begin with assessment area review, performance evaluation analysis, and immediate examination strategy across retail lending, services, and community development. Our CRA work spans bank compliance program design, examination response, merger application CRA strategy, and fair lending audit. Effective CRA practice requires HMDA data analysis, lending pattern review, and community development investment documentation from intake. Strong CRA framework integrates assessment area mapping, lending performance analysis, and parallel ECOA/FHA compliance review.

### Cra Framework and Federal Bank Regulators

Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 (12 U.S.C. § 2901 et seq.) requires federal bank regulators to encourage insured depository institutions to serve credit needs of communities including low- and moderate-income (LMI) areas. Three federal regulators administer CRA based on institution charter: OCC for national banks and federal savings associations, FDIC for state nonmember banks, and Federal Reserve for state member banks. CRA examinations evaluate bank performance against established standards through performance evaluation publicly disclosed under § 2906 with rating influencing branch approval, merger application, and public reputation. Joint Final Rule (Oct 24, 2023, effective April 1, 2024) by OCC/FDIC/FRB modernized CRA framework with revised tests, assessment areas, and data requirements. Strong [ECOA compliance](https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/ecoa-compliance) counsel coordinates CRA framework analysis, regulator engagement, and parallel fair lending compliance.

### When Does the 2024 Cra Final Rule Apply?

2024 CRA Final Rule (effective April 1, 2024 for most provisions, January 1, 2026 for full implementation) significantly modernizes CRA framework with size-based tests differentiation. Large banks ($2B+ assets) face four tests: Retail Lending Test, Retail Services and Products Test, Community Development Financing Test, and Community Development Services Test under new framework. Intermediate banks ($600M-$2B) face Retail Lending Test and Community Development Test with simplified evaluation framework. Small banks (under $600M) retain streamlined Lending Test option or may elect Strategic Plan with public consultation requirements. Strong [fair housing act](https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/fair-housing-act) counsel coordinates size-based test analysis, transition planning, and effective date implementation.

## 2. How Do Fair Lending and Community Development Obligations Apply?

Fair lending compliance, community development obligations, and bank product accessibility form the substantive compliance work in CRA practice. Each area requires specific HMDA data analysis, ECOA review, and regulatory engagement framework.

### When Does Ecoa and Fair Housing Act Overlap with Cra?

Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA, 15 U.S.C. § 1691) prohibits discrimination in credit transactions on protected characteristics with Regulation B (12 C.F.R. Part 1002) implementation. Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.) prohibits discrimination in residential housing finance with overlap to ECOA mortgage lending. CRA examination considers ECOA and FHA compliance as gating issue with consistent ECOA/FHA findings necessary for satisfactory CRA rating. DOJ pattern-or-practice fair lending cases (Wells Fargo $175M 2012, Bank of America $335M 2012 settlements) demonstrate parallel enforcement landscape. Strong [federal housing act](https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/federal-housing-act) counsel coordinates ECOA-FHA-CRA tri-statute compliance and parallel DOJ engagement.

### Community Development Loans, Investments, and Services

Community development activities under CRA include affordable housing (Section 8, LIHTC), economic development (small business loans, microfinance), revitalization (NMTC, opportunity zones), and essential community services (healthcare, education). Investment Test eligibility requires positive impact on LMI areas, with bank investments in CDFIs, Section 8 housing, and LIHTC commonly receiving credit. Service Test considers retail bank delivery systems (branches, ATMs, online banking accessibility) and community development services (board service, financial education). Public welfare investment authority under 12 C.F.R. § 24 (national banks) and 12 C.F.R. § 208.22 (state member banks) authorizes specific CRA-eligible investments. Strong [affordable housing law](https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/affordable-housing-law) counsel coordinates community development investment review, eligibility analysis, and CRA credit documentation.

## 3. Cra Examinations and Compliance Risk Pressure Points

CRA examination preparation, performance evaluation response, and ongoing compliance form the regulatory dimensions of CRA practice. Each area requires specific data analysis, regulatory engagement, and parallel proceeding management. The table below summarizes principal CRA rating tiers and merger implications.

| CRA Rating | Description | Merger Approval Impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outstanding | Exceeds standards | Strong support |
| Satisfactory | Meets standards | Usually approved |
| Needs to Improve | Below standards | Heightened scrutiny + delay |
| Substantial Noncompliance | Failing | Likely denial or conditions |

#### Outstanding

#### Satisfactory

#### Needs to Improve

#### Substantial Noncompliance

### Why Do Cra Ratings Affect Merger Approval?

Bank Merger Act (12 U.S.C. § 1828(c)) requires federal regulators to consider CRA performance evaluation when approving bank mergers, acquisitions, and branch openings with public protest opportunity. CRA performance evaluation publicly available under § 2906 enables community groups, advocates, and competitors to file protests during merger application comment period. Heightened scrutiny applied to applicants with Needs to Improve or Substantial Noncompliance ratings frequently results in conditional approval, divestiture requirements, or denial. Recent merger CRA protests (TD-First Horizon abandoned 2023, BB&T-SunTrust 2019 Truist conditions, BMO-Bank of the West) demonstrate CRA protest impact. Strong [housing finance](https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/housing-finance) counsel coordinates merger CRA strategy, protest response, and conditional approval negotiation.

### Performance Evaluation, Strategic Plan, and Public Disclosure

Performance evaluation conducted by federal regulator examiners evaluates bank against test framework over evaluation period (typically 3-5 years) with public report published. Strategic plan option (under both old and new CRA framework) allows banks to develop measurable performance goals subject to public comment and regulator approval with annual reporting. Public files (under former Reg BB § 25.43) and new public engagement requirements provide community input opportunities throughout CRA cycle. CRA Performance Context including local economic conditions, peer comparisons, and limitation factors inform examiner findings. Strong [predatory lending](https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/predatory-lending) counsel coordinates performance evaluation response, strategic plan development, and public disclosure compliance.

## 4. Regulatory Enforcement, Merger Reviews, and Banking Litigation

CRA enforcement, merger application defense, and parallel fair lending litigation form the resolution dimension of CRA practice. Each pathway requires specific procedural framework, evidence development, and damages analysis.

### How Are Cra Protests Filed in Merger Applications?

Community group CRA protests during merger application comment period (typically 30-day public notice) trigger heightened regulator review with potential public hearings and additional information requests. Protests commonly cite CRA rating deficiencies, specific lending pattern failures, branch closures in LMI areas, and inadequate community input. Bank applicant response includes additional community commitments, post-merger CRA pledges, branch retention agreements, and community advisory board commitments. National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and local community groups coordinate protests with $620B+ in merger commitments negotiated through CRA protest framework. Strong [lending transactions](https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/lending-transactions) counsel coordinates merger CRA protest defense, community commitment negotiation, and regulatory engagement.

### Doj Fair Lending Enforcement and Pattern-or-Practice Claims

DOJ Civil Rights Division Fair Lending Unit prosecutes redlining and discriminatory lending claims under FHA, ECOA, and federal banking laws with pattern-or-practice authority under 12 U.S.C. § 3535. Recent DOJ enforcement targets (City National Bank $31M 2023, Trident Mortgage $24M 2022) demonstrate Combating Redlining Initiative (launched 2021) enforcement scope. CFPB parallel authority under Equal Credit Opportunity Act enforcement includes Regulation B implementation and consent orders against discriminatory lending practices. State attorney general parallel enforcement under state fair lending laws (NY Banking Law § 29, Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A) creates multi-jurisdictional exposure. Coordinated [discrimination litigation](https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/discrimination-litigation) counsel manages DOJ enforcement, CFPB parallel proceedings, and state AG fair lending claims simultaneously.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Do CRA Ratings Reflect Differences in Performance ---
URL: https://ncrc.org/do-cra-ratings-reflect-differences-in-performance-an-examination-using-federal-reserve-data

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NCRC (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) report examines whether Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) ratings reflect real differences in bank performance, using a new Federal Reserve database of 6,300 CRA exams conducted from 2005 through 2017. The analysis was authored by Josh Silver (Senior Advisor, Policy and Government Affairs) and Jason Richardson (Director of Research & Evaluation).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Retail loan performance measures generally showed higher ratings corresponding to better outcomes, but the differences were narrower than expected.
- Community development (CD) loan and investment measures showed much larger performance differences across ratings categories (often ~100% differences) compared to retail measures (often just 1 percentage point differences).
- Approximately 90% of banks received a Satisfactory rating, indicating the four-tier rating system fails to adequately differentiate performance. NCRC recommends splitting Satisfactory into High and Low Satisfactory tiers.
- Large banks significantly lagged smaller banks in percent of loans to LMI borrowers and to the smallest businesses, though they did not trail on LMI tract lending.
- Anomalies existed, including banks with High Satisfactory ratings sometimes outperforming banks with Outstanding ratings (e.g., median LMI borrower lending of 12.78% for High Satisfactory vs. 11.83% for Outstanding), potentially explained by large banks being downgraded for fair lending violations during the financial crisis.
- The sharpest performance differences occurred between Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings (e.g., 10.43% vs. 2.13% for LMI borrower lending).

RECOMMENDATIONS:
- NCRC advocates for incremental reform rather than radical overhaul, contrary to the OCC's final rule.
- Proposes a peer-relative rating scale comparing bank performance to aggregate peers (Outstanding: >100% of peer level; High Satisfactory: 80-99%; Low Satisfactory: 60-79%; Needs-to-Improve: 40-60%; Substantial Noncompliance: <39%).
- Suggests different peer benchmarks may be needed for different business models (branch-based vs. non-branch banks) and asset sizes.
- Recommends retaining qualitative factors (20-30% of ratings) and compensation mechanisms where strong performance on one test can offset weaker performance elsewhere.
- Calls for the OCC to withdraw its final rule, which NCRC argues is not evidence-based, and to collaborate with the Federal Reserve Board and FDIC on new rulemaking with a publicly available database.
- Recommends annual agency reports analyzing performance measures after new regulations are implemented.

METHODOLOGY NOTES:
- Banks classified as community (up to $10B assets), regional ($10B-$50B), and large (over $50B).
- The Federal Reserve database lacked service test variables (e.g., percent of branches in LMI tracts), limiting analysis.
- Banks with Substantial Noncompliance ratings were excluded due to insufficient observations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results suggest the need for refinement of performance measures, especially for the retail loan indicators, rather than a complete overhaul. The Federal Reserve data indicates a rating system that is not fundamentally broken or arbitrary but a system that should be sharpened."
</key_excerpts>

<summary>
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a news announcement (News Release 2024-128) on December 2, 2024, disclosing Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) performance evaluations for 19 national banks and federal savings associations. These evaluations became public during the period of November 1, 2024, through November 30, 2024. Under the CRA, the OCC assesses an institution's record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound banking operations. Possible CRA ratings include outstanding, satisfactory, needs to improve, and substantial noncompliance.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the official webpage of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the central bank of the United States), specifically focusing on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The page explains how the Federal Reserve evaluates how well state member banks have helped meet the needs of their communities.

Key points include:
- The Federal Reserve uses one of five evaluation methods tailored to a bank's size or business strategy to assess CRA performance.
- The Board continues to apply the 1995 regulations to banks.
- Banks' Performance Evaluations are made public through an online database searchable by institution, exam criteria, or bank branch location. Each bank must also maintain a copy of its Performance Evaluation in its public file and make it available to customers upon request.

The page describes the types of CRA ratings:

- **State Rating or Multistate MSA Rating**: A state rating is generally assigned if a bank has branches in more than one state (interstate bank). A multistate MSA rating is assigned if a bank has branches in two or more states within a multistate metropolitan statistical area. CRA activity is captured in either a state rating or a multistate MSA rating, but not both.
- **Component Ratings**: Assigned to two types of banks, with two gradations of satisfactory for large bank component tests (high-satisfactory and low-satisfactory).

Important note: Small banks, wholesale and limited purpose banks, and banks with strategic plans DO NOT receive component ratings.

The page also lists the broader scope of Federal Reserve responsibilities, including monetary policy (Federal Open Market Committee), supervision, financial stability, payment policies, research and data resources (including interest rates, exchange rates, bank structure data, financial accounts, etc.), community development, and consumer resources. --- SOURCE 6: Community Reinvestment Act: When Do CRA Ratings Threaten Mergers? ---
URL: https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/community-reinvestment-act

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a legal practice article from SJKP LLP Law Firm (a U.S. law firm, also associated with Daeryun Law) titled "Community Reinvestment Act: When Do CRA Ratings Threaten Mergers?" published May 14, 2026. The article provides comprehensive guidance on Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) compliance, examinations, ratings, and their impact on bank mergers.

KEY CONTENT:
- The CRA (12 U.S.C. § 2901 et seq., enacted 1977) requires federal bank regulators to encourage insured depository institutions to serve credit needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. Three regulators administer CRA by charter type: OCC (national banks/federal savings associations), FDIC (state nonmember banks), and Federal Reserve (state member banks).
- The 2024 CRA Final Rule (Joint Final Rule by OCC/FDIC/FRB, Oct 24, 2023; effective April 1, 2024, full implementation January 1, 2026) modernized the CRA framework with size-based tests: Large banks ($2B+ assets) face four tests (Retail Lending, Retail Services and Products, Community Development Financing, Community Development Services); Intermediate banks ($600M-$2B) face Retail Lending and Community Development Tests; Small banks (under $600M) retain streamlined Lending Test or may elect a Strategic Plan.
- CRA ratings and merger impact: Outstanding (strong support), Satisfactory (usually approved), Needs to Improve (heightened scrutiny + delay), and Substantial Noncompliance (likely denial or conditions).
- Under the Bank Merger Act (12 U.S.C. § 1828(c)), regulators must consider CRA performance evaluations in merger approvals, with public protest opportunities. Notable merger cases affected by CRA protests include TD-First Horizon (abandoned 2023), BB&T-SunTrust (2019 Truist conditions), and BMO-Bank of the West.
- ECOA (15 U.S.C. § 1691, Reg B at 12 C.F.R. Part 1002) and Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.) overlap with CRA compliance as gating issues. DOJ pattern-or-practice enforcement examples include Wells Fargo ($175M, 2012), Bank of America ($335M, 2012), City National Bank ($31M, 2023), and Trident Mortgage ($24M, 2022) under the Combating Redlining Initiative (launched 2021).
- Community development activities include affordable housing (Section 8, LIHTC), economic development (small business loans, microfinance), revitalization (NMTC, opportunity zones), and essential community services.
- CRA protests during the ~30-day merger comment period trigger heightened review; the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and local groups have negotiated $620B+ in merger commitments through the protest framework.
- CFPB and state attorneys general (e.g., NY Banking Law § 29, Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A) can pursue parallel enforcement, creating multi-jurisdictional exposure.
- The firm offers CRA services including examination preparation, fair lending audits, merger CRA strategy, and enforcement defense.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations ---
URL: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/12/2026-16454/community-reinvestment-act-regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Register notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) regarding the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Regulations, jointly issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) on August 12, 2026.

**Key Details:**
- Document Number: 2026-16454 (91 FR 52114)
- Docket ID: OCC-2026-0694
- RINs: 1557-AF57 (OCC) and 3064-AG31 (FDIC)
- Affects 12 CFR Parts 5, 24, 25, 35 (OCC) and 12 CFR Parts 345, 346 (FDIC)
- 105 pages (52114-52218)
- Comment period ends October 13, 2026 (54 days from publication)
- 7 comments received at Regulations.gov as of publication

**Purpose of the Proposal:**
The OCC and FDIC propose targeted amendments to their CRA rules to: (1) refocus on the statutory objective of encouraging banks to meet credit needs of their communities; (2) better ensure community development grants reach intended communities; (3) reduce unnecessary burden, particularly for community banks; and (4) provide greater clarity for obtaining CRA consideration. The proposal also includes technical changes to CRA sunshine requirements under the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, and similar technical changes to OCC's Public Welfare Investments rule and corporate activities rules.

**Key Background/History:**
- The CRA was enacted in 1977, requiring banks to meet the credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.
- Current rules largely date back to 1995.
- 2018: OCC received 1,500+ comment letters on a CRA ANPRM.
- 2019: Joint NPRM received 7,500+ comment letters; OCC finalized its rule in 2020 (later rescinded in 2021).
- 2022: Joint NPRM to modernize CRA rules; ~950 comments received.
- October 24, 2023: Final 2023 CRA rules issued.
- February 5, 2024: Trade associations sued in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas.
- March 29, 2024: Court granted preliminary injunction, enjoining enforcement of 2023 CRA rules. Court found agencies exceeded authority on "entire community" interpretation and the "Major Questions Doctrine" was considered.
- April 18, 2024: Agencies appealed to the Fifth Circuit.
- March 28, 2025: Agencies filed to stay appeal pending new rulemakings; Fifth Circuit granted stay April 1, 2025.
- July 16, 2025: Rescission proposal published (received ~47 comments); agencies decided not to finalize it but issued this new proposal instead.
- July 1, 2026: OCC and FDIC filed unopposed motion to dismiss appeal; Fifth Circuit dismissed on July 9, 2026.
- The agencies are now seeking a final judgment that would prohibit future CRA amendments based on expansive views of "entire community" (allowing assessment outside geographic areas where banks operate deposit-taking facilities) or expansive views of "credit needs" (including deposit products).

**Proposal Overview (Key Components):**
- **Increase focus on lending** toward statutory objectives
- **Ensure community development grants benefit communities**
- **Reduce burden**, especially for community banks
- **Increase clarity and objectivity**

URL: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/22/2025-23547/community-reinvestment-act-simplified-strategic-plan-process-for-community-banks

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Register proposed rule by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), published on 12/22/2025 (Document 2025-23547, 90 FR 59744, Docket ID OCC-2025-0669). The OCC is proposing supplemental guidance on a simplified strategic plan process for community banks under the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The proposal addresses 12 CFR Part 25 and spans 21 pages (59744-59764).

KEY DETAILS:
- Comments close February 20, 2026, via Regulations.gov (Docket OCC-2025-0669) or by mail/hand delivery to the Chief Counsel's Office, 400 7th Street SW, Suite 3E-218, Washington, DC 20219.
- Contact: Emily Boyes (202-649-5490), Andrea Shearin and Cassandra Remmenga (202-649-5470).
- The OCC defines community banks as those with up to $30 billion in assets.
- The CRA was enacted in 1977, requiring regulated financial institutions to demonstrate that their deposit facilities serve the convenience and needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE:
- The CRA strategic plan option allows banks to have their CRA performance assessed under an approved strategic plan instead of the standard performance tests (lending test, investment test, service test; small bank performance standards; or CD test for wholesale/limited purpose banks).
- The OCC cites stakeholder feedback that strategic plans should be available to all banks, particularly branchless banks and those with unique business models.
- The current strategic plan process is complex and difficult to navigate, with limited guidance (OCC Bulletin 2019-39 and Interagency Q&As), leading community banks to perceive the burden as outweighing the benefits. This has had a "chilling effect" on strategic plan adoption, especially among community banks.
- The proposal aligns with Executive Order 14192, "Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation."

PROPOSED SIMPLIFIED PROCESS COMPONENTS:
1. Measurable Goals: The OCC would provide more specific guidance on types of measurable goals, including elective goals (with specific performance measures like percentages, numbers, dollar amounts, and performance levels) that community banks could adopt, based on the agency's supervisory experience. Banks may also include custom goals if elective goals are unsuitable based on performance context (capacity, constraints, product offerings, business strategy, historical CRA performance).
2. Performance Measures: Goals typically expressed in dollar amounts, percent of tier one (T1) capital, or total assets; allocations typically based on percentage of deposits assigned to each assessment area. Multi-year plans require annual interim measurable goals, with annual increases in dollar-denominated thresholds.
3. Performance Levels: Elective goals would reflect what the OCC historically considers "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" for community banks, with different levels for smaller/less complex vs. larger/more complex banks. Goals focusing on only one performance category would generally require higher performance levels.
4. Simplified Strategic Plan Form: A standardized form with guidance for when elective goals may be appropriate.
5. The process includes consultation, plan receipt/acknowledgement, case-specific waiver requests, compliance with public participation requirements, and OCC review/approval.

KEY CAVEATS: The elective goals are NOT safe harbors and do not guarantee approval. The OCC would periodically assess and update elective goals. The proposal does not establish new requirements—it provides transparency into the types of measurable goals the OCC has generally found to reflect "Satisfactory" or "Outstanding" performance.

The document also includes three questions for comment: (1) whether elective goals provide clarity and reduce burden, (2) other factors the OCC should consider, and (3) whether performance expectations should be increased or decreased for community banks using the simplified process.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Analysis of the OCC's Final CRA Rule - NCRC ---
URL: https://ncrc.org/analysis-of-the-occs-final-cra-rule

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is NCRC's (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) analysis and critique of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) final Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule, released on May 20. NCRC argues the final rule weakens CRA enforcement and will result in fewer loans, investments, and services for low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

Key criticisms across the rule's components:

**What Activities Count:** The rule significantly dilutes the focus on LMI communities by: adding essential infrastructure and community facilities (roads, bridges, mass transit, hospitals) to the definition of community development; allowing activities to "partially benefit" (less than majority of dollars) LMI people rather than requiring primary (50%+) benefit—with no floor set by OCC (NCRC recommends a 30% floor); and adding "CRA deserts" as discretionary underserved areas that banks can self-designate through a secretive, closed-off process, with qualified activities there multiplied by up to four. The OCC retained arbitrary multipliers (e.g., doubling certain community development loans, quadrupling "innovative and complex" activities deemed so subjectively by examiners), which NCRC says introduce grade inflation and subjectivity. The CRA illustrative list process remains ad hoc, with additions made annually and public notice/comment only once every five years; examples added without proposal include loans for workforce housing near a multinational's warehouse and tax increment bonds that can finance gentrification.

**How It Counts:** The CRA evaluation measure—a ratio of CRA activities divided by bank deposits—remains the dominant, determinative factor on exams. OCC scrapped its proposed thresholds (6% for Satisfactory, 11% for Outstanding) and retail test thresholds (e.g., 65%) admitting it lacked data to support them, leaving them for future rulemaking—NCRC calls this irresponsible and a "giant leap into subjectivity." The final rule eliminates the large bank service test and any evaluation of bank deposit accounts for LMI customers (NCRC notes current exams do quantify accounts), devalues branches (a typical bank's branch distribution contributes only ~0.56 to the numerator), and quantifies all types of volunteering. The retail lending test becomes pass/fail (counting far less than the current 50% weight), and consumer lending excludes overdrafts and credit cards. Large banks must now pass in 80% of assessment areas (up from 50%), but if tests remain easy this won't increase rigor.

**Where It Counts:** New deposit-based assessment areas are based on deposits (a bank must gather >50% of deposits outside branches and >5% from an area), but lack of data makes impacts unclear. Banks may designate areas larger than the smallest 5%-deposit area, giving discretion to neglect smaller needier areas. Credit is allowed for activities outside AAs regardless of AA performance, encouraging large national deals over local ones.

**Public Input/Accountability:** Public comments are narrowed to local needs/opportunities rather than bank CRA performance; community development data is only reported at total bank level (not census tract/county), frustrating public oversight; exams become bank-driven (banks calculate their own ratings for examiners to verify); Outstanding-rated banks are examined only once every five years; affiliates are generally excluded from exams unless acting as "intermediaries"; and the small bank threshold was raised to $600 million (reclassifying ~181 intermediate small banks), with ~89% of OCC banks now exempt from the new exams.

NCRC concludes the rule "signals an abrogation of the OCC's statutory responsibilities" and "must be rescinded or overturned."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It will lessen the public accountability of banks to their communities by enacting performance measures on CRA exams that will be complex and opaque, while at the same time over-simplifying how to measure a bank's responsiveness to local needs. The result will be significantly fewer loans, investments and services to low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities most in need of more credit and capital."

"The OCC did not place a floor on a partial benefit... However, without a floor, the temptation is too great since 5% of an interstate bridge is a large dollar amount... At the very least, the OCC should have specified a floor such as 30% of the benefit must be for LMI people and neighborhoods."

"The OCC scrapped the thresholds for its CRA evaluation measure, admitting it does not have data to support this core part of its proposal... the final rule does not contain benchmarks for the CRA evaluation measure, a specific CD minimum, or thresholds for the retail lending distribution tests."

--- SOURCE 9: OCC and FDIC Propose Targeted Revisions to CRA Regulations ---
URL: https://www.sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2026/August/OCC-FDIC-Propose-Targeted-Revisions-CRA-Regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 31, 2026, the OCC and FDIC jointly issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (the "CRA Proposal") to amend their regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The Federal Reserve Board did not join the proposal. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

**Background:** The CRA was enacted in 1977 to encourage banks to help meet credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. The current CRA rule is based on interagency regulations from 1995. In October 2023, the agencies adopted a substantially revised 2023 CRA Rule, which was challenged by banking trade associations and preliminarily enjoined by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas in March 2024 before taking effect. In July 2025, the agencies proposed rescinding the 2023 CRA Rule, but the OCC and FDIC instead issued this new CRA Proposal. The Board did not participate and its next steps remain unclear, raising the possibility of differing CRA requirements across federal banking agencies.

**Key Changes in the CRA Proposal:**

1. **Bank Size Categories:** Raises the small bank threshold to $1 billion or less (up from $412 million), creates a new "intermediate bank" category for banks between $1 billion and $10 billion, and designates "large banks" as those over $10 billion (up from $1.649 billion). Based on 2024-2025 Call Report data, approximately 636 of 3,577 supervised banks would be intermediate banks and ~86 would be large banks. The percentage of large banks would decrease from 13.4% to 2.4%.

2. **Revised Ratings for Intermediate Banks:** An intermediate bank would need only a "satisfactory" rating on the lending test (not both lending and community development tests) to receive an overall "satisfactory" rating.

3. **Retained Assessment Area Framework:** The proposal retains the Current CRA Rule's assessment area delineation (facility-based), unlike the 2023 CRA Rule which required separate retail lending assessment areas.

4. **Revised Lending Tests:** Lending tests would be limited to "major product lines" (consumer, home mortgage, small business, small farm loans), with two proposed options for determining major product lines. Consumer lending would be a major product line if it constitutes a majority of retail lending by both dollar amount and loan count. The agencies are considering eliminating the separate limited purpose bank category. 30 loans generally would be considered sufficient for meaningful assessment of lending performance.

5. **Service Test:** The retail banking services criterion under the large bank service test would be limited to credit services only, eliminating consideration of deposit products (consistent with the Texas district court ruling that the CRA does not authorize assessing deposit products).

6. **Community Development Clarifications:** Would clarify definitions for affordable housing (including both subsidized and unsubsidized), codify guidance on distressed/underserved tracts, provide lists of community services (recharacterized as "civic assistance"), define three categories of economic development, and add Tribal/native lands and government-targeted redevelopment areas to revitalization/stabilization categories.

7. **Geographic Flexibility:** Community development activities outside assessment areas would be eligible for consideration only after a bank demonstrates adequate in-assessment-area activity. Two options proposed: (1) quantitative thresholds (large banks: 0.625% of tier 1 capital to CD loans and 0.625% to CD investments/grants; intermediate/wholesale/limited purpose banks: 1.25%), or (2) qualitative determination based on the "low satisfactory" performance level.

8. **Community Development Grants:** Would require written commitments on qualifying use of proceeds, documentation requirements, and limit consideration to grants where recipient indirect costs do not exceed 15%.

9. **Strategic Plans:** Would clarify measurable goal requirements (performance measure + performance level), permit preliminary agency feedback, require written notice of technical completeness, and deem technically complete plans approved if the agency does not act within 60 days.

10. **Illegal Credit Practices:** Two options proposed—considering only violations cited in public enforcement actions, or also considering nonpublic enforcement actions (generally codifying current practice).

11. **Public File:** Would require public files to be available on the bank's website rather than physical copies, and revise required branch services lists to cover "credit products" rather than "loan and deposit products."

**Implications:** The proposal would significantly reduce burden for banks in the new intermediate category (no longer subject to large bank investment/service tests or related data requirements). Banks would need to reassess community development grant programs, geographic flexibility eligibility, and major product line methodologies. The Federal Reserve's non-participation could create differing CRA requirements depending on a bank's charter type, potentially influencing chartering decisions.
</summary>

"The CRA Proposal would increase the asset threshold for treatment as a large bank to more than $10 billion from $1.649 billion, establish a new 'intermediate bank' category for banks generally having between $1 billion and $10 billion in assets, revise the manner in which retail lending is evaluated, eliminate consideration of deposit products under the large-bank service test and modify the standards governing community development activities, including grants and activities outside a bank's assessment areas."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Register document page for the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) final rule on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Regulations, published on June 5, 2020 (Document 2020-11220, 85 FR 34734). The rule, effective October 1, 2020, strengthens and modernizes the CRA by making four key changes: (1) clarifying and expanding the bank lending, investment, and services (qualifying activities) that receive CRA credit; (2) updating how banks delineate assessment areas, including requiring deposit-based assessment areas for banks that collect deposits above a threshold outside their physical branch footprint (capturing internet banks and other non-traditional models); (3) providing more consistent and objective methods for evaluating CRA performance through new performance standards measuring retail lending distribution and dollar-value impact of CD activities; and (4) requiring more timely and transparent data collection, recordkeeping, and reporting.

The rule was issued by the Department of the Treasury's OCC, amending 12 CFR Parts 25 and 195 (Docket ID OCC-2018-0008, RIN 1557-AE34), spanning 101 pages. Banks must comply by October 1, 2020, January 1, 2023, or January 1, 2024, as applicable, with appendix C to part 25 expiring January 1, 2024.

Background: The reform effort began with an August 2018 Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (over 1,500 comments received), followed by a joint December 2019 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking with the FDIC (over 7,500 comments received). Under the prior framework, nearly 74% of banks were rated satisfactory and almost 24% outstanding, with less than 3% in the two lowest ratings, and the OCC found only a weak positive relationship between CRA ratings and actual CRA activity. The new framework moves from a primarily subjective to a primarily objective evaluation system to make ratings more reliable, reproducible, and comparable.

Key provisions include: qualifying activities criteria covering underserved areas, distressed areas, disaster areas, and Indian country beyond LMI areas; a publicly available illustrative list of qualifying activities; a process for banks to seek agency confirmation of qualifying status; and the exclusion of certain activities that previously received credit (e.g., loans to middle- and upper-income borrowers in LMI census tracts) to emphasize LMI support. The rule also addresses the small bank exemption ($500 million threshold), performance standards, and data collection burden concerns raised in comments. The OCC stated the rule takes a more incremental approach to reform that accounts for differences among categories of institutions subject to the CRA.
