--- SOURCE 8: Analysis of the OCC's Final CRA Rule - NCRC ---
URL: https://ncrc.org/analysis-of-the-occs-final-cra-rule

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is NCRC's (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) analysis and critique of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) final Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule, released on May 20. NCRC argues the final rule weakens CRA enforcement and will result in fewer loans, investments, and services for low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

Key criticisms across the rule's components:

**What Activities Count:** The rule significantly dilutes the focus on LMI communities by: adding essential infrastructure and community facilities (roads, bridges, mass transit, hospitals) to the definition of community development; allowing activities to "partially benefit" (less than majority of dollars) LMI people rather than requiring primary (50%+) benefit—with no floor set by OCC (NCRC recommends a 30% floor); and adding "CRA deserts" as discretionary underserved areas that banks can self-designate through a secretive, closed-off process, with qualified activities there multiplied by up to four. The OCC retained arbitrary multipliers (e.g., doubling certain community development loans, quadrupling "innovative and complex" activities deemed so subjectively by examiners), which NCRC says introduce grade inflation and subjectivity. The CRA illustrative list process remains ad hoc, with additions made annually and public notice/comment only once every five years; examples added without proposal include loans for workforce housing near a multinational's warehouse and tax increment bonds that can finance gentrification.

**How It Counts:** The CRA evaluation measure—a ratio of CRA activities divided by bank deposits—remains the dominant, determinative factor on exams. OCC scrapped its proposed thresholds (6% for Satisfactory, 11% for Outstanding) and retail test thresholds (e.g., 65%) admitting it lacked data to support them, leaving them for future rulemaking—NCRC calls this irresponsible and a "giant leap into subjectivity." The final rule eliminates the large bank service test and any evaluation of bank deposit accounts for LMI customers (NCRC notes current exams do quantify accounts), devalues branches (a typical bank's branch distribution contributes only ~0.56 to the numerator), and quantifies all types of volunteering. The retail lending test becomes pass/fail (counting far less than the current 50% weight), and consumer lending excludes overdrafts and credit cards. Large banks must now pass in 80% of assessment areas (up from 50%), but if tests remain easy this won't increase rigor.

**Where It Counts:** New deposit-based assessment areas are based on deposits (a bank must gather >50% of deposits outside branches and >5% from an area), but lack of data makes impacts unclear. Banks may designate areas larger than the smallest 5%-deposit area, giving discretion to neglect smaller needier areas. Credit is allowed for activities outside AAs regardless of AA performance, encouraging large national deals over local ones.

**Public Input/Accountability:** Public comments are narrowed to local needs/opportunities rather than bank CRA performance; community development data is only reported at total bank level (not census tract/county), frustrating public oversight; exams become bank-driven (banks calculate their own ratings for examiners to verify); Outstanding-rated banks are examined only once every five years; affiliates are generally excluded from exams unless acting as "intermediaries"; and the small bank threshold was raised to $600 million (reclassifying ~181 intermediate small banks), with ~89% of OCC banks now exempt from the new exams.

NCRC concludes the rule "signals an abrogation of the OCC's statutory responsibilities" and "must be rescinded or overturned."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It will lessen the public accountability of banks to their communities by enacting performance measures on CRA exams that will be complex and opaque, while at the same time over-simplifying how to measure a bank's responsiveness to local needs. The result will be significantly fewer loans, investments and services to low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities most in need of more credit and capital."

"The OCC did not place a floor on a partial benefit... However, without a floor, the temptation is too great since 5% of an interstate bridge is a large dollar amount... At the very least, the OCC should have specified a floor such as 30% of the benefit must be for LMI people and neighborhoods."

"The OCC scrapped the thresholds for its CRA evaluation measure, admitting it does not have data to support this core part of its proposal... the final rule does not contain benchmarks for the CRA evaluation measure, a specific CD minimum, or thresholds for the retail lending distribution tests."

--- SOURCE 9: OCC and FDIC Propose Targeted Revisions to CRA Regulations ---
URL: https://www.sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2026/August/OCC-FDIC-Propose-Targeted-Revisions-CRA-Regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 31, 2026, the OCC and FDIC jointly issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (the "CRA Proposal") to amend their regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The Federal Reserve Board did not join the proposal. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

**Background:** The CRA was enacted in 1977 to encourage banks to help meet credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. The current CRA rule is based on interagency regulations from 1995. In October 2023, the agencies adopted a substantially revised 2023 CRA Rule, which was challenged by banking trade associations and preliminarily enjoined by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas in March 2024 before taking effect. In July 2025, the agencies proposed rescinding the 2023 CRA Rule, but the OCC and FDIC instead issued this new CRA Proposal. The Board did not participate and its next steps remain unclear, raising the possibility of differing CRA requirements across federal banking agencies.

**Key Changes in the CRA Proposal:**

1. **Bank Size Categories:** Raises the small bank threshold to $1 billion or less (up from $412 million), creates a new "intermediate bank" category for banks between $1 billion and $10 billion, and designates "large banks" as those over $10 billion (up from $1.649 billion). Based on 2024-2025 Call Report data, approximately 636 of 3,577 supervised banks would be intermediate banks and ~86 would be large banks. The percentage of large banks would decrease from 13.4% to 2.4%.

2. **Revised Ratings for Intermediate Banks:** An intermediate bank would need only a "satisfactory" rating on the lending test (not both lending and community development tests) to receive an overall "satisfactory" rating.

3. **Retained Assessment Area Framework:** The proposal retains the Current CRA Rule's assessment area delineation (facility-based), unlike the 2023 CRA Rule which required separate retail lending assessment areas.

4. **Revised Lending Tests:** Lending tests would be limited to "major product lines" (consumer, home mortgage, small business, small farm loans), with two proposed options for determining major product lines. Consumer lending would be a major product line if it constitutes a majority of retail lending by both dollar amount and loan count. The agencies are considering eliminating the separate limited purpose bank category. 30 loans generally would be considered sufficient for meaningful assessment of lending performance.

5. **Service Test:** The retail banking services criterion under the large bank service test would be limited to credit services only, eliminating consideration of deposit products (consistent with the Texas district court ruling that the CRA does not authorize assessing deposit products).

6. **Community Development Clarifications:** Would clarify definitions for affordable housing (including both subsidized and unsubsidized), codify guidance on distressed/underserved tracts, provide lists of community services (recharacterized as "civic assistance"), define three categories of economic development, and add Tribal/native lands and government-targeted redevelopment areas to revitalization/stabilization categories.

7. **Geographic Flexibility:** Community development activities outside assessment areas would be eligible for consideration only after a bank demonstrates adequate in-assessment-area activity. Two options proposed: (1) quantitative thresholds (large banks: 0.625% of tier 1 capital to CD loans and 0.625% to CD investments/grants; intermediate/wholesale/limited purpose banks: 1.25%), or (2) qualitative determination based on the "low satisfactory" performance level.

8. **Community Development Grants:** Would require written commitments on qualifying use of proceeds, documentation requirements, and limit consideration to grants where recipient indirect costs do not exceed 15%.

9. **Strategic Plans:** Would clarify measurable goal requirements (performance measure + performance level), permit preliminary agency feedback, require written notice of technical completeness, and deem technically complete plans approved if the agency does not act within 60 days.

10. **Illegal Credit Practices:** Two options proposed—considering only violations cited in public enforcement actions, or also considering nonpublic enforcement actions (generally codifying current practice).

11. **Public File:** Would require public files to be available on the bank's website rather than physical copies, and revise required branch services lists to cover "credit products" rather than "loan and deposit products."

**Implications:** The proposal would significantly reduce burden for banks in the new intermediate category (no longer subject to large bank investment/service tests or related data requirements). Banks would need to reassess community development grant programs, geographic flexibility eligibility, and major product line methodologies. The Federal Reserve's non-participation could create differing CRA requirements depending on a bank's charter type, potentially influencing chartering decisions.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: Federal Register :: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations ---
URL: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/06/05/2020-11220/community-reinvestment-act-regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Register document page for the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) final rule on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Regulations, published on June 5, 2020 (Document 2020-11220, 85 FR 34734). The rule, effective October 1, 2020, strengthens and modernizes the CRA by making four key changes: (1) clarifying and expanding the bank lending, investment, and services (qualifying activities) that receive CRA credit; (2) updating how banks delineate assessment areas, including requiring deposit-based assessment areas for banks that collect deposits above a threshold outside their physical branch footprint (capturing internet banks and other non-traditional models); (3) providing more consistent and objective methods for evaluating CRA performance through new performance standards measuring retail lending distribution and dollar-value impact of CD activities; and (4) requiring more timely and transparent data collection, recordkeeping, and reporting.

The rule was issued by the Department of the Treasury's OCC, amending 12 CFR Parts 25 and 195 (Docket ID OCC-2018-0008, RIN 1557-AE34), spanning 101 pages. Banks must comply by October 1, 2020, January 1, 2023, or January 1, 2024, as applicable, with appendix C to part 25 expiring January 1, 2024.

Background: The reform effort began with an August 2018 Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (over 1,500 comments received), followed by a joint December 2019 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking with the FDIC (over 7,500 comments received). Under the prior framework, nearly 74% of banks were rated satisfactory and almost 24% outstanding, with less than 3% in the two lowest ratings, and the OCC found only a weak positive relationship between CRA ratings and actual CRA activity. The new framework moves from a primarily subjective to a primarily objective evaluation system to make ratings more reliable, reproducible, and comparable.

Key provisions include: qualifying activities criteria covering underserved areas, distressed areas, disaster areas, and Indian country beyond LMI areas; a publicly available illustrative list of qualifying activities; a process for banks to seek agency confirmation of qualifying status; and the exclusion of certain activities that previously received credit (e.g., loans to middle- and upper-income borrowers in LMI census tracts) to emphasize LMI support. The rule also addresses the small bank exemption ($500 million threshold), performance standards, and data collection burden concerns raised in comments. The OCC stated the rule takes a more incremental approach to reform that accounts for differences among categories of institutions subject to the CRA.
</summary>

This is NCRC's (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) analysis and critique of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) final Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule, released on May 20. NCRC argues the final rule weakens CRA enforcement and will result in fewer loans, investments, and services for low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

Key criticisms across the rule's components:

**What Activities Count:** The rule significantly dilutes the focus on LMI communities by: adding essential infrastructure and community facilities (roads, bridges, mass transit, hospitals) to the definition of community development; allowing activities to "partially benefit" (less than majority of dollars) LMI people rather than requiring primary (50%+) benefit—with no floor set by OCC (NCRC recommends a 30% floor); and adding "CRA deserts" as discretionary underserved areas that banks can self-designate through a secretive, closed-off process, with qualified activities there multiplied by up to four. The OCC retained arbitrary multipliers (e.g., doubling certain community development loans, quadrupling "innovative and complex" activities deemed so subjectively by examiners), which NCRC says introduce grade inflation and subjectivity. The CRA illustrative list process remains ad hoc, with additions made annually and public notice/comment only once every five years; examples added without proposal include loans for workforce housing near a multinational's warehouse and tax increment bonds that can finance gentrification.

**How It Counts:** The CRA evaluation measure—a ratio of CRA activities divided by bank deposits—remains the dominant, determinative factor on exams. OCC scrapped its proposed thresholds (6% for Satisfactory, 11% for Outstanding) and retail test thresholds (e.g., 65%) admitting it lacked data to support them, leaving them for future rulemaking—NCRC calls this irresponsible and a "giant leap into subjectivity." The final rule eliminates the large bank service test and any evaluation of bank deposit accounts for LMI customers (NCRC notes current exams do quantify accounts), devalues branches (a typical bank's branch distribution contributes only ~0.56 to the numerator), and quantifies all types of volunteering. The retail lending test becomes pass/fail (counting far less than the current 50% weight), and consumer lending excludes overdrafts and credit cards. Large banks must now pass in 80% of assessment areas (up from 50%), but if tests remain easy this won't increase rigor.

**Where It Counts:** New deposit-based assessment areas are based on deposits (a bank must gather >50% of deposits outside branches and >5% from an area), but lack of data makes impacts unclear. Banks may designate areas larger than the smallest 5%-deposit area, giving discretion to neglect smaller needier areas. Credit is allowed for activities outside AAs regardless of AA performance, encouraging large national deals over local ones.

**Public Input/Accountability:** Public comments are narrowed to local needs/opportunities rather than bank CRA performance; community development data is only reported at total bank level (not census tract/county), frustrating public oversight; exams become bank-driven (banks calculate their own ratings for examiners to verify); Outstanding-rated banks are examined only once every five years; affiliates are generally excluded from exams unless acting as "intermediaries"; and the small bank threshold was raised to $600 million (reclassifying ~181 intermediate small banks), with ~89% of OCC banks now exempt from the new exams.

NCRC concludes the rule "signals an abrogation of the OCC's statutory responsibilities" and "must be rescinded or overturned."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It will lessen the public accountability of banks to their communities by enacting performance measures on CRA exams that will be complex and opaque, while at the same time over-simplifying how to measure a bank's responsiveness to local needs. The result will be significantly fewer loans, investments and services to low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities most in need of more credit and capital."

"The OCC did not place a floor on a partial benefit... However, without a floor, the temptation is too great since 5% of an interstate bridge is a large dollar amount... At the very least, the OCC should have specified a floor such as 30% of the benefit must be for LMI people and neighborhoods."

"The OCC scrapped the thresholds for its CRA evaluation measure, admitting it does not have data to support this core part of its proposal... the final rule does not contain benchmarks for the CRA evaluation measure, a specific CD minimum, or thresholds for the retail lending distribution tests."

"Moving to the OCC's approach will greatly diminish the importance of bank branches in CRA compliance, which will likely lead to significant branch loss in LMI communities and a decrease in lending as documented in NCRC's comment letter."

"In sum, this final rule signals an abrogation of the OCC's statutory responsibilities to ensure that banks continually and affirmatively respond to credit needs of LMI borrowers and in LMI communities. It must be rescinded or overturned."
</key_excerpts>

institutions are required by law to demonstrate that their deposit
facilities serve the convenience and needs of the communities in which
they are chartered to do business; the convenience and needs of
communities include the need for credit services as well as deposit

neighborhood. By using this approach, CB&T has been able to focus on

development loans and its CRA qualified investments totaled $78 million.

service during the exam period.

said David Blackford, chief executive officer of California Bank &

investment of both time and financial resources. CB&T's outstanding CRA

community development."

# What happens if a bank gets a bad CRA rating?

1. [Knowledge Base](/cra-knowledge-base)
2. [CRA Basics](https://www.learncra.com/knowledgebase-category/cra-basics/)
3. What happens if a bank gets a bad CRA rating?



Of the four ratings a bank can receive for their CRA performance, only the Needs to Improve and Substantial Non-Compliance are viewed as “bad” ratings. However, especially in the case of a Needs to Improve rating, just because the bank received a negative rating doesn’t mean that the bank is ignoring the community.

In some cases, a bank may receive a technical downgrade to their CRA rating based on other compliance matters or issues within the bank. This can result in a bank that would otherwise have a Satisfactory CRA rating receive a lower rating. In those cases the banks may have a good record of meeting community needs even though other problems exist within the bank.

Regardless, if a bank receives a negative rating, it can be time-consuming. It effectively pauses the bank’s long-term strategy for growth by preventing the banks from opening new branches, merging with another bank or acquiring a bank.

It also poses significant reputation risk to the banks since the CRA rating is public. A negative rating brings a higher level of scrutiny both from the bank’s regulator and the general public.

Also, banks are expected to take immediate action to begin correcting the negative CRA rating. Therefore, the bank’s CRA regulator will often shorten the time frame before their next examination. This can be shortened to as little as twelve months before the bank is re-examined to determine if it has taken the necessary steps to increase its CRA performance.

# CBA Outlines Recommendations To Strengthen Joint CRA Modernization Proposal

Lindsey Johnson

  ![img](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB3aWR0aD0iMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)  

To Whom It May Concern:

The Consumer Bankers Association (“CBA”)[[1]](#_ftn1) is pleased to submit these comments to the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (“Board”), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (“OCC”), and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”) (collectively, the “Agencies”) on behalf of its members in response to the Joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NPR” or “Proposal”) entitled “Community Reinvestment Act.”[[2]](#_ftn2) The CBA welcomes the Agencies’ unified approach to Community Reinvestment Act (“CRA”) regulation and their efforts to propose rules that adapt to changes in the banking industry and provide greater clarity and consistency in CRA compliance.

The CBA supports the goals of the CRA, and its members acknowledge an affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income (“LMI”) areas, consistent with safe and sound banking practices. As noted by a leading advocacy group, the CRA “has leveraged trillions of dollars of responsible loans, investments and services for traditionally underserved communities.”[[3]](#_ftn3) Through the CRA, banks across the nation invest hundreds of billions of dollars in their communities, demonstrably benefitting them. Our members remain committed to further supporting their communities and emphatically reject any notion that current CRA ratings are inflated or reflect anything other than the Agencies’ recognition of that commitment.

In reviewing the proposed rulemaking, the CBA’s objective was to make sure that changes to the existing 1995 regulatory structure facilitate this commitment by providing banks with a flexible yet predictable mechanism to satisfy their CRA obligations, perhaps for the next quarter century. In furtherance of this objective, our members carefully analyzed the NPR and several provided relevant data on a confidential basis.[[4]](#_ftn4) We offer the following comments to facilitate the implementation of a streamlined, modernized rule that reasonably accounts for the operational realities of the banking industry.

The CBA endorses a more quantitative approach to CRA examinations, an expansion of community development categories, and a pre-clearance mechanism for activities not expressly authorized. But our analysis also shows some aspects of the NPR would be counterproductive to modernization and serving our communities. Specifically:

* Retail Lending Assessment Areas (“RLAAs”) are contrary to the plain language of the CRA and congressional intent. In fact, RLAAs turn CRA on its head by effectively requiring banks to use deposits gathered from their local communities to make loans in places potentially thousands of miles away. We urge the Agencies to dispense with the notion of RLAAs and to instead examine each bank’s facility-based assessment areas (“FBAAs”) and institution-wide performance.
* The Major Product Line (“MPL”) determination process will lead to uncertainty and inaccurately depict a bank’s AA lending. MPL determinations at the AA level will make it challenging for banks to implement credit programs that meet community needs since banks will not know which products constitute MPLs until examination time. Additionally, basing MPL determinations on a dollar-volume metric creates statistical anomalies by devaluing small business loans for banks with high mortgage and/or auto lending volumes. We urge the Agencies to determine MPLs at an institution level, using a unit-based metric, to afford banks greater clarity, consistency, and assurance.
* Consumer auto loans should not be evaluated under the Retail Lending Test (“RLT”). The Agencies have not substantiated their inference that LMI individuals have little or no access to auto loans, nor have they adequately articulated why auto loans warrant vastly different treatment than other consumer lending under the NPR. We urge the Agencies to exclude auto loans from the RLT and to refocus the CRA on mortgage loans and small business loans, which are instrumental to helping LMI individuals build wealth.
* Banks will have less flexibility in how to serve their communities. The NPR adopts a one-size-fits-all approach for large banks, deemphasizing performance context and adopting strict compliance thresholds. We urge the Agencies to continue to use performance context as the foundation of a bank’s performance evaluation, recognizing that banks require flexibility to address different needs and issues across different markets.
* An “Outstanding” rating will be largely out-of-reach, which may mean more banks will be content with “Satisfactory.” The NPR would require an “Outstanding” bank to perform at 125% of market, creating an unsustainable race to the top. We urge the Agencies to set this benchmark between 90% and 100% of market and supplement it with an analysis of discretionary factors that may boost ratings.
* Rating downgrades should only be based on discriminatory or other illegal practices that have a nexus to the CRA. The NPR proposes to expand the types of discriminatory practices that could result in a CRA rating downgrade to include any practice, not just ones related to providing financial products and services. We urge the Agencies to limit the scope of practices that could result in a downgrade to practices with a nexus to CRA, i.e., related to the provision of financial products and services.
* Banks will have less incentive to engage in community development (“CD”) financing because CD lending would no longer be eligible for consideration under the more heavily weighted lending test. Instead, lending and investments would be aggregated and assessed under a less heavily weighted CD Financing Test. We urge the Agencies to redress this imbalance by providing banks with the option of receiving qualitative consideration for CD lending under the RLT and weighting combined CD activities at 50%.
* Limiting the strategic plan option will deprive banks of the flexibility needed to serve their communities in ways consistent with their business orientations. The NPR raises the bar for strategic plans by requiring banks to be evaluated under the same performance tests and standards as traditional banks unless they are “substantially engaged” in other activities. We urge the Agencies retain strategic plans in their current form.
* The transition period is much too short. The 12-month period for large banks to implement the Proposal’s significant new administrative and data collection requirements is insufficient because it does not give banks nearly enough time to come into compliance. We urge the Agencies provide at least a 24-month implementation period and establish all standards and benchmarks at the beginning of an examination cycle based on two years of performance.
* Restrictions within CD financing categories will complicate banks’ efforts to serve LMI communities. The NPR’s 30/60 affordable housing standard presupposes an abundance of 30/60 projects, which the data does not support. We urge the Agencies to adopt a 30/80 affordable housing standard, if they adopt one at all, with higher thresholds in high-cost areas, to appropriately serve both low- and moderate-income neighborhoods and individuals.
* Consideration for CD services should be based on LMI community needs and not be limited to the provision of financial services. The NPR’s focus on CD services that are related to the provision of financial services (in metropolitan but not rural areas) unduly restricts banks’ efforts to prioritize the unique, varying needs of urban LMI communities. We urge the Agencies to eliminate this restriction and allow banks to receive consideration for all CD services, regardless of whether such services are related to the provision of financial services.

Read the full letter [here](https://consumerbankers.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/CBA-Joint-Agency-CRA-NPR-Comment-Letter-08.05.2022.pdf).

This is a comment letter from the Consumer Bankers Association (CBA) submitted to the Federal Reserve Board, OCC, and FDIC regarding the Joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The CBA, the only member-driven trade association focused exclusively on retail banking, welcomes the Agencies' unified approach to CRA modernization but raises significant concerns about specific aspects of the proposal.

The CBA endorses a more quantitative approach to CRA examinations, expansion of community development categories, and a pre-clearance mechanism for activities not expressly authorized. However, the letter outlines ten key objections and recommendations:

1. Retail Lending Assessment Areas (RLAAs) are contrary to the plain language of the CRA and congressional intent—they would require banks to use local deposits to make loans thousands of miles away. CBA urges examination of facility-based assessment areas (FBAAs) instead.
2. Major Product Line (MPL) determinations at the AA level create uncertainty and statistical anomalies; MPLs should be determined at the institution level using a unit-based metric rather than dollar-volume.
3. Consumer auto loans should be excluded from the Retail Lending Test (RLT); CRA should focus on mortgage and small business loans that help LMI individuals build wealth.
4. The NPR's one-size-fits-all approach for large banks de-emphasizes performance context; CBA urges continued use of performance context as the foundation of evaluations.
5. The "Outstanding" rating benchmark of 125% of market is unsustainable; CBA recommends 90-100% of market with discretionary factors.
6. Rating downgrades should only be based on discriminatory/illegal practices with a nexus to CRA (provision of financial products and services).
7. Community development (CD) lending should remain eligible for consideration under the more heavily weighted lending test, with combined CD activities weighted at 50%.
8. Strategic plan options should be retained in their current form rather than requiring banks to be evaluated under the same performance tests as traditional banks.
9. The 12-month transition period is too short; CBA urges at least a 24-month implementation period with standards set at the beginning of an examination cycle.
10. The 30/60 affordable housing standard should be replaced with a 30/80 standard (with higher thresholds in high-cost areas) to serve both low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
11. CD services consideration should not be limited to financial services-related activities; all CD services should be eligible regardless of relationship to financial services.

The letter was authored by Lindsey Johnson and submitted on August 5, 2022. The full letter is available as a PDF from the CBA website.

args.summary:
This webpage is American Banker's Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) news and coverage hub, aggregating articles on the federal anti-redlining law and related regulatory developments. The content primarily tracks the ongoing battle over the 2023 CRA overhaul and its reversal under the Trump administration.

Key regulatory developments covered include:
- The Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC proposed a rule to revert the anti-discrimination framework to its 1995 standards (July 16), citing litigation concerns about the 2023 rule.
- The FDIC and OCC issued a joint notice of proposed rulemaking that would tailor requirements for smaller institutions and monitor which groups receive community development grants (July 31).
- The FDIC, Fed, and OCC announced plans to rescind the 2023 CRA reform in March.
- Regulators tweaked new CRA rules ahead of implementation, delaying when certain banks would change assessment areas until 2026 (March 22).

Political and legal developments include:
- Sen. Elizabeth Warren and other Senate Democrats urged regulators to keep the 2023 CRA overhaul, arguing the rule was carefully crafted with bipartisan input (September 16).
- Warren and Rep. Maxine Waters blasted an "industry lawsuit" against CRA reform, saying the banking industry gets a "free pass" in CRA examinations.
- An industry-led legal challenge to the new rules is opposed by some banks and consumer groups, including Beneficial State Bank, which joined civil rights groups in an amicus brief opposing the lawsuit.
- Even opponents of the Biden-era CRA rule agree that pre-approving CRA-eligible activities was a good idea.

Other stories include: a $100M affordable housing fund effort by financial literacy advocate John Hope Bryant raising up to $300 million from banks; TD creating a $25 million fund for Philadelphia neighborhoods; OceanFirst in NJ receiving a top CRA rating after settling redlining allegations; New Jersey lawmakers considering a state-level CRA bill covering nonbanks and credit unions; and a CFPB report examining state CRA laws. The page also includes opinion pieces, including one arguing the expanded definition of "large" banks (those with at least $2 billion in assets) is a feature, not a bug, and another on JPMorgan Chase's plans to open 100 banking centers in "banking deserts."

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Do CRA Ratings Reflect Differences in Performance ---
URL: https://ncrc.org/do-cra-ratings-reflect-differences-in-performance-an-examination-using-federal-reserve-data

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NCRC (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) report examines whether Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) ratings reflect real differences in bank performance, using a new Federal Reserve database of 6,300 CRA exams conducted from 2005 through 2017. The analysis was authored by Josh Silver (Senior Advisor, Policy and Government Affairs) and Jason Richardson (Director of Research & Evaluation).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Retail loan performance measures generally showed higher ratings corresponding to better outcomes, but the differences were narrower than expected.
- Community development (CD) loan and investment measures showed much larger performance differences across ratings categories (often ~100% differences) compared to retail measures (often just 1 percentage point differences).
- Approximately 90% of banks received a Satisfactory rating, indicating the four-tier rating system fails to adequately differentiate performance. NCRC recommends splitting Satisfactory into High and Low Satisfactory tiers.
- Large banks significantly lagged smaller banks in percent of loans to LMI borrowers and to the smallest businesses, though they did not trail on LMI tract lending.
- Anomalies existed, including banks with High Satisfactory ratings sometimes outperforming banks with Outstanding ratings (e.g., median LMI borrower lending of 12.78% for High Satisfactory vs. 11.83% for Outstanding), potentially explained by large banks being downgraded for fair lending violations during the financial crisis.
- The sharpest performance differences occurred between Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings (e.g., 10.43% vs. 2.13% for LMI borrower lending).

RECOMMENDATIONS:
- NCRC advocates for incremental reform rather than radical overhaul, contrary to the OCC's final rule.
- Proposes a peer-relative rating scale comparing bank performance to aggregate peers (Outstanding: >100% of peer level; High Satisfactory: 80-99%; Low Satisfactory: 60-79%; Needs-to-Improve: 40-60%; Substantial Noncompliance: <39%).
- Suggests different peer benchmarks may be needed for different business models (branch-based vs. non-branch banks) and asset sizes.
- Recommends retaining qualitative factors (20-30% of ratings) and compensation mechanisms where strong performance on one test can offset weaker performance elsewhere.
- Calls for the OCC to withdraw its final rule, which NCRC argues is not evidence-based, and to collaborate with the Federal Reserve Board and FDIC on new rulemaking with a publicly available database.
- Recommends annual agency reports analyzing performance measures after new regulations are implemented.

METHODOLOGY NOTES:
- Banks classified as community (up to $10B assets), regional ($10B-$50B), and large (over $50B).
- The Federal Reserve database lacked service test variables (e.g., percent of branches in LMI tracts), limiting analysis.
- Banks with Substantial Noncompliance ratings were excluded due to insufficient observations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results suggest the need for refinement of performance measures, especially for the retail loan indicators, rather than a complete overhaul. The Federal Reserve data indicates a rating system that is not fundamentally broken or arbitrary but a system that should be sharpened."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/apps/CRAPubWeb/CRA/BankRatingResult

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Federal Reserve Board's Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) search page, which provides a searchable database of Performance Evaluations & Ratings for Federal Reserve-supervised state member banks. The page is part of the official Federal Reserve System website and covers the CRA framework under the Federal Open Market Committee.

The search tool allows users to filter results by several criteria: institution name or ID, overall CRA rating (All, Outstanding, Satisfactory, Needs to Improve, Substantial Noncompliance), city, county, state (all 50 states plus Puerto Rico and DC), asset size range (from 0-$350K up to $100M+), exam year (1995-2026), public year (1995-2026), and exam method (Intermediate Small Bank, Small Bank, Large Bank, Limited Purpose, Strategic Plan, Wholesale). Users can also filter by component test ratings including Lending Test, Investment Test, Service Test, and Community Development Test ratings.

The results table displays a paginated list (64 pages total) of bank evaluation records, showing for each bank: Bank Name with RSSD ID, Headquarters Location, Overall Rating, Exam Date (Performance Evaluation), Public Date, Exam Method, and Asset Size (in thousands). Each entry includes a link to download the full Performance Evaluation (PE) PDF.

Sample data from the first page shows 30 banks, including examples like:

The page includes records dating back to 1998 and forward through 2026 exam years, with most banks receiving "Satisfactory" ratings and only a few receiving "Outstanding."
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Community Reinvestment Act: When Do CRA Ratings Threaten Mergers? ---
URL: https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/community-reinvestment-act

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a legal practice article from SJKP LLP Law Firm (a U.S. law firm, also associated with Daeryun Law) titled "Community Reinvestment Act: When Do CRA Ratings Threaten Mergers?" published May 14, 2026. The article provides comprehensive guidance on Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) compliance, examinations, ratings, and their impact on bank mergers.

KEY CONTENT:
- The CRA (12 U.S.C. § 2901 et seq., enacted 1977) requires federal bank regulators to encourage insured depository institutions to serve credit needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. Three regulators administer CRA by charter type: OCC (national banks/federal savings associations), FDIC (state nonmember banks), and Federal Reserve (state member banks).
- The 2024 CRA Final Rule (Joint Final Rule by OCC/FDIC/FRB, Oct 24, 2023; effective April 1, 2024, full implementation January 1, 2026) modernized the CRA framework with size-based tests: Large banks ($2B+ assets) face four tests (Retail Lending, Retail Services and Products, Community Development Financing, Community Development Services); Intermediate banks ($600M-$2B) face Retail Lending and Community Development Tests; Small banks (under $600M) retain streamlined Lending Test or may elect a Strategic Plan.
- CRA ratings and merger impact: Outstanding (strong support), Satisfactory (usually approved), Needs to Improve (heightened scrutiny + delay), and Substantial Noncompliance (likely denial or conditions).
- Under the Bank Merger Act (12 U.S.C. § 1828(c)), regulators must consider CRA performance evaluations in merger approvals, with public protest opportunities. Notable merger cases affected by CRA protests include TD-First Horizon (abandoned 2023), BB&T-SunTrust (2019 Truist conditions), and BMO-Bank of the West.
- ECOA (15 U.S.C. § 1691, Reg B at 12 C.F.R. Part 1002) and Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.) overlap with CRA compliance as gating issues. DOJ pattern-or-practice enforcement examples include Wells Fargo ($175M, 2012), Bank of America ($335M, 2012), City National Bank ($31M, 2023), and Trident Mortgage ($24M, 2022) under the Combating Redlining Initiative (launched 2021).
- Community development activities include affordable housing (Section 8, LIHTC), economic development (small business loans, microfinance), revitalization (NMTC, opportunity zones), and essential community services.
- CRA protests during the ~30-day merger comment period trigger heightened review; the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and local groups have negotiated $620B+ in merger commitments through the protest framework.
- CFPB and state attorneys general (e.g., NY Banking Law § 29, Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A) can pursue parallel enforcement, creating multi-jurisdictional exposure.
- The firm offers CRA services including examination preparation, fair lending audits, merger CRA strategy, and enforcement defense.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Do CRA Ratings Reflect Differences in Performance ---
URL: https://ncrc.org/do-cra-ratings-reflect-differences-in-performance-an-examination-using-federal-reserve-data

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NCRC (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) report examines whether Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) ratings reflect real differences in bank performance, using a new Federal Reserve database of 6,300 CRA exams conducted from 2005 through 2017. The analysis was authored by Josh Silver (Senior Advisor, Policy and Government Affairs) and Jason Richardson (Director of Research & Evaluation).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Retail loan performance measures generally showed higher ratings corresponding to better outcomes, but the differences were narrower than expected.
- Community development (CD) loan and investment measures showed much larger performance differences across ratings categories (often ~100% differences) compared to retail measures (often just 1 percentage point differences).
- Approximately 90% of banks received a Satisfactory rating, indicating the four-tier rating system fails to adequately differentiate performance. NCRC recommends splitting Satisfactory into High and Low Satisfactory tiers.
- Large banks significantly lagged smaller banks in percent of loans to LMI borrowers and to the smallest businesses, though they did not trail on LMI tract lending.
- Anomalies existed, including banks with High Satisfactory ratings sometimes outperforming banks with Outstanding ratings (e.g., median LMI borrower lending of 12.78% for High Satisfactory vs. 11.83% for Outstanding), potentially explained by large banks being downgraded for fair lending violations during the financial crisis.
- The sharpest performance differences occurred between Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings (e.g., 10.43% vs. 2.13% for LMI borrower lending).

RECOMMENDATIONS:
- NCRC advocates for incremental reform rather than radical overhaul, contrary to the OCC's final rule.
- Proposes a peer-relative rating scale comparing bank performance to aggregate peers (Outstanding: >100% of peer level; High Satisfactory: 80-99%; Low Satisfactory: 60-79%; Needs-to-Improve: 40-60%; Substantial Noncompliance: <39%).
- Suggests different peer benchmarks may be needed for different business models (branch-based vs. non-branch banks) and asset sizes.
- Recommends retaining qualitative factors (20-30% of ratings) and compensation mechanisms where strong performance on one test can offset weaker performance elsewhere.
- Calls for the OCC to withdraw its final rule, which NCRC argues is not evidence-based, and to collaborate with the Federal Reserve Board and FDIC on new rulemaking with a publicly available database.
- Recommends annual agency reports analyzing performance measures after new regulations are implemented.

METHODOLOGY NOTES:
- Banks classified as community (up to $10B assets), regional ($10B-$50B), and large (over $50B).
- The Federal Reserve database lacked service test variables (e.g., percent of branches in LMI tracts), limiting analysis.
- Banks with Substantial Noncompliance ratings were excluded due to insufficient observations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results suggest the need for refinement of performance measures, especially for the retail loan indicators, rather than a complete overhaul. The Federal Reserve data indicates a rating system that is not fundamentally broken or arbitrary but a system that should be sharpened."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (New York Fed) website, describing its mission and the various functions and services it provides. The New York Fed's core mission is to make the U.S. economy stronger and the financial system more stable for all segments of society, accomplished through executing monetary policy, providing financial services, supervising banks, and conducting research on issues impacting the nation and communities.

The page outlines several key areas of the New York Fed's work:
- Supervising and regulating financial institutions in the Second District to maintain a safe and competitive U.S. and global banking system.
- Providing financial services and advancing infrastructure reform in key markets, plus training and educational support to international institutions.
- The Governance & Culture Reform hub, which fosters discussion about corporate governance and reform of culture and behavior in the financial services industry.
- The New York Innovation Center, which bridges finance, technology, and innovation to generate insights into high-value central bank-related opportunities.
- Addressing the growing role of nonbank financial institutions (NBFIs) in U.S. financial markets, described as a transformational trend with implications for monetary policy and financial stability.
- Offering the Central Banking Seminar and specialized courses for central bankers and financial supervisors.
- Providing consumer protection resources on frauds and scams.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Fed Communities explains four ways the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) encourages banks to work with their neighbors. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining—the discriminatory practice of denying credit based on the ethnic or racial composition of neighborhoods despite residents being creditworthy borrowers. Redlining has caused persistent economic disparities, including lower homeownership rates and household income for those born in formerly redlined neighborhoods in the 1970s-1980s, and higher rates of COVID-19 complications among residents of these areas. The CRA encourages banks to distribute resources more equitably to underserved (LMI) communities, with the Fed and other regulators conducting performance evaluations and assigning publicly available CRA ratings.

The four ways the CRA encourages banks are: (1) Connect with their neighbors—evaluators collect demographic data and interview community contacts, and any member of the public can comment on a bank's performance; (2) Tailor community development work to specific community needs—beyond housing, this includes early childhood development, healthcare, and workforce training; (3) Contribute financial know-how to community-led initiatives—such as volunteering expertise in financial literacy or serving on a nonprofit lender's loan committee; (4) Develop new strategies and partnerships—such as partnering with community development financial institutions (CDFIs), and participating in events like Investment Connection workshops hosted by regional Federal Reserve Banks.

The article notes that on May 5, 2022, the Federal Reserve Board, OCC, and FDIC jointly released a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) to reform CRA regulations. The post was originally published on July 15, 2021, updated May 11, 2022, and last updated October 23, 2023. It was written by Benjamin Horowitz, a senior policy analyst for the Community Development team at the Minneapolis Fed.

--- SOURCE 11: The Fed - Perspectives from Main Street: Stakeholder Feedback on Modernizing the Community Reinvestment Act ---
URL: https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/stakeholder-feedback-on-modernizing-the-community-reinvestment-act-201906.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an official Federal Reserve report titled "Perspectives from Main Street: Stakeholder Feedback on Modernizing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)." It summarizes feedback gathered from 29 roundtables hosted by the Federal Reserve Board of Governors and Reserve Banks between October 2018 and January 2019 across diverse urban and rural locations (including Lynchburg, Virginia; Dallas, Texas; San Juan, Puerto Rico; Rapid City, South Dakota; and Salt Lake City, Utah), with over 400 bankers and community group members attending. Federal Reserve staff also read nearly 1,500 comments submitted in response to the OCC's 2018 Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on CRA reform.

The report organizes feedback by topic:

1. ASSESSMENT AREAS: Participants generally agreed the geography-based assessment area definition needs updating due to technology changes, though smaller community banks with branch-based operations find the current approach workable. Bankers with online/digital presence find requirements challenging. Concerns raised about relying on deposits to define assessment areas (tracking difficulties, urban concentration bias against rural areas), inclusion of loan production offices, partial vs. full county areas, and fair lending concerns deterring branch expansion. Community groups stressed maintaining branch focus since LMI individuals, elderly, and rural populations rely heavily on branches.

2. CRA IN UNDERSERVED COMMUNITIES: Suggestions included creating "CRA zones" designated by regulators or local jurisdictions (potentially overlapping Opportunity Zones or disaster areas); clear standards for when banks can operate outside assessment areas (e.g., allowing 30% of activity outside); more full-scope reviews in rural areas; updating LMI definitions (statewide median income calculations exclude some rural poor populations); considering underserved populations by people rather than geography (elderly, racial minorities, immigrants, students, veterans, disabled); and adding an explicit racial lens.

3. PERFORMANCE TEST STRUCTURE: Widespread agreement that reform is needed while maintaining different evaluation methods for different bank sizes. Bankers suggested raising intermediate small bank (ISB) threshold to $1-5 billion (currently $321 million-$1.284 billion) and adding an "intermediate large" category. One cited study said eliminating ISBs' community development test would cause $3 billion in annual community development lending/investment losses. Significant concern about a single community development metric; nearly all bankers supported performance context. Debate over combining community development loans, investments, and services into one "bucket"—some favored flexibility, while others feared reduced investment demand for LIHTC, NMTC, and CDFI ecosystems.

4. EVALUATING PERFORMANCE: Nearly all participants stressed need for more clarity, consistency, and timeliness in CRA examinations. Bankers wanted transparency on how much activity is "enough" for ratings. Concerns that metrics could incentivize focus on high-value markets. Few specific metrics were proposed; suggestions included basing metrics on tier 1 capital, deposits, income, employees, or share of CRA activities. Participants wanted qualitative factors (innovation, complexity, responsiveness) clarified, community needs assessments standardized, and more data collection/transparency. Some suggested switching from the current rating system (outstanding/satisfactory/needs to improve/substantial noncompliance) to letter grades or numerical ratings, splitting "satisfactory" into high/low tiers, and providing benefits (e.g., discounted FDIC insurance) for "outstanding" ratings.

5. DEFINING COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES: Both banks and community groups wanted clearer definitions of eligible activities, including a "hotline" or national registry/menu. CDFI participants suggested CRA credit for the life of loans rather than just origination year, automatic favorable treatment for CDFI and disaster relief activities, and credit for volunteer services (e.g., Habitat for Humanity). Some urged expanding eligible products (educational loans, payday loan alternatives, auto loans, individual development accounts, affordable checking/savings accounts) and giving automatic credit for public infrastructure investments (school buses, fire trucks, health clinics). Debate over mortgage-backed securities and secondary market purchases eligibility.

6. ADDITIONAL COMMENTS: Many participants wanted CRA expanded to cover credit unions, insurance companies, fintech companies, mortgage brokers, and other non-depository institutions. Community groups asked for regulatory oversight/enforcement of community benefits agreements (CBAs). Concerns about examination timeliness, burdensome paper public files, and inconsistent examiner training across agencies.

Appendices include a table of all 29 roundtable dates/locations/attendee groups, and lists of questions posed separately to community groups and bankers.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve propose amendments to CRA regulations | Consumer Finance Monitor ---
URL: https://www.consumerfinancemonitor.com/2022/05/18/occ-fdic-and-federal-reserve-propose-amendments-to-cra-regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Consumer Finance Monitor blog (by the Consumer Financial Services Group at Ballard Spahr LLP) reports that the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve Board jointly issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPR) proposing amendments to their regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). This follows the OCC's December 2021 rescission of its 2020 CRA final rule (which had moved from a primarily subjective to a primarily objective ratings system) and its replacement with a rule largely based on the 1995 framework. Comments on the NPR must be received by August 5, 2022.

Key highlights of the proposal include:

**Assessment Areas**: Banks would continue to delineate facility-based assessment areas where they have main offices, branches, and deposit-taking remote service facilities. Geographic requirements would be tailored by bank size. Large banks would be required to establish retail assessment areas in any MSA or combined non-MSA areas where they originated at least 100 home mortgage loans or 250 small business loans outside their facility-based assessment area. Small and intermediate banks would not be subject to this requirement.

**Performance Tests and Ratings**: The evaluation framework would include four tests: Retail Lending Test, Retail Services and Products Test, Community Development Financing Test, and Community Development Services Test. Banks' "operations subsidiaries" would be included in CRA performance evaluations. Five performance scores would be used: Outstanding, High Satisfactory, Low Satisfactory, Needs to Improve, and Substantial Noncompliance, which would then be combined into the four statutorily-required ratings.

**Retail Lending Test**: Intended to standardize retail lending evaluations through retail lending metrics and performance standards based on local and tailored benchmarks.

**Community Development Services Test**: Would include a qualitative assessment plus, for large banks with assets over $10 billion, a metric measuring hours of community development services per full-time equivalent bank employee. Activities reflecting areas of expertise such as HR, IT, and legal services would be considered related to financial services. In nonmetropolitan areas, banks can receive credit for certain volunteer activities meeting community development needs even if unrelated to financial services.

**Assigned Scores and Ratings**: Scores would be combined across tests with weights varying by bank asset size. For large banks, weights are: Retail Lending Test (45%), Retail Services and Products Test (15%), Community Development Financing Test (30%), and Community Development Services Test (10%). For intermediate banks, the Retail Lending Test and current community development test would be weighted equally.
</summary>

"After moving alone in 2020 to reform its Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) regulation, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has joined the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and Federal Reserve Board in issuing a joint notice of proposed rulemaking setting forth proposed amendments to their regulations implementing the CRA."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 13: Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Compliance Guide ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Compliance Guide published by NETBankAudit, a banking regulatory compliance and audit firm with over 25 years of experience. The guide provides a detailed overview of the CRA, its purpose, scope, key definitions, examination procedures for different bank sizes, and the history of the 2023 proposed modernization and its subsequent rescission.

**CRA Purpose and Scope:** Enacted in 1977, the CRA ensures financial institutions serve the credit needs of their entire communities, particularly low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. It applies to national banks, federal savings associations, and state savings associations, is codified at 12 CFR Part 25, and is administered by the OCC, Federal Reserve, and FDIC. Key definitions covered include Affiliate, Assessment Area, Community Development, Small Bank/Intermediate Small Bank (classified by asset size with thresholds adjusted annually), and Qualified Investment.

**Performance Evaluations:** Banks are evaluated under various tests: Lending, Investment, and Service Tests for large institutions; Community Development Test for wholesale/limited purpose banks; Small Bank/Intermediate Small Bank Standards; and a Strategic Plan Option. Ratings range from "Outstanding" to "Substantial Noncompliance," based on quantitative and qualitative factors.

**The 2023 CRA Final Rule and Rescission:** In October 2023, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC issued a new CRA Final Rule—the first modernization since 1995—aimed at expanding credit access, recognizing digital/online banking, and using a metrics-based approach. However, litigation was filed, a preliminary injunction halted its implementation in February 2024, and in March 2025 the agencies announced their intent to rescind the rule. As of April 2025, the 2023 rule is not in effect, and banks continue to operate under the 1995/2021 regulatory framework.

**Examination Procedures:**
- **Large Institutions:** Examiners select assessment areas for full-scope review (at least one per state and multistate MSA). The Lending Test covers home mortgage, small business, small farm, and community development lending; the Investment Test assesses qualified investments; the Service Test evaluates retail and community development services.
- **Intermediate Small Banks (ISBs):** Evaluated under a Lending Test (loan-to-deposit ratio analysis, credit distribution inside vs. outside assessment areas, geographic and borrower distribution) and a Community Development Test.
- **Small Banks** (assets ≤ $600 million, adjusted annually): Primarily evaluated on lending performance under the OCC's 2020 rule, with new data collection requirements for retail domestic deposit accounts and deposit-based assessment areas required if 50%+ of retail domestic deposits come from outside facility-based assessment areas.

**CRA Public File Requirements:** All banks must maintain a public file containing public comments, the most recent CRA Performance Evaluation, assessment area maps, branch lists, loan-to-deposit ratios, and HMDA disclosure statements.

**Impact on Applications:** CRA performance is a critical factor in regulatory applications for new branches, relocations, mergers, conversions, and acquisitions. Poor performance can result in denial or conditional approval.

**CRA Timeline:** 1977 (enacted), 1995 (comprehensive revision), 2021 (OCC final rule), October 2023 (new Final Rule issued), February 2024 (rule published but halted by litigation), March 2025 (agencies announce rescission), April 2025 (1995/2021 framework reinstated).

The page concludes with best practices for CRA compliance professionals and a promotional section describing NETBankAudit's CRA audit and consulting services. The rest of the page contains unrelated links to NETBankAudit's learning center articles on topics including cybersecurity, AML/BSA, FDIC supervision, IT audits, ransomware, and other banking compliance regulations.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Do CRA Ratings Reflect Differences in Performance ---
URL: https://ncrc.org/do-cra-ratings-reflect-differences-in-performance-an-examination-using-federal-reserve-data

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This NCRC (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) report examines whether Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) ratings reflect real differences in bank performance, using a new Federal Reserve database of 6,300 CRA exams conducted from 2005 through 2017. The analysis was authored by Josh Silver (Senior Advisor, Policy and Government Affairs) and Jason Richardson (Director of Research & Evaluation).

KEY FINDINGS:
- Retail loan performance measures generally showed higher ratings corresponding to better outcomes, but the differences were narrower than expected.
- Community development (CD) loan and investment measures showed much larger performance differences across ratings categories (often ~100% differences) compared to retail measures (often just 1 percentage point differences).
- Approximately 90% of banks received a Satisfactory rating, indicating the four-tier rating system fails to adequately differentiate performance. NCRC recommends splitting Satisfactory into High and Low Satisfactory tiers.
- Large banks significantly lagged smaller banks in percent of loans to LMI borrowers and to the smallest businesses, though they did not trail on LMI tract lending.
- Anomalies existed, including banks with High Satisfactory ratings sometimes outperforming banks with Outstanding ratings (e.g., median LMI borrower lending of 12.78% for High Satisfactory vs. 11.83% for Outstanding), potentially explained by large banks being downgraded for fair lending violations during the financial crisis.
- The sharpest performance differences occurred between Low Satisfactory and Needs-to-Improve ratings (e.g., 10.43% vs. 2.13% for LMI borrower lending).

RECOMMENDATIONS:
- NCRC advocates for incremental reform rather than radical overhaul, contrary to the OCC's final rule.
- Proposes a peer-relative rating scale comparing bank performance to aggregate peers (Outstanding: >100% of peer level; High Satisfactory: 80-99%; Low Satisfactory: 60-79%; Needs-to-Improve: 40-60%; Substantial Noncompliance: <39%).
- Suggests different peer benchmarks may be needed for different business models (branch-based vs. non-branch banks) and asset sizes.
- Recommends retaining qualitative factors (20-30% of ratings) and compensation mechanisms where strong performance on one test can offset weaker performance elsewhere.
- Calls for the OCC to withdraw its final rule, which NCRC argues is not evidence-based, and to collaborate with the Federal Reserve Board and FDIC on new rulemaking with a publicly available database.
- Recommends annual agency reports analyzing performance measures after new regulations are implemented.

METHODOLOGY NOTES:
- Banks classified as community (up to $10B assets), regional ($10B-$50B), and large (over $50B).
- The Federal Reserve database lacked service test variables (e.g., percent of branches in LMI tracts), limiting analysis.
- Banks with Substantial Noncompliance ratings were excluded due to insufficient observations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The results suggest the need for refinement of performance measures, especially for the retail loan indicators, rather than a complete overhaul. The Federal Reserve data indicates a rating system that is not fundamentally broken or arbitrary but a system that should be sharpened."
</key_excerpts>

<summary>
This webpage is from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York (New York Fed) website, describing its mission and the various functions and services it provides. --- SOURCE 5: Community Reinvestment Act: When Do CRA Ratings Threaten Mergers? ---
URL: https://www.daeryunlaw.com/us/practices/detail/community-reinvestment-act

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a legal practice article from SJKP LLP Law Firm (a U.S. law firm, also associated with Daeryun Law) titled "Community Reinvestment Act: When Do CRA Ratings Threaten Mergers?" published May 14, 2026. The article provides comprehensive guidance on Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) compliance, examinations, ratings, and their impact on bank mergers.

KEY CONTENT:
- The CRA (12 U.S.C. § 2901 et seq., enacted 1977) requires federal bank regulators to encourage insured depository institutions to serve credit needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. Three regulators administer CRA by charter type: OCC (national banks/federal savings associations), FDIC (state nonmember banks), and Federal Reserve (state member banks).
- The 2024 CRA Final Rule (Joint Final Rule by OCC/FDIC/FRB, Oct 24, 2023; effective April 1, 2024, full implementation January 1, 2026) modernized the CRA framework with size-based tests: Large banks ($2B+ assets) face four tests (Retail Lending, Retail Services and Products, Community Development Financing, Community Development Services); Intermediate banks ($600M-$2B) face Retail Lending and Community Development Tests; Small banks (under $600M) retain streamlined Lending Test or may elect a Strategic Plan.
- CRA ratings and merger impact: Outstanding (strong support), Satisfactory (usually approved), Needs to Improve (heightened scrutiny + delay), and Substantial Noncompliance (likely denial or conditions).
- Under the Bank Merger Act (12 U.S.C. § 1828(c)), regulators must consider CRA performance evaluations in merger approvals, with public protest opportunities. Notable merger cases affected by CRA protests include TD-First Horizon (abandoned 2023), BB&T-SunTrust (2019 Truist conditions), and BMO-Bank of the West.
- ECOA (15 U.S.C. § 1691, Reg B at 12 C.F.R. Part 1002) and Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.) overlap with CRA compliance as gating issues. DOJ pattern-or-practice enforcement examples include Wells Fargo ($175M, 2012), Bank of America ($335M, 2012), City National Bank ($31M, 2023), and Trident Mortgage ($24M, 2022) under the Combating Redlining Initiative (launched 2021).
- Community development activities include affordable housing (Section 8, LIHTC), economic development (small business loans, microfinance), revitalization (NMTC, opportunity zones), and essential community services.
- CRA protests during the ~30-day merger comment period trigger heightened review; the National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) and local groups have negotiated $620B+ in merger commitments through the protest framework.
- CFPB and state attorneys general (e.g., NY Banking Law § 29, Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A) can pursue parallel enforcement, creating multi-jurisdictional exposure.
- The firm offers CRA services including examination preparation, fair lending audits, merger CRA strategy, and enforcement defense.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 (12 U.S.C. § 2901 et seq.) requires federal bank regulators to encourage insured depository institutions to serve credit needs of communities including low- and moderate-income (LMI) areas."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:

California Bank & Trust (CB&T), a subsidiary of Zions Bancorporation (NASDAQ: ZION) and one of California's leading banks with over $10 billion in assets and 89 offices statewide, announced it has again been awarded an "Outstanding" rating from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) under the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The examination, which began in May and was recently completed, evaluated the institution's community reinvestment activities.

The Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 requires regulated financial institutions to demonstrate that their deposit facilities serve the convenience and needs of the communities in which they operate, including credit and deposit services.

During the review period, CB&T originated over $250 million in community development loans, its CRA qualified investments totaled $78 million, and CB&T employees completed over 6,500 hours of community service. The bank partners with nonprofit agencies in each branch community to identify economic issues and unique needs of each neighborhood, focusing on community-specific lending initiatives to meet the credit needs of individuals and businesses.

David Blackford, chief executive officer of California Bank & Trust, commented on the achievement. CB&T provides a full range of financial solutions for businesses and individuals, including cash management, international banking, commercial and small business lending, and online banking.

--- SOURCE 7: What happens if a bank gets a bad CRA rating? | socrates | CRA Learning Center | curated by findCRA ---
URL: https://www.learncra.com/knowledgebase/what-happens-if-a-bank-gets-a-bad-cra-rating

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from LearnCRA explains the consequences a bank faces when it receives a "bad" CRA (Community Reinvestment Act) rating. Of the four possible CRA ratings, only "Needs to Improve" and "Substantial Non-Compliance" are considered bad ratings. The page notes that a bank may receive a technical downgrade based on other compliance matters, meaning a bank that would otherwise receive a Satisfactory rating could receive a lower one despite having a good record of meeting community needs.

The key consequences of a negative CRA rating include:
- It pauses the bank's long-term growth strategy by preventing it from opening new branches, merging with another bank, or acquiring a bank.
- It creates significant reputation risk since the CRA rating is public, bringing higher scrutiny from both regulators and the public.
- The bank is expected to take immediate corrective action, and the regulator will typically shorten the time frame before the next examination — potentially to as little as twelve months — to determine if the bank has taken the necessary steps to improve its CRA performance.

The page was last modified on April 28, 2023, and is categorized under CRA Basics and CRA Examinations.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: CBA Outlines Recommendations To Strengthen Joint CRA Modernization Proposal - consumerbankers.com ---
URL: https://consumerbankers.com/comment-letter/cba-outlines-recommendations-to-strengthen-joint-cra-modernization-proposal

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comment letter from the Consumer Bankers Association (CBA) submitted to the Federal Reserve Board, OCC, and FDIC regarding the Joint Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The CBA, the only member-driven trade association focused exclusively on retail banking, welcomes the Agencies' unified approach to CRA modernization but raises significant concerns about specific aspects of the proposal.

The CBA endorses a more quantitative approach to CRA examinations, expansion of community development categories, and a pre-clearance mechanism for activities not expressly authorized. However, the letter outlines ten key objections and recommendations:

1. Retail Lending Assessment Areas (RLAAs) are contrary to the plain language of the CRA and congressional intent—they would require banks to use local deposits to make loans thousands of miles away. CBA urges examination of facility-based assessment areas (FBAAs) instead.
2. Major Product Line (MPL) determinations at the AA level create uncertainty and statistical anomalies; MPLs should be determined at the institution level using a unit-based metric rather than dollar-volume.
3. Consumer auto loans should be excluded from the Retail Lending Test (RLT); CRA should focus on mortgage and small business loans that help LMI individuals build wealth.
4. The NPR's one-size-fits-all approach for large banks de-emphasizes performance context; CBA urges continued use of performance context as the foundation of evaluations.
5. The "Outstanding" rating benchmark of 125% of market is unsustainable; CBA recommends 90-100% of market with discretionary factors.
6. Rating downgrades should only be based on discriminatory/illegal practices with a nexus to CRA (provision of financial products and services).
7. Community development (CD) lending should remain eligible for consideration under the more heavily weighted lending test, with combined CD activities weighted at 50%.
8. Strategic plan options should be retained in their current form rather than requiring banks to be evaluated under the same performance tests as traditional banks.
9. The 12-month transition period is too short; CBA urges at least a 24-month implementation period with standards set at the beginning of an examination cycle.
10. The 30/60 affordable housing standard should be replaced with a 30/80 standard (with higher thresholds in high-cost areas) to serve both low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
11. CD services consideration should not be limited to financial services-related activities; all CD services should be eligible regardless of relationship to financial services.

The letter was authored by Lindsey Johnson and submitted on August 5, 2022. The full letter is available as a PDF from the CBA website.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The CBA supports the goals of the CRA, and its members acknowledge an affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income ('LMI') areas, consistent with safe and sound banking practices."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: 4 ways the CRA encourages banks to work hand-in- ... ---
URL: https://fedcommunities.org/four-ways-cra-encourages-equitable-community-investment

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Fed Communities explains four ways the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) encourages banks to work with their neighbors. The CRA was passed by Congress in 1977 in response to redlining—the discriminatory practice of denying credit based on the ethnic or racial composition of neighborhoods despite residents being creditworthy borrowers. Redlining has caused persistent economic disparities, including lower homeownership rates and household income for those born in formerly redlined neighborhoods in the 1970s-1980s, and higher rates of COVID-19 complications among residents of these areas. The CRA encourages banks to distribute resources more equitably to underserved (LMI) communities, with the Fed and other regulators conducting performance evaluations and assigning publicly available CRA ratings.

The four ways the CRA encourages banks are: (1) Connect with their neighbors—evaluators collect demographic data and interview community contacts, and any member of the public can comment on a bank's performance; (2) Tailor community development work to specific community needs—beyond housing, this includes early childhood development, healthcare, and workforce training; (3) Contribute financial know-how to community-led initiatives—such as volunteering expertise in financial literacy or serving on a nonprofit lender's loan committee; (4) Develop new strategies and partnerships—such as partnering with community development financial institutions (CDFIs), and participating in events like Investment Connection workshops hosted by regional Federal Reserve Banks.

The article notes that on May 5, 2022, the Federal Reserve Board, OCC, and FDIC jointly released a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) to reform CRA regulations. The post was originally published on July 15, 2021, updated May 11, 2022, and last updated October 23, 2023. It was written by Benjamin Horowitz, a senior policy analyst for the Community Development team at the Minneapolis Fed.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

## OCC Issues Guidance on CRA Performance Evaluation Process

[Adam Witmer](/blog?author=5181ccc0e4b03000ce6fc3e5)

[Regulatory Update](/blog/category/Regulatory+Update), [CRA](/blog/category/CRA)

On June 15, 2018, the OCC issued a bulletin (2018-17) on supervisory policy and processes for Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) performance evaluations.  This bulletin was issued to inform national banks, federal savings associations, and federal branches and agencies (collectively, banks) regulated by the OCC about clarification to the OCC’s supervisory policies and processes regarding how examiners will now evaluate and communicate bank performance under the CRA.  This new guidance is effective immediately, though financial institutions that are currently in the middle of a CRA examination may see the use of transitional procedures.

Highlights of this guidance include:

* Implementation of full-scope and limited-scope reviews;
* Consideration of activities that promote economic development;
* Use of demographic, aggregate, and market share data;
* Evaluation of the borrower distribution of loans outside bank assessment areas (AA);
* Evaluation frequency and timing;
* The CRA performance evaluation period; and
* Evaluation of home mortgage loans.

While this guidance will have the greatest impact on large financial institutions, all financial institutions (including small, and intermediate-small banks) regulated by the OCC should review this bulletin which outlines the OCC’s new approach to CRA evaluations.

The full bulletin can be found **[here](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2018/bulletin-2018-17.html)**.
