--- SOURCE 11: Federal Register :: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations ---
URL: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/06/05/2020-11220/community-reinvestment-act-regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Register document page for the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) final rule on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Regulations, published on June 5, 2020 (Document 2020-11220, 85 FR 34734). The rule, effective October 1, 2020, strengthens and modernizes the CRA by making four key changes: (1) clarifying and expanding the bank lending, investment, and services (qualifying activities) that receive CRA credit; (2) updating how banks delineate assessment areas, including requiring deposit-based assessment areas for banks that collect deposits above a threshold outside their physical branch footprint (capturing internet banks and other non-traditional models); (3) providing more consistent and objective methods for evaluating CRA performance through new performance standards measuring retail lending distribution and dollar-value impact of CD activities; and (4) requiring more timely and transparent data collection, recordkeeping, and reporting.

The rule was issued by the Department of the Treasury's OCC, amending 12 CFR Parts 25 and 195 (Docket ID OCC-2018-0008, RIN 1557-AE34), spanning 101 pages. Banks must comply by October 1, 2020, January 1, 2023, or January 1, 2024, as applicable, with appendix C to part 25 expiring January 1, 2024.

Background: The reform effort began with an August 2018 Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (over 1,500 comments received), followed by a joint December 2019 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking with the FDIC (over 7,500 comments received). Under the prior framework, nearly 74% of banks were rated satisfactory and almost 24% outstanding, with less than 3% in the two lowest ratings, and the OCC found only a weak positive relationship between CRA ratings and actual CRA activity. The new framework moves from a primarily subjective to a primarily objective evaluation system to make ratings more reliable, reproducible, and comparable.

Key provisions include: qualifying activities criteria covering underserved areas, distressed areas, disaster areas, and Indian country beyond LMI areas; a publicly available illustrative list of qualifying activities; a process for banks to seek agency confirmation of qualifying status; and the exclusion of certain activities that previously received credit (e.g., loans to middle- and upper-income borrowers in LMI census tracts) to emphasize LMI support. The rule also addresses the small bank exemption ($500 million threshold), performance standards, and data collection burden concerns raised in comments. The OCC stated the rule takes a more incremental approach to reform that accounts for differences among categories of institutions subject to the CRA.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On Dec. 11, 2024, Truist Financial Corporation (NYSE: TFC) announced it received the highest possible overall rating of "Outstanding" from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) for its most recent Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) examination period, covering 2020-2022. The CRA encourages banks to help meet credit needs of communities they operate in, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods.

Key achievements during the examination period (Jan. 1, 2020 – Dec. 31, 2022):
- Made 845,332 home mortgage, small business, and small farm loans totaling $151.9 billion to support LMI individuals and geographies.
- Originated 7,174 community development loans totaling $16.1 billion (a 304.6% increase in loan count and 154.7% increase in dollars from the prior 2017-2019 exam period).
- Delivered 6,143 qualified investments totaling $5.8 billion (up from $1.8 billion in the prior period), including $4.4 billion supporting affordable housing.
- Delivered 12,938 community development service activities, a 55.2% increase from 8,334 in the prior exam period.

COVID-19 pandemic response achievements:
- Truist was the fourth-largest lender by dollars in the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), funding approximately $16.3 billion across nearly 120,000 loans to assist ~80,000 small business clients and support over 2 million jobs.
- Launched the Truist Cares initiative in March 2020, providing more than $50 million in aid.
- Provided approximately 900,000 COVID-19 related payment relief accommodations between March 2020 and December 2021, impacting ~$50 billion in loan balances.

Truist completed its three-year $60 billion Community Benefits Plan (from its 2019 merger of equals), delivering $75.4 billion in combined lending, investing, and philanthropic activities—exceeding the target. Truist also recently announced "Truist Cares for Western North Carolina," a three-year, $725 million commitment to support hurricane recovery in areas impacted by Hurricane Helene.

Truist is headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, and is a top-10 commercial bank with total assets of $523 billion as of Sept. 30, 2024.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: Analysis of the OCC's Final CRA Rule - NCRC ---
URL: https://ncrc.org/analysis-of-the-occs-final-cra-rule

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is NCRC's (National Community Reinvestment Coalition) analysis and critique of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) final Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rule, released on May 20. NCRC argues the final rule weakens CRA enforcement and will result in fewer loans, investments, and services for low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

Key criticisms across the rule's components:

**What Activities Count:** The rule significantly dilutes the focus on LMI communities by: adding essential infrastructure and community facilities (roads, bridges, mass transit, hospitals) to the definition of community development; allowing activities to "partially benefit" (less than majority of dollars) LMI people rather than requiring primary (50%+) benefit—with no floor set by OCC (NCRC recommends a 30% floor); and adding "CRA deserts" as discretionary underserved areas that banks can self-designate through a secretive, closed-off process, with qualified activities there multiplied by up to four. The OCC retained arbitrary multipliers (e.g., doubling certain community development loans, quadrupling "innovative and complex" activities deemed so subjectively by examiners), which NCRC says introduce grade inflation and subjectivity. The CRA illustrative list process remains ad hoc, with additions made annually and public notice/comment only once every five years; examples added without proposal include loans for workforce housing near a multinational's warehouse and tax increment bonds that can finance gentrification.

**How It Counts:** The CRA evaluation measure—a ratio of CRA activities divided by bank deposits—remains the dominant, determinative factor on exams. OCC scrapped its proposed thresholds (6% for Satisfactory, 11% for Outstanding) and retail test thresholds (e.g., 65%) admitting it lacked data to support them, leaving them for future rulemaking—NCRC calls this irresponsible and a "giant leap into subjectivity." The final rule eliminates the large bank service test and any evaluation of bank deposit accounts for LMI customers (NCRC notes current exams do quantify accounts), devalues branches (a typical bank's branch distribution contributes only ~0.56 to the numerator), and quantifies all types of volunteering. The retail lending test becomes pass/fail (counting far less than the current 50% weight), and consumer lending excludes overdrafts and credit cards. Large banks must now pass in 80% of assessment areas (up from 50%), but if tests remain easy this won't increase rigor.

**Where It Counts:** New deposit-based assessment areas are based on deposits (a bank must gather >50% of deposits outside branches and >5% from an area), but lack of data makes impacts unclear. Banks may designate areas larger than the smallest 5%-deposit area, giving discretion to neglect smaller needier areas. Credit is allowed for activities outside AAs regardless of AA performance, encouraging large national deals over local ones.

**Public Input/Accountability:** Public comments are narrowed to local needs/opportunities rather than bank CRA performance; community development data is only reported at total bank level (not census tract/county), frustrating public oversight; exams become bank-driven (banks calculate their own ratings for examiners to verify); Outstanding-rated banks are examined only once every five years; affiliates are generally excluded from exams unless acting as "intermediaries"; and the small bank threshold was raised to $600 million (reclassifying ~181 intermediate small banks), with ~89% of OCC banks now exempt from the new exams.

NCRC concludes the rule "signals an abrogation of the OCC's statutory responsibilities" and "must be rescinded or overturned."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It will lessen the public accountability of banks to their communities by enacting performance measures on CRA exams that will be complex and opaque, while at the same time over-simplifying how to measure a bank's responsiveness to local needs. The result will be significantly fewer loans, investments and services to low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities most in need of more credit and capital."

"The OCC did not place a floor on a partial benefit... However, without a floor, the temptation is too great since 5% of an interstate bridge is a large dollar amount... At the very least, the OCC should have specified a floor such as 30% of the benefit must be for LMI people and neighborhoods."

"The OCC scrapped the thresholds for its CRA evaluation measure, admitting it does not have data to support this core part of its proposal... the final rule does not contain benchmarks for the CRA evaluation measure, a specific CD minimum, or thresholds for the retail lending distribution tests."

"Moving to the OCC's approach will greatly diminish the importance of bank branches in CRA compliance, which will likely lead to significant branch loss in LMI communities and a decrease in lending as documented in NCRC's comment letter."

"In sum, this final rule signals an abrogation of the OCC's statutory responsibilities to ensure that banks continually and affirmatively respond to credit needs of LMI borrowers and in LMI communities. It must be rescinded or overturned."
</key_excerpts>

NCRC argues the final rule weakens CRA enforcement and will result in fewer loans, investments, and services for low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities.

Key criticisms across the rule's components:

**What Activities Count:** The rule significantly dilutes the focus on LMI communities by: adding essential infrastructure and community facilities (roads, bridges, mass transit, hospitals) to the definition of community development; allowing activities to "partially benefit" (less than majority of dollars) LMI people rather than requiring primary (50%+) benefit—with no floor set by OCC (NCRC recommends a 30% floor); and adding "CRA deserts" as discretionary underserved areas that banks can self-designate through a secretive, closed-off process, with qualified activities there multiplied by up to four. The OCC retained arbitrary multipliers (e.g., doubling certain community development loans, quadrupling "innovative and complex" activities deemed so subjectively by examiners), which NCRC says introduce grade inflation and subjectivity. The CRA illustrative list process remains ad hoc, with additions made annually and public notice/comment only once every five years; examples added without proposal include loans for workforce housing near a multinational's warehouse and tax increment bonds that can finance gentrification.

**How It Counts:** The CRA evaluation measure—a ratio of CRA activities divided by bank deposits—remains the dominant, determinative factor on exams. OCC scrapped its proposed thresholds (6% for Satisfactory, 11% for Outstanding) and retail test thresholds (e.g., 65%) admitting it lacked data to support them, leaving them for future rulemaking—NCRC calls this irresponsible and a "giant leap into subjectivity." The final rule eliminates the large bank service test and any evaluation of bank deposit accounts for LMI customers (NCRC notes current exams do quantify accounts), devalues branches (a typical bank's branch distribution contributes only ~0.56 to the numerator), and quantifies all types of volunteering. The retail lending test becomes pass/fail (counting far less than the current 50% weight), and consumer lending excludes overdrafts and credit cards. Large banks must now pass in 80% of assessment areas (up from 50%), but if tests remain easy this won't increase rigor.

**Where It Counts:** New deposit-based assessment areas are based on deposits (a bank must gather >50% of deposits outside branches and >5% from an area), but lack of data makes impacts unclear. Banks may designate areas larger than the smallest 5%-deposit area, giving discretion to neglect smaller needier areas. Credit is allowed for activities outside AAs regardless of AA performance, encouraging large national deals over local ones.

**Public Input/Accountability:** Public comments are narrowed to local needs/opportunities rather than bank CRA performance; community development data is only reported at total bank level (not census tract/county), frustrating public oversight; exams become bank-driven (banks calculate their own ratings for examiners to verify); Outstanding-rated banks are examined only once every five years; affiliates are generally excluded from exams unless acting as "intermediaries"; and the small bank threshold was raised to $600 million (reclassifying ~181 intermediate small banks), with ~89% of OCC banks now exempt from the new exams.

NCRC concludes the rule "signals an abrogation of the OCC's statutory responsibilities" and "must be rescinded or overturned."
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: OCC and FDIC Propose Targeted Revisions to CRA Regulations ---
URL: https://www.sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2026/August/OCC-FDIC-Propose-Targeted-Revisions-CRA-Regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 31, 2026, the OCC and FDIC jointly issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (the "CRA Proposal") to amend their regulations implementing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The Federal Reserve Board did not join the proposal. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

**Background:** The CRA was enacted in 1977 to encourage banks to help meet credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods. The current CRA rule is based on interagency regulations from 1995. In October 2023, the agencies adopted a substantially revised 2023 CRA Rule, which was challenged by banking trade associations and preliminarily enjoined by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas in March 2024 before taking effect. In July 2025, the agencies proposed rescinding the 2023 CRA Rule, but the OCC and FDIC instead issued this new CRA Proposal. The Board did not participate and its next steps remain unclear, raising the possibility of differing CRA requirements across federal banking agencies.

**Key Changes in the CRA Proposal:**

1. **Bank Size Categories:** Raises the small bank threshold to $1 billion or less (up from $412 million), creates a new "intermediate bank" category for banks between $1 billion and $10 billion, and designates "large banks" as those over $10 billion (up from $1.649 billion). Based on 2024-2025 Call Report data, approximately 636 of 3,577 supervised banks would be intermediate banks and ~86 would be large banks. The percentage of large banks would decrease from 13.4% to 2.4%.

2. **Revised Ratings for Intermediate Banks:** An intermediate bank would need only a "satisfactory" rating on the lending test (not both lending and community development tests) to receive an overall "satisfactory" rating.

3. **Retained Assessment Area Framework:** The proposal retains the Current CRA Rule's assessment area delineation (facility-based), unlike the 2023 CRA Rule which required separate retail lending assessment areas.

4. **Revised Lending Tests:** Lending tests would be limited to "major product lines" (consumer, home mortgage, small business, small farm loans), with two proposed options for determining major product lines. Consumer lending would be a major product line if it constitutes a majority of retail lending by both dollar amount and loan count. The agencies are considering eliminating the separate limited purpose bank category. 30 loans generally would be considered sufficient for meaningful assessment of lending performance.

5. **Service Test:** The retail banking services criterion under the large bank service test would be limited to credit services only, eliminating consideration of deposit products (consistent with the Texas district court ruling that the CRA does not authorize assessing deposit products).

6. **Community Development Clarifications:** Would clarify definitions for affordable housing (including both subsidized and unsubsidized), codify guidance on distressed/underserved tracts, provide lists of community services (recharacterized as "civic assistance"), define three categories of economic development, and add Tribal/native lands and government-targeted redevelopment areas to revitalization/stabilization categories.

7. **Geographic Flexibility:** Community development activities outside assessment areas would be eligible for consideration only after a bank demonstrates adequate in-assessment-area activity. Two options proposed: (1) quantitative thresholds (large banks: 0.625% of tier 1 capital to CD loans and 0.625% to CD investments/grants; intermediate/wholesale/limited purpose banks: 1.25%), or (2) qualitative determination based on the "low satisfactory" performance level.

8. **Community Development Grants:** Would require written commitments on qualifying use of proceeds, documentation requirements, and limit consideration to grants where recipient indirect costs do not exceed 15%.

9. **Strategic Plans:** Would clarify measurable goal requirements (performance measure + performance level), permit preliminary agency feedback, require written notice of technical completeness, and deem technically complete plans approved if the agency does not act within 60 days.

10. **Illegal Credit Practices:** Two options proposed—considering only violations cited in public enforcement actions, or also considering nonpublic enforcement actions (generally codifying current practice).

11. **Public File:** Would require public files to be available on the bank's website rather than physical copies, and revise required branch services lists to cover "credit products" rather than "loan and deposit products."

**Implications:** The proposal would significantly reduce burden for banks in the new intermediate category (no longer subject to large bank investment/service tests or related data requirements). Banks would need to reassess community development grant programs, geographic flexibility eligibility, and major product line methodologies. The Federal Reserve's non-participation could create differing CRA requirements depending on a bank's charter type, potentially influencing chartering decisions.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: CBA Comments to OCC and FDIC on CRA NPR - consumerbankers.com ---
URL: https://consumerbankers.com/comment-letter/cba-comments-to-occ-and-fdic-on-cra-npr

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comment letter from the Consumer Bankers Association (CBA) submitted to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in response to their Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) on the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Regulations. The letter was prepared by Stephen Congdon of Buckley LLP.

**Key Position:** CBA supports the goals of the CRA and acknowledges banks have an affirmative obligation to help meet the credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) areas. However, CBA has significant concerns about several elements of the proposed NPR framework and proposes alternative approaches.

**Main Concerns with the NPR:**
1. **CRA Evaluation Measure (the "Measure"):** The proposed metric divides eligible activities by deposits, shifting focus from the number of LMI loans originated to the aggregate dollar volume of LMI loans outstanding. This imposes substantial regulatory burdens requiring new data systems and fails to give sufficient credit to LMI mortgage and small business loan programs that don't produce large dollar volumes.
2. **Mandatory consumer lending inclusion:** Would significantly expand a bank's affirmative CRA obligations and add regulatory burdens.
3. **Deposit-based assessment areas:** Would inflame (not reduce) "hot spots" since Internet deposits largely come from population centers, and would not help CRA deserts (rural areas, distressed communities, Indian country) since these areas don't generate enough deposits to qualify.
4. **Balance sheet-based metrics:** Would be a regulatory disincentive for LMI mortgages and small business loans and skew evaluations geographically toward high-cost areas.
5. **Lack of sufficient data:** Insufficient relevant data exists for banks to assess the NPR's impact, including the proposed 11%/6%/3% rating thresholds.
6. **Call Report data challenges:** Information required for data collection is not easily obtainable from Call Reports (e.g., loan balances by LMI census tracts, geographic location of borrowers/depositors).
7. **Too fluid rating thresholds:** Frequent adjustments would create inconsistent examinations and unlevel playing fields.

**CBA's Proposed Alternative – "Reinvestment Redistribution":**
- Maintains existing facility-based assessment areas only
- Treats Internet deposits as sourced from the broad U.S. "cyber-community" rather than any particular geography
- Retains an origination-based approach (unit basis for retail lending, not balance sheet)
- Preserves optional consumer loan reporting
- Excludes corporate deposits from denominators (along with brokered deposits)
- Provides weighted incentives for CRA qualifying activities in banking deserts
- Uses two metrics: (1) assessment area qualified retail lending on a unit basis for all retail banks, and (2) dollar volume of CD activity as a percentage of non-corporate, non-brokered domestic retail deposits for large/wholesale/limited purpose banks
- Allows CRA obligations based on Internet deposits to be fulfilled with qualifying activities anywhere

**Recommendations:**
- The OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve should issue a uniform CRA rule (the Federal Reserve was absent from this NPR)
- Rating thresholds should be set after collecting two years of bank data under the new requirements
- Thresholds should be durable and adjusted infrequently
- A safe harbor (similar to the CFPB's 2018 HMDA grace period) should be provided for data reporting

Federal banking regulators sharply downgraded Wells Fargo’s score on the Community Reinvestment Act, citing a pattern of violations that go well beyond the sales scandal that has badly damaged the firm’s reputation.

Processing Content

In a report released Tuesday, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency found that the San Francisco-based bank “needs to improve” its compliance with the 1977 law, which requires banks to meet the credit needs of the communities in which they operate.

Previously, Wells Fargo had an “outstanding” rating from the OCC, so its downgrade was substantial.

The new rating, which puts Wells in the bottom tier of banks, is not only a black eye in terms of public perception. It could also have substantial negative consequences for the megabank’s ability to grow and compete for business.

A Wells Fargo & Co. sign sits on display outside the company's offices in San Francisco, California, U.S., on Tuesday, April 27, 2010. Wells Fargo & Co., the fourth-largest U.S. bank by assets and deposits, may raise its dividend once capital levels satisfy regulators and if the economic recovery continues, said Chief Executive Officer John Stumpf. Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg

“The findings reflect an extensive and pervasive pattern and practice of violations across multiple lines of business within the bank, resulting in significant harm to large numbers of consumers,” the OCC stated.

“The bank failed to implement an effective compliance and risk management program designed to properly prevent, identify and correct violations. Further, bank management instituted policies, procedures and performance standards that contributed to several of the violations for which evidence has been identified.”

The report cited 10 legal cases that show evidence of discrimination or illegal credit practices at Wells. Among them is the company’s recent blockbuster $190 million settlement with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau over the creation of roughly 2 million fake accounts by more than 5,000 branch employees.

Also included on the list is an agreement by Wells in 2012 to pay $175 million to settle charges with the Department of Justice that the company discriminated against black and Hispanic mortgage borrowers during the housing boom by steering them into costly subprime loans.

Additionally, the report cited a 2011 settlement with the Federal Reserve, which accused Wells of falsifying mortgage applications and steering prime borrowers into higher-rate subprime loans in the run-up to the financial meltdown.

The cases demonstrate that Wells failed to effectively monitor its various businesses for discrimination and other legal risks, the OCC said in its report, describing the violations as “egregious.”

The exam covered 2009 through 2012, though the OCC’s new report also considered more recent regulatory actions against the bank.

Wells Fargo noted in a securities filing Tuesday that the low rating imposes a wide range of regulatory restrictions.

For example, the score could hurt the bank’s ability to engage in certain nonbank mergers and acquisitions. In addition, regulators consider CRA performance when reviewing applications to establish branches and in considering proposed bank mergers and acquisitions.

Wells also said that the low rating could affect its relationships with states, municipalities and other public agencies, to the extent that those entities are restricted from doing business with banks that score poorly.

In a press release Tuesday, Wells said that the new report marks the first time since 1994, when exam results were first publicly disclosed, that it received any score other than “outstanding” for its overall compliance with the Community Reinvestment Act.

“We are disappointed with this rating given Wells Fargo’s strong track record of lending to, investing in and providing service to low- and moderate-income communities,” CEO Tim Sloan said in the press release.

Sloan also indicated that Wells will seek to get its score revised upward as quickly as possible.

“With more than four years having passed since the end of our last CRA evaluation period, Wells Fargo intends to ask the OCC to accelerate the timing of its next exam so that we may continue to serve most effectively the low-and moderate-income communities in which we operate,” he stated.

More than 95% of banks receive at least a “satisfactory” rating on their exams, the California Reinvestment Coalition said Tuesday.

“This should be a wake-up call to the board of directors at Wells that the status quo isn’t working, that regulators like the OCC expect better, and that the bank has a long road ahead of it in repairing trust with its customers and with communities,” Paulina Gonzalez, the California group’s executive director, said in a press release.

The steep downgrade came despite the fact that Wells Fargo scored well on several components of the exam.

The $1.9 trillion-asset bank received an “outstanding” score on the regulators’ lending test, which looks partly at banks’ provision of credit to borrowers with low incomes, as well as on the investment test, which considers banks’ community development efforts.

Wells Fargo received a “high satisfactory” score on the regulators’ service test, which evaluates whether banks are operating branches in places where people with low incomes live.

args.summary:
On March 28, 2017, federal banking regulators (the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency) sharply downgraded Wells Fargo's Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rating from "outstanding" to "needs to improve," placing the bank in the bottom tier of institutions. This was the first time since 1994 (when exam results were first publicly disclosed) that Wells Fargo received anything other than an "outstanding" rating.

The downgrade was based on an extensive pattern of violations across multiple business lines, going well beyond the bank's well-publicized sales scandal. The OCC report cited 10 legal cases demonstrating discrimination or illegal credit practices, including:
- The $190 million settlement with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau over approximately 2 million fake accounts created by more than 5,000 branch employees
- A 2012 $175 million settlement with the Department of Justice over discrimination against Black and Hispanic mortgage borrowers who were steered into costly subprime loans during the housing boom
- A 2011 settlement with the Federal Reserve over falsifying mortgage applications and steering prime borrowers into higher-rate subprime loans

The exam covered 2009-2012, though more recent regulatory actions were also considered. The OCC described the violations as "egregious" and stated the bank "failed to implement an effective compliance and risk management program designed to properly prevent, identify and correct violations."

The low rating imposes significant regulatory restrictions, potentially hampering Wells Fargo's ability to:
- Engage in certain nonbank mergers and acquisitions
- Establish new branches (regulators consider CRA performance in such applications)
- Maintain relationships with states, municipalities, and public agencies that restrict doing business with poorly-rated banks

Despite the overall downgrade, Wells Fargo (a $1.9 trillion-asset bank) scored "outstanding" on the lending and investment tests and "high satisfactory" on the service test. CEO Tim Sloan expressed disappointment, noting the bank's "strong track record of lending to, investing in and providing service to low- and moderate-income communities," and said the bank intends to ask the OCC to accelerate the timing of its next exam. The California Reinvestment Coalition noted that more than 95% of banks receive at least a "satisfactory" rating, with executive director Paulina Gonzalez calling the downgrade "a wake-up call to the board of directors at Wells."
args.key_excerpts: "The findings reflect an extensive and pervasive pattern and practice of violations across multiple lines of business within the bank, resulting in significant harm to large numbers of consumers," the OCC stated. "The bank failed to implement an effective compliance and risk management program designed to properly prevent, identify and correct violations. Further, bank management instituted policies, procedures and performance standards that contributed to several of the violations for which evidence has been identified.", "We are disappointed with this rating given Wells Fargo's strong track record of lending to, investing in and providing service to low- and moderate-income communities," CEO Tim Sloan said in the press release., "With more than four years having passed since the end of our last CRA evaluation period, Wells Fargo intends to ask the OCC to accelerate the timing of its next exam so that we may continue to serve most effectively the low-and moderate-income communities in which we operate," he stated., "This should be a wake-up call to the board of directors at Wells that the status quo isn't working, that regulators like the OCC expect better, and that the bank has a long road ahead of it in repairing trust with its customers and with communities," Paulina Gonzalez, the California group's executive director, said in a press release.

This is Zions Bancorporation, National Association's Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024. The company is incorporated in the United States (IRS Employer Identification Number 87-0189025) with principal executive offices at One South Main, Salt Lake City, Utah 84133-1109.

**Trading Symbols:** Common Stock (ZION) and Depositary Shares representing Series A Floating-Rate Non-Cumulative Perpetual Preferred Stock (ZIONP) are both registered on The NASDAQ Stock Market LLC.

**Capital Position (December 31, 2024):** The company exceeded all minimum capital requirements and "well capitalized" thresholds. CET1 to risk-weighted assets was 10.9% (vs. 7.0% requirement with buffer), Tier 1 risk-based capital was 11.0% (vs. 8.5%), Total risk-based capital was 13.3% (vs. 10.5%), and Tier 1 leverage was 8.3% (vs. 4.0%).

**Share Repurchases:** In 2024, the bank repurchased 900,725 common shares at an average price of $39.53, with 890,167 purchased in Q1 as part of publicly announced plans.

**Financial Highlights (2024 vs. 2023):**
- Net interest income: $2,430M (flat vs. $2,438M)
- Noninterest income: $700M (+3%, from $677M)
- Total net revenue: $3,130M
- Provision for credit losses: $72M (down 45% from $132M)
- Noninterest expense: $2,046M (down 2% from $2,097M)
- Net income: $784M (+15% from $680M)
- Net earnings applicable to common shareholders: $737M (+14% from $648M)
- Diluted EPS: $4.95 (up from $4.35)
- Tangible book value at year-end: $33.85 (up 20% from $28.30)
- Market price end of year: $54.25 (up from $43.87)
- Assets: $88,775M; Loans: $59,410M; Deposits: $76,223M
- Common equity: $6,058M

**Performance Ratios (2024):** Return on average assets 0.88%, return on average common equity 13.1%, return on average tangible common equity 16.2%, net interest margin 3.00%, net charge-offs to average loans 0.10%, total allowance for credit losses to loans 1.25%, efficiency ratio 64.2%.

**Capital Ratios at Year-End (2024):** CET1 capital 10.9%, Tier 1 leverage 8.3%, tangible common equity 5.7%.

**Interest Rate Analysis:** Average yield on total interest-earning assets was 5.26% in 2024 (vs. 4.86% in 2023), cost of interest-bearing liabilities was 3.32% (vs. 2.91%). Total cost of deposits was 2.06% (vs. 1.46%).

**Noninterest Income Breakdown (2024):** Commercial account fees $182M, capital markets fees $110M (up 36%), card fees $96M, loan-related fees $70M, retail/business banking fees $67M, wealth management fees $58M.

**Noninterest Expense (2024):** Salaries and employee benefits $1,287M, technology/telecom/information processing $260M, deposit insurance and regulatory expense $91M (down 46% from $169M), occupancy and equipment $161M. Total technology spend was $466M. Full-time equivalent employees: 9,406 (down 3% from 9,679).

**Stock Performance (cumulative, indexed to 100 in 2019):** Zions 124.1, KBW Regional Bank Index 131.0, S&P 500 196.8, S&P MidCap 400 163.1 for 2024.

**Taxes:** Income before income taxes $1,012M, income tax expense $228M, effective tax rate 22.5% (vs. 23.3% in 2023).

**Dividends:** Dividends declared per common share were $1.66 (up 1% from $1.64), with a common dividend payout ratio of 33.6%.

SALT LAKE CITY, Oct. 20, 2025 /PRNewswire/ -- Zions Bancorporation, N.A. (NASDAQ: [ZION](#financial-modal)) ("Zions" or "the Bank") today reported net earnings applicable to common shareholders for the third quarter of 2025 of $221 million, or $1.48 per diluted common share, compared with net earnings applicable to common shareholders of $204 million, or $1.37 per diluted common share, for the third quarter of 2024, and net earnings applicable to common shareholders of $243 million, or $1.63 per diluted common share, for the second quarter of 2025.

Harris H. Simmons, Chairman and CEO of Zions Bancorporation, commented, "We're pleased with the Company's core earnings, which included 14% growth in pre-provision net revenue over the prior year period, and 18% on an adjusted basis. The net interest margin increased 25 basis points over the prior year period, while customer-related noninterest income, adjusted for the net credit valuation adjustment, grew 8%. Although loans contracted at a 3% annualized linked-quarter rate in the quarter, deposits, excluding brokered deposits, grew at an annualized rate of 7%. Over the past year, tangible book value per share grew 17%."

Mr. Simmons continued, "The quarter's credit results were marred by a $50 million charge-off, and a $10 million specific reserve established against the approximate remaining balance, arising from loans to two related companies in which apparent irregularities and misrepresentations were recently detected. Legal action has been initiated to pursue recovery of the amounts owed from guarantors of the credits. Excluding this loss, remaining net charge-offs were very benign at $6 million, or 4 basis points of average loans on an annualized basis."

For the full version of the Bank's 2025 third quarter earnings release, including financial schedules, please visit www.[zionsbancorporation.com](http://zionsbancorporation.com/).

**Supplemental Presentation and Conference Call**

Zions has posted a supplemental presentation to its website, which will be used to discuss the third quarter results at 5:30 p.m. ET on October 20, 2025. Media representatives, analysts, investors, and the public are invited to join this discussion by calling (877) 709-8150 (domestic and international) and using the meeting number 13756405, or via on-demand webcast. A link to the webcast will be available on the Zions Bancorporation website at [www.zionsbancorporation.com](https://www.zionsbancorporation.com/). The webcast of the conference call will also be archived and available for 30 days.

**About Zions Bancorporation, N.A.**

Zions Bancorporation, N.A. is one of the nation's premier financial services companies with annual net revenue of $3.1 billion in 2024, and total assets of approximately $89 billion at December 31, 2024. Zions operates under local management teams and distinct brands in 11 western states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Texas, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming. The Bank is a consistent recipient of national and state-wide customer survey awards in small- and middle-market banking, as well as a leader in public finance advisory services and Small Business Administration lending. In addition, Zions is included in the S&P MidCap 400 and NASDAQ Financial 100 indices. Investor information and links to local banking brands can be accessed at [www.zionsbancorporation.com](https://www.zionsbancorporation.com/).

The company posted net earnings applicable to common shareholders of $221 million, or $1.48 per diluted common share for Q3 2025, compared to $204 million ($1.37 per share) in Q3 2024 and $243 million ($1.63 per share) in Q2 2025.

Key highlights from CEO Harris H. Simmons:
- Pre-provision net revenue grew 14% over the prior year period (18% on an adjusted basis)
- Net interest margin increased 25 basis points year-over-year
- Customer-related noninterest income, adjusted for net credit valuation adjustment, grew 8%
- Loans contracted at a 3% annualized linked-quarter rate, while deposits (excluding brokered) grew at a 7% annualized rate
- Tangible book value per share grew 17% over the past year

Credit results were impacted by a $50 million charge-off and a $10 million specific reserve related to loans to two related companies where irregularities and misrepresentations were detected. Legal action has been initiated against guarantors. Excluding this loss, remaining net charge-offs were very benign at $6 million (4 basis points of average loans on an annualized basis).

The company hosted a conference call and webcast on October 20, 2025 at 5:30 p.m. ET (call number: 877-709-8150, meeting number 13756405). The webcast is archived for 30 days.

About the company: Zions Bancorporation is a premier financial services company with annual net revenue of $3.1 billion in 2024 and total assets of approximately $89 billion at December 31, 2024. It operates under local management teams and distinct brands in 11 western states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Texas, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming). Zions is included in the S&P MidCap 400 and NASDAQ Financial 100 indices.

args.summary:
This is an official page from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) website's Banker Resource Center providing the Monthly List of Banks Examined for CRA (Community Reinvestment Act) Compliance. The page serves as an index of downloadable monthly lists of banks that were examined for CRA compliance, organized by year.

The lists are categorized by year and cover the following periods:
- 2026: Monthly lists available from January through August 2026
- 2025: Monthly lists available from January through December 2025
- 2024: Monthly lists available from January through December 2024
- 2023: Monthly lists available from January through December 2023
- 2022: Monthly lists available from January through December 2022
- 2021: Monthly lists available from January through December 2021
- 2020: Monthly lists available from January through December 2020
- 2019: Monthly lists available from January through December 2019
- 2018: Monthly lists available from January through December 2018
- 2017: Monthly lists available from January through December 2017

Additionally, there is an "Older Reports" section linking to archived FDIC records covering the period 1996-2016 via the FDIC archive (archive.fdic.gov). The page was last updated on August 5, 2026. The lists are published monthly and provide documentation of banks examined for compliance with the Community Reinvestment Act.

# Community Reinvestment Act

The [Community Reinvestment Act (CRA)](http://www.federalreserve.gov/communitydev/cra_about.htm) is intended to encourage depository institutions to help meet the credit needs of the communities in which they operate, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations. It was enacted by Congress in 1977 ([12 U.S.C. 2901](https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/granule/USCODE-2011-title12/USCODE-2011-title12-chap30-sec2901)) and is implemented by [Regulation BB (12 CFR 228)](https://www.federalreserve.gov/bankinforeg/regbbcg.htm).

The CRA requires that each depository institution’s record in helping meet the credit needs of its entire community be evaluated periodically by the appropriate federal financial supervisory agency. A bank’s CRA performance record is taken into account when considering an institution’s application for deposit facilities.

## How does the CRA work?

The regulators evaluate a bank’s performance in its assessment areas. Assessment areas are geographic areas defined by the bank where the bank maintains deposit-taking facilities, such as branches or ATMs. CRA evaluations focus on how well banks serve their assessment areas, particularly LMI neighborhoods within their assessment areas.

In evaluating a bank’s CRA performance, the agencies consider three main criteria: (1) the bank’s lending to LMI individuals, businesses, and geographies; (2) the bank’s investment in community development projects; and (3) the banking services (including branch locations and online banking) and community development services offered by the bank. The number of criteria vary by bank size, for example, with smaller banks evaluated just on retail lending.

Public involvement is also a key component of the CRA. Community organizations and individuals are encouraged to provide input to the agencies during the CRA evaluation process, which informs the evaluations, and allows communities to help shape their financial future.

## Why is the CRA important?

The CRA plays a critical role in building stronger communities. For example, banks may receive CRA credit for:

*   Lending to, and investing in, projects that create affordable housing in LMI areas;
*   Making loans to LMI individuals and in LMI areas to support homeownership;
*   Lending to small business owners who may rely on financing to grow their business, create jobs, and contribute to local economic development; and
*   Providing access to branches, ATMs, and retail banking services to LMI individuals and in LMI areas.

In all, the CRA remains a vital tool to help meet the credit needs of communities across the nation.

This webpage from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (clevelandfed.org) covers the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) and provides an overview of the Cleveland Fed's broader activities, resources, and organizational structure.

**Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Core Content:**
- The CRA is intended to encourage depository institutions to help meet the credit needs of the communities in which they operate, including low- and moderate-income (LMI) neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations.
- It was enacted by Congress in 1977 (12 U.S.C. 2901) and is implemented by Regulation BB (12 CFR 228).
- Each depository institution's record is evaluated periodically by the appropriate federal financial supervisory agency, and a bank's CRA performance record is considered when applying for deposit facilities.
- Regulators evaluate a bank's performance in its assessment areas (geographic areas where the bank maintains deposit-taking facilities like branches or ATMs), focusing particularly on LMI neighborhoods.
- Three main evaluation criteria: (1) lending to LMI individuals, businesses, and geographies; (2) investment in community development projects; (3) banking services (branches, online banking) and community development services. The number of criteria varies by bank size, with smaller banks evaluated only on retail lending.
- Public involvement is a key component; community organizations and individuals are encouraged to provide input during evaluations.
- Banks may receive CRA credit for lending/investing in affordable housing in LMI areas, making loans to LMI individuals for homeownership, lending to small business owners, and providing access to branches, ATMs, and retail banking services in LMI areas.

**CRA Evaluation Resources:**
- Performance evaluations of state member banks examined by the Federal Reserve (including the Cleveland Fed) are available on the Board's performance evaluation database; evaluations for banks supervised by FDIC and OCC are also available.
- Interagency CRA information is available from the FFIEC.
- An interactive timeline of CRA history is available from fedcommunities.org.

**Cleveland Fed Organizational Overview:**
- The Cleveland Fed serves the Fourth Federal Reserve District, spanning Ohio and parts of Pennsylvania, West Virginia, and Kentucky.
- Offices located in Cleveland (1455 East 6th Street, OH), Cincinnati (150 East Fourth Street, OH), and Pittsburgh (One Oxford Centre, 301 Grant Street, PA).
- Key functions include: Banking Supervision (promoting safe and sound banking and consumer protection compliance), Credit Risk (providing liquidity to the banking system), and Statistics and Analysis (collecting financial and survey data).
- The Community Development team works from Cleveland, Pittsburgh, and Cincinnati to promote economic resilience and mobility of LMI people and communities.
- Major offerings include the Center for Inflation Research, indicators/data (Median CPI, Median PCE Inflation, Inflation Expectations, Inflation Nowcasting, Yield Curve and GDP Growth, Simple Monetary Policy Rules, SORCE, BOTS, Small Business Credit Survey), research publications (Economic Commentaries, Working Papers, Beige Book), and education/financial literacy resources.

City National Bank of Florida Earns "Outstanding" Community Reinvestment Act Rating For 24th Consecutive Year

City National Bank of Florida Earns "Outstanding" Community Reinvestment Act Rating For 24th consecutive Year, Fueled by More than $1.3 Billion in Community Development Loans

**MIAMI, FL — June 27, 2025 —** The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has awarded City National Bank of Florida (CNB) an ‘Outstanding’ rating in its latest performance evaluation. The period covered three years between 2021 and 2024, marking the eighth-straight exam period in which CNB earned an ‘Outstanding’ rating. CNB is currently one of only 7 banks in Florida with the OCC’s highest rating and holds the longest-running streak of Outstanding ratings of any bank in Florida, dating back to 2003.

‍  
During the exam, the OCC analyzed CNB’s performance meeting the credit needs of low-to-moderate income individuals, the bank’s activity deploying capital, and its track record of service in underserved communities. The OCC spotlighted CNB’s extensive efforts to assist its clients and communities particularly in the areas of lending, investments, and community development. All told, CNB originated more than $1.3 billion in community development loans during the exam period.  
‍

“Earning the OCC’s highest CRA rating for 24 straight years reflects CNB’s deep commitment to strengthening communities in Florida and delivering a direct, positive impact in underserved areas,” Vice Chairman and CEO Jorge Gonzalez said. “CNB has been focused on this mission for decades, and we will continue investing heavily in the health and prosperity of our communities in the future.”

‍  
CNB programs which contributed to the Outstanding CRA rating include:

* **CitySmart Mortgage Program**, CNB helped more families achieve the dream of homeownership by enhancing its CitySmart Mortgage Program, which assists borrowers purchasing homes in low- and moderate-income communities.
* **The Down Payment Assistance Program**, in partnership with local governments, has provided critical financial support to families who otherwise may not have been able to purchase a home.
* Through the **CNB Housing Foundation**, CNB has taken a proactive approach to addressing Florida’s affordable housing challenges.
* Partnering with organizations like **Housing United for Broward,** the bank has helped fund new housing developments, including the recently launched Parcview Townhomes in Miramar.
* The **Community Advantage City Line** and SBA 7(a) Loan Program have provided flexible financing solutions to support small businesses and entrepreneurs, helping them access working capital and grow their businesses.

The OCC commended CNB for completing 186 community development loans totaling $1.3 billion during the exam period. By dollar volume, 69.5 percent funded revitalization and stabilization efforts, 14.6 percent funded community services targeted to low-and moderate-income individuals, 9.6 percent of these loans funded affordable housing, and 6.3 percent funded economic development.

Over the past three years, Florida's population has grown by approximately 5 percent. According to the Florida Housing Coalition, in 2024 over 2.4 million low-income Florida households are spent more than 30% of their income toward housing costs, with 1.3 million of these households spending more than 50% of their income on housing, an approximately 14.3% increase of cost-burdened low-income households over a three-year period.

‍  
The Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rating is issued by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) reflecting exceptional efforts in lending, investments, and community development, demonstrating the bank's commitment to supporting economic growth in underserved areas.

## About City National Bank of Florida

City National Bank of Florida (CNB) is the financial institution to which Floridians have turned for more than 75 years. Based in Miami, CNB has a presence across South and Central Florida, with 1,000 employees statewide. With more than $26 billion in assets, CNB is one of the state’s largest financial institutions and one of the nation’s fastest-growing banks. CNB is a subsidiary of Chilean bank Banco de Credito e Inversiones (Bci) and remains a community-centric bank guided by local decision-making, with services including commercial banking, real estate lending, private banking, wealth management, international banking, treasury management, corporate services, commercial real estate, residential mortgages, and a capital markets group which offers loan syndication, specialty finance and capital placement. CNB is rated 5 stars "Superior" by BauerFinancial and has earned an “Outstanding” Community Reinvestment Act rating for its lending in underserved communities for more than 20 consecutive years. The bank has been certified a Great Place to Work ® and has repeatedly been recognized as one of the nation’s “Best Banks to Work For” by American Banker magazine. CNB is Member FDIC.

City National Bank of Florida (CNB) announced on June 27, 2025, that it earned an "Outstanding" Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) rating from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for the 24th consecutive year. This marks the eighth-straight exam period with an 'Outstanding' rating, covering the period between 2021 and 2024. CNB is one of only 7 banks in Florida with the OCC's highest rating and holds the longest-running streak of Outstanding ratings of any bank in Florida, dating back to 2003.

The OCC analyzed CNB's performance in meeting the credit needs of low-to-moderate income individuals, capital deployment activity, and service record in underserved communities. CNB originated more than $1.3 billion in community development loans during the exam period, including 186 community development loans. By dollar volume: 69.5% funded revitalization and stabilization efforts, 14.6% funded community services for low- and moderate-income individuals, 9.6% funded affordable housing, and 6.3% funded economic development.

Programs contributing to the Outstanding rating include: the CitySmart Mortgage Program (assists borrowers in low/moderate-income communities), the Down Payment Assistance Program (in partnership with local governments), the CNB Housing Foundation (addressing Florida's affordable housing challenges), partnerships like Housing United for Broward (including the Parcview Townhomes in Miramar), and the Community Advantage City Line and SBA 7(a) Loan Program (supporting small businesses).

The article also highlights that Florida's population grew ~5% over three years, and according to the Florida Housing Coalition, over 2.4 million low-income Florida households spent more than 30% of income on housing in 2024 (1.3 million spending over 50%), a ~14.3% increase in cost-burdened households.

Vice Chairman and CEO Jorge Gonzalez commented on the achievement. CNB is based in Miami with 1,000 employees, more than $26 billion in assets, and is a subsidiary of Chilean bank Banco de Credito e Inversiones (Bci). CNB has served Florida for over 75 years, is rated 5 stars "Superior" by BauerFinancial, and is certified as a Great Place to Work.

(9) “Commission” means the Financial Services Commission.  (10) “Control,” including the terms “controlling,” “controlled by,” and “under common control with,” means the possession, directly or indirectly, of the power to direct or cause the direction of the management or policies of a person, whether through the ownership of voting securities, by contract, or otherwise. (12)(a) “Dealer” includes, unless otherwise specified, a person, other than an associated person of a dealer, that engages, for all or part of the person’s time, directly or indirectly, as agent or principal in the business of offering, buying, selling, or otherwise dealing or trading in securities issued by another person. (13) “Director” means a person appointed or elected to sit on a board that manages the affairs of a corporation or other organization by electing or exercising control over its officers.  (14) “Federal covered adviser” means a person that is registered or required to be registered under s. 203 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, as amended. (16) “General partner” has the same meaning as in s. 620.1102. The term includes a co-owner or manager of a partnership who has unlimited liability for the partnership’s debts. (18) “Guaranty” means an agreement in writing in which one party either agrees, or holds itself out to the public as agreeing, to pay the indebtedness of another when due, including, without limitation, payments of principal and interest on a bond, debenture, note, or other evidence of indebtedness, without resort by the holder to any other obligor, whether or not such writing expressly states that the person signing is signing as a guarantor. Words of guaranty or equivalent words that otherwise do not specify guaranty of payment create a presumption that payment, rather than collection, is guaranteed by the guarantor. Any guaranty in writing is enforceable notwithstanding any statute of frauds.  (19) “Intermediary” means a person that facilitates through its website the offer or sale of securities of an issuer with a principal place of business in this state.  (20)(a) “Investment adviser” means a person, other than an associated person of an investment adviser or a federal covered adviser, that receives compensation, directly or indirectly, and engages for all or part of the person’s time, directly or indirectly, or through publications or writings, in the business of advising others as to the value of securities or as to the advisability of investments in, purchasing of, or selling of securities.  (b) The term does not include any of the following: 1. A dealer or an associated person of a dealer whose performance of services in paragraph (a) is solely incidental to the conduct of the dealer’s or associated person’s business as a dealer and who does not receive special compensation for those services.  2. A licensed practicing attorney or certified public accountant whose performance of such services is solely incidental to the practice of the attorney’s or accountant’s profession.  3. A bank authorized to do business in this state.  4. A bank holding company as defined in the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended, authorized to do business in this state.  5. A trust company having trust powers, as defined in s. 658.12, which it is authorized to exercise in this state, which trust company renders or performs investment advisory services in a fiduciary capacity incidental to the exercise of its trust powers.  6. A person that renders investment advice exclusively to insurance or investment companies.  7. A person that, during the preceding 12 months, has fewer than six clients who are residents of this state. (21) “Issuer” means a person that proposes to issue, has issued, or shall hereafter issue any security. A person that acts as a promoter for and on behalf of a corporation, trust, partnership, limited liability company, association, or other legal entity of any kind to be formed shall be deemed an issuer.  (22) “Limited liability company” has the same meaning as in s. 605.0102. The term includes a foreign limited liability company as defined in s. 605.0102.  (23) “Limited liability company manager” or “limited liability managing member” means a person who is responsible alone, or in concert with others, for performing the management functions of a limited liability company.  (24) “Limited partner” has the same meaning as in s. 620.1102. The term includes a co-owner of a partnership who has limited liability for the partnership’s debts.  (25) “Offer to sell,” “offer for sale,” or “offer” means an attempt or offer to dispose of, or solicitation of an offer to buy, a security or interest in a security, or an investment or interest in an investment, for value.  (26) “Office” means the Office of Financial Regulation of the commission.  (27) “Partnership” means two or more persons who are the co-owners of a business, including those operating as a foreign limited liability limited partnership, a foreign limited partnership, a limited liability limited partnership, or a limited partnership as those terms are defined in s. 620.1102.  (28) “Predecessor” means a person whose major portion of assets has been acquired directly or indirectly by an issuer.  (29) “Principal” means an executive officer of a corporation, partner of a partnership, sole proprietor of a sole proprietorship, trustee of a trust, or any other person with similar supervisory functions with respect to any organization, whether incorporated or unincorporated.  (30) “Promoter” includes the following: (a) A person that, acting alone or in conjunction with one or more other persons, directly or indirectly takes the initiative in founding and organizing the business or enterprise of an issuer.  (b) A person that, in connection with the founding or organizing of the business or enterprise of an issuer, directly or indirectly receives in consideration of services or property, or both services and property, 10 percent or more of any class of securities of the issuer or 10 percent or more of the proceeds from the sale of any class of securities. However, a person that receives such securities or proceeds either solely as underwriting commissions or solely in connection with property shall not be deemed a promoter if such person does not otherwise take part in founding and organizing the enterprise.  (31) “Qualified institutional buyer” means a qualified institutional buyer, as defined in Securities and Exchange Commission Rule 144A, 17 C.F.R. s. 230.144A(a), under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, or any foreign buyer that satisfies the minimum financial requirements set forth in such rule.  (32) “Sale” or “sell” means a contract of sale or disposition of an investment, security, or interest in a security, for value. With respect to a security or interest in a security, the term does not include preliminary negotiations or agreements between an issuer or any person on whose behalf an offering is to be made and any underwriter or among underwriters who are or are to be in privity of contract with an issuer. Any security given or delivered with, or as a bonus on account of, any purchase of securities or any other thing shall be conclusively presumed to constitute a part of the subject of such purchase and to have been offered and sold for value. Every sale or offer of a warrant or right to purchase or subscribe to another security of the same or another issuer, as well as every sale or offer of a security which gives the holder a present or future right or privilege to convert into another security or another issuer, is considered to include an offer of the other security.  (33) “Security” includes any of the following: (a) A note.  (b) A stock.  (c) A treasury stock.  (d) A bond.  (e) A debenture.  (f) An evidence of indebtedness.  (g) A certificate of deposit.  (h) A certificate of deposit for a security.  (i) A certificate of interest or participation.  (j) A whiskey warehouse receipt or other commodity warehouse receipt.  (k) A certificate of interest in a profit-sharing agreement or the right to participate therein.  (l) A certificate of interest in an oil, gas, petroleum, mineral, or mining title or lease or the right to participate therein.  (m) A collateral trust certificate.  (n) A reorganization certificate.  (o) A preorganization subscription.  (p) A transferable share.  (q) An investment contract.  (r) A beneficial interest in title to property, profits, or earnings.  (s) An interest in or under a profit-sharing or participation agreement or scheme.  (t) An option contract that entitles the holder to purchase or sell a given amount of the underlying security at a fixed price within a specified period of time.  (u) Any other instrument commonly known as a security, including an interim or temporary bond, debenture, note, or certificate.  (v) A receipt for a security, or for subscription to a security, or a right to subscribe to or purchase any security.  (w) A viatical settlement investment.  (34) “Trust” has the same meaning as in s. 731.201.  (35) “Underwriter” means a person that has purchased from an issuer or an affiliate of an issuer with a view to, or offers or sells for an issuer or an affiliate of an issuer in connection with, the distribution of any security, or participates or has a direct or indirect participation in any such undertaking, or participates or has a participation in the direct or indirect underwriting of any such undertaking; except that a person is presumed not to be an underwriter with respect to any security which it has owned beneficially for at least 1 year; and, further, a dealer is not considered an underwriter with respect to any securities which do not represent part of an unsold allotment to or subscription by the dealer as a participant in the distribution of such securities by the issuer or an affiliate of the issuer; and, further, in the case of securities acquired on the conversion of another security without payment of additional consideration, the length of time such securities have been beneficially owned by a person includes the period during which the convertible security was beneficially owned and the period during which the security acquired on conversion has been beneficially owned.  (36) “Viatical settlement investment” means an agreement for the purchase, sale, assignment, transfer, devise, or bequest of all or any portion of a legal or equitable interest in a viaticated policy as defined in chapter 626. This webpage is the official Florida Statutes (2025) Chapter 517, titled "Securities Transactions," from the Florida Legislature's official website (leg.state.fl.us). The chapter is formally known as the "Florida Securities and Investor Protection Act" (Section 517.011).

**Key Sections Preserved:**

**Section 517.021 (Definitions):** Provides extensive statutory definitions for securities law terms including "accredited investor" (defined by SEC Rule 501), "affiliate," "angel investor group," "associated person," "boiler room" (enterprise soliciting investors via telephone, email, text, social media, chat rooms), "branch manager," "branch office," "business entity," "commission" (Financial Services Commission), "control," "dealer," "federal covered adviser," "federal covered security," "guarantor," "guaranty," "intermediary," "investment adviser," "issuer," "offer to sell," "office" (Office of Financial Regulation), "predecessor," "principal," "promoter," "qualified institutional buyer" (per SEC Rule 144A), "sale," "security" (enumerating 23 types including notes, stocks, bonds, debentures, investment contracts, viatical settlement investments, etc.), "trust," "underwriter," and "viatical settlement investment."

**Section 517.03 (Rulemaking):** The Office of Financial Regulation administers and enforces the chapter. The commission may adopt rules implementing the chapter. Acts done in conformity with commission rules are immune from liability under the chapter, even if the rule is later amended, repealed, or invalidated.

**Section 517.051 (Exempt Securities):** Exemptions from registration are self-executing (no filing required), and the claimant bears the burden of proving entitlement. Exempt securities include: (1) securities issued/guaranteed by the US, states, territories, or political subdivisions (with disclosure requirements for issuers in default since Dec 31, 1975); (2) securities of foreign governments with US diplomatic relations; (3) securities of international banks, US banks, Federal Reserve member banks, and FDIC-insured depository institutions; (4) securities of regulated railroads, common carriers, and public utilities (collateral must be at least 125% of par value); (5) securities of state-regulated banks, trust companies, savings institutions, credit unions, etc.; (6) fixed-return securities outstanding in public hands for at least 5 years with no defaults in the preceding 5 years; (7) nonprofit agricultural cooperative securities; (8) cooperative housing shares for residential occupancy; (9) cooperative membership interests/retention certificates; (10) securities of religious/charitable/educational nonprofit organizations (subject to offering circular disclosure requirements); and (11) insurance/endowment policies and annuity contracts.

**Section 517.061 (Exempt Transactions):** Also self-executing. Exempt transactions include: (1) judicial sales and sales by executors, administrators, guardians, receivers, or bankruptcy trustees; (2) notes/bonds issued in connection with real property acquisition; (3) stock dividends with no value given; (4) offers to existing security holders; (5) securities issued in business reorganizations; (6) merger/consolidation transactions; (7) transfers of eligible privately held companies through merger and acquisition brokers; (8) employee stock purchase, savings, option, profit-sharing, and pension plans; (9) sales to institutional purchasers (banks, trust companies, insurance companies, dealers, investment companies, qualified institutional buyers, federal covered advisers, business development companies, small business investment companies, pension plans with assets over $5 million, 501(c)(3) organizations, family offices with assets over $5 million, and entities with investments over $5 million); (10) private offerings to no more than 35 purchasers in the state (with 3-day rescission rights and no general solicitation); and (11) offerings to accredited investors only, with specific general announcement content requirements, prohibitions on telephone solicitation to non-accredited persons, and notice filing requirements with the office.

**Chapter Overview:** The chapter also includes sections covering: the Florida Limited Offering Exemption (517.0611), Florida Invest Local Exemption (517.0612), failure to comply with exemptions (517.0613), integration of offerings (517.0614), solicitations of interest (517.0615), disqualification (517.0616), registration of securities (517.07), viatical settlement investments (517.072), Cuba prospectus disclosure (517.075), registration procedure (517.081), registration by notification (517.082), consent to service (517.101), revocation/denial of registration (517.111), registration of dealers/associated persons/intermediaries/investment advisers (517.12), notice filings for federal covered advisers (517.1201), branch office notice filings (517.1202), books and records (517.121), continuing education (517.1214), investment adviser conduct rules (517.1215), dealer conduct rules (517.1217), arbitration (517.122), Securities Guaranty Fund (517.131-517.151), revocation/suspension of registrations (517.161), burden of proof (517.171), enforcement (517.191), investigations and subpoenas (517.201), confidentiality (517.2015), public records exemption (517.2016), private remedies for unlawful sales (517.211), commodities prohibited practices (517.275), fraudulent transactions (517.301), criminal penalties (517.302), records destruction (517.313), fees (517.315), excise tax exemption (517.32), and protection of specified adults (517.34).
