args.summary:
This article from the Review of Banking & Financial Law (Vol. 40) examines the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's (OCC) June 2020 final rule modernizing the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), which was enacted unilaterally without the support of the other two CRA regulators—the Federal Reserve and the FDIC.

**Background on the CRA:** The CRA was enacted in 1977 in response to redlining and discriminatory lending practices that denied credit to creditworthy individuals in "disfavored" neighborhoods. The Act imposes a "continuing and affirmative obligation" on banks to help meet the credit needs of low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities. It applies to national banks, savings associations, and FDIC-insured state-chartered banks (but not credit unions or nonbank entities). The three regulators—OCC, Federal Reserve, and FDIC—had historically promulgated nearly identical regulations, promoting uniformity and preventing banks from switching jurisdictions to avoid compliance. Banks receive one of four CRA ratings: outstanding, satisfactory, needs to improve, or substantial noncompliance.

**OCC's Modernization:** The OCC proposed an overhaul in August 2018 and finalized changes in June 2020, despite calls to postpone during the COVID-19 pandemic. Comptroller Joseph Otting stated the changes would "help ensure the CRA remains a relevant and powerful tool for the revitalization of our communities and for our nation's civil rights." The new rule introduces metrics-based performance standards, expands qualifying activities for CRA compliance, and updates where bank activity counts. Critics argued the changes could "defang" the CRA by making compliance easier. The FDIC declined to sign on citing the "burden on banks responding to the coronavirus pandemic," while an FDIC commissioner called the amendments "a deeply misconceived proposal."

**Concerns with Unilateral Action:** The OCC's unilateral action creates two versions of the CRA. While the OCC regulates roughly 70% of CRA-related bank assets, the remaining 30% (including large commercial banks like PNC and Goldman Sachs) fall under Federal Reserve or FDIC jurisdiction. The American Bankers Association warned the split would "perpetuate confusion and inconsistency and would create competitive inequities." There is concern banks could change charters to escape stricter rules—eleven banks already switched to OCC jurisdiction after the proposal. The OCC regulates the largest U.S. banks including Bank of America, Citibank, and Fifth Third Bank.

**Legal Challenge:** In June 2020, the National Community Reinvestment Coalition and California Reinvestment Coalition sued the OCC in the Northern District of California to block the rule, alleging the OCC "severed the previously unified CRA regulatory framework." The court denied the OCC's motion to dismiss in January 2021, with a hearing set for January 20, 2022.

**Future Outlook:** The article notes the next Comptroller (potentially Michael Barr, a former Treasury official favored by community advocates) may reexamine the CRA rule. The article concludes that without support from all three partner agencies, the future of the CRA as a resource for expanding credit access in LMI neighborhoods is unclear.

News Release 2026-63|July 30, 2026

# OCC Releases CRA Performance Evaluations for 14 National Banks and Federal Savings Associations

Share This Page:

*   ![Image 8: print sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/print.svg) ![Image 9: facebook sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/facebook.svg) ![Image 10: twitter sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/twitter.svg) ![Image 11: linkedin sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/linkedin.svg) ![Image 12: email sharing button](https://platform-cdn.sharethis.com/img/email.svg) 

WASHINGTON—The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today released a list of Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) performance evaluations that became public during the period of July 1, 2026, through July 30, 2026.

Under the CRA, the OCC assesses an institution’s record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with the safe and sound operation of such institution.

The list includes the national banks, federal savings associations, and insured federal branches of foreign banks that have received CRA ratings. Possible ratings assigned are outstanding, satisfactory, needs to improve, and substantial noncompliance. The CRA evaluations released are:

| Institution | City | State | CRA Rating |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Desjardins Bank, National Association](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/23852.pdf) | Hallandale Beach | FL | Satisfactory |
| [Hinsdale Bank & Trust Company, National Association](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/25212.pdf) | Hinsdale | IL | Outstanding |
| [Midland FS & LA](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/704475.pdf) | Bridgeview | IL | Needs to Improve |
| [The First National Bank of Carmi](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/4934.pdf) | Carmi | IL | Satisfactory |
| [The First National Bank of Hutchinson](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/3180.pdf) | Hutchinson | KS | Outstanding |
| [First National Bank](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/446.pdf) | Damariscotta | ME | Satisfactory |
| [Merchants Bank, National Association](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/14488.pdf) | Winona | MN | Satisfactory |
| [My Kind of Bank, National Association](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/6906.pdf) | Ottertail | MN | Outstanding |
| [The Citizens National Bank of Park Rapids](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/13692.pdf) | Park Rapids | MN | Outstanding |
| [Woodlands National Bank](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/23926.pdf) | Hinckley | MN | Satisfactory |
| [Waterford Bank, National Association](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/24685.pdf) | Toledo | OH | Satisfactory |
| [Kress National Bank](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/15168.pdf) | Kress | TX | Satisfactory |
| [Trinity Bank, National Association](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/24397.pdf) | Fort Worth | TX | Satisfactory |
| [John Deere Financial, f.s.b.](https://occ.gov/static/cra/craeval/Jul26/715685.pdf) | Madison | WI | Satisfactory |

The OCC's website offers access to a searchable list of all public [CRA evaluations](https://www.occ.gov/publications-and-resources/tools/index-cra-search.html "CRA Performance Evaluations") issued since April 1996. The OCC also publishes a [list](https://www.occ.gov/topics/consumers-and-communities/cra/exam-schedule/index-cra-evaluations-coming-due.html "Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Evaluations Coming Due") of institutions to be examined for compliance with the CRA.

To receive alerts for news releases announcing CRA performance evaluations, subscribe to [OCC News](https://www.occ.gov/about/connect-with-us/subscribe-to-occ-email-updates.html "Subscribe to OCC Email Updates") email list.

This is the Federal Reserve Board of Governors' Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) public search portal, specifically the "Evaluations & Ratings" page for Federal Reserve supervised banks (State Member Banks). The page provides a searchable database of CRA performance evaluations and ratings for state member banks.

**Search Filters Available:**
- Institution Name or ID
- Overall CRA Rating (Outstanding, Satisfactory, Needs to Improve, Substantial Noncompliance)
- Geographic filters (City, County, State - all 50 states plus DC and Puerto Rico)
- Asset Size Range (in thousands): 0-350K, 350K-1M, 1M-10M, 10M-100M, 100M+
- Exam Year (1995-2026)
- Public Year (1995-2026)
- Exam Method (Intermediate Small Bank, Large Bank, Limited Purpose Small Bank, Strategic Plan, Wholesale)
- Individual test ratings: Lending Test, Investment Test, Service Test, and Community Development Test (each with Outstanding, Satisfactory, Needs to Improve, Substantial Noncompliance options)

# Fitch Affirms Zions Bancorporation at 'BBB+'; Outlook Stable

Fri 26 Sep, 2025 - 3:59 PM ET

[](https://www.facebook.com/share.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fitchratings.com%2Fresearch%2Fbanks%2Ffitch-affirms-zions-bancorporation-at-bbb-outlook-stable-26-09-2025&title=Fitch%20Affirms%20Zions%20Bancorporation%20at%20%27BBB%2B%27%3B%20Outlook%20Stable)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fitchratings.com%2Fresearch%2Fbanks%2Ffitch-affirms-zions-bancorporation-at-bbb-outlook-stable-26-09-2025&status=Fitch%20Affirms%20Zions%20Bancorporation%20at%20%27BBB%2B%27%3B%20Outlook%20Stable+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fitchratings.com%2Fresearch%2Fbanks%2Ffitch-affirms-zions-bancorporation-at-bbb-outlook-stable-26-09-2025)[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fitchratings.com%2Fresearch%2Fbanks%2Ffitch-affirms-zions-bancorporation-at-bbb-outlook-stable-26-09-2025&title=Fitch%20Affirms%20Zions%20Bancorporation%20at%20%27BBB%2B%27%3B%20Outlook%20Stable&source=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fitchratings.com%2Fresearch%2Fbanks%2Ffitch-affirms-zions-bancorporation-at-bbb-outlook-stable-26-09-2025)[](mailto:?subject=Fitch%20Affirms%20Zions%20Bancorporation%20at%20'BBB%2B'%3B%20Outlook%20Stable&body=Check%20out%20this%20site%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fitchratings.com%2Fresearch%2Fbanks%2Ffitch-affirms-zions-bancorporation-at-bbb-outlook-stable-26-09-2025)[](https://www.fitchratings.com/research/banks/fitch-affirms-zions-bancorporation-at-bbb-outlook-stable-26-09-2025#)

**Related Content:**

[Zions Bancorporation, N.A. - Ratings Navigator](https://www.fitchratings.com/research/banks/zions-bancorporation-na-ratings-navigator-30-09-2025)[Zions Bancorporation, N.A.](https://www.fitchratings.com/research/banks/zions-bancorporation-na-13-10-2025)

Fitch Ratings - New York - 26 Sep 2025: Fitch Ratings has affirmed the Long- and Short-Term Issuer Default Ratings (IDRs) of Zions Bancorporation N.A. (ZION) at 'BBB+' and 'F2', respectively. Fitch has also affirmed the Viability Rating (VR) at 'bbb+'. The Rating Outlook is Stable.

### Key Rating Drivers

**Affirmation Reflects Substantial Headroom at Current Rating:** The affirmation of ZION's Long-Term IDR, VR and Stable Outlook reflects the company's solid financial performance and Fitch's expectation that the impact of an economic downturn should prove manageable in the context of its current rating.

**Solid Franchise in Western U.S.:** ZION has a solid franchise in its core markets, with strong penetration in small-business lending within its footprint. However, it has limited fee-revenue diversity and a higher reliance on spread-based income compared to peers. This lack of revenue diversity constrains its ratings.

**Adequate Risk Management:** Fitch views ZION's risk controls and underwriting standards as appropriate for the rating. The bank's centralized risk function maintains suitable influence over credit policy decisions. However, ZION has a higher concentration risk tolerance than most peers, evidenced by the highest CRE concentration among peers at 161% of risk-based capital as of 2Q25.

Fitch also considers ZION to have higher interest rate risk in its securities portfolio than Category IV peers, partly due to the need to offset its primarily floating-rate loan portfolio. Notably, ZION is more asset-sensitive than peers, reflected by its substantially lower use of cash flow hedges compared to Category IV peers.

**Strong Asset Quality:** ZION's credit quality remains benign, although impaired loans increased in 1H25 due to continued pressure in commercial real estate and higher residential mortgage nonaccruals. The impaired loan ratio was 1.29% at 2Q25, up from 0.79% at 4Q24. ZION consistently has the lowest net charge-off rate among the peer group, at 9 bps in 1H25 versus a peer median of 37 bps. Fitch expects the ratio to increase in FY26, though it should continue to compare favorably against the large regional peer group. ZION's 'a-‌' Asset Quality score has sufficient headroom to absorb a moderate increase in loan losses in a weaker economic environment.

**Net Interest Margin Expansion;****Revenue Diversity a Constraint:** ZION's earnings improved in 1H25, supported by fixed-rate pricing tailwinds in the securities portfolio, loan growth, and a focus on reducing deposit costs. Operating profit to risk-weighted assets (RWA) rose to 1.61% in 1H25 from 1.49% in FY24. Fitch expects higher net interest income to drive further growth in operating profit to RWA in FY26, albeit at a modest pace given ZION's asset-sensitive balance sheet in a rate-cutting cycle. ZION remains the most spread-reliant bank among major regional peers; this reliance has contributed to volatility in net interest income over time, and limited revenue diversification remains a ratings constraint.

**Capital Accretion Continues:** ZION's common equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio was 10.97% as of 2Q25, up from 10.6% a year earlier and in line with the peer median. On an AOCI-adjusted basis, CET1 was approximately 7.83% — the lowest among peers — though it increased by 109 bps over the same period. Fitch expects CET1 to accrete to 11.4% by 4Q25, supported by the continued suspension of share repurchases. Overall, Fitch views ZION's capital as appropriate for its current rating and anticipates further capital build toward the peer median over the rating horizon.

**Liquidity Profile Approaches Pre-Pandemic Levels:** ZION's focus on optimizing net interest margin led to an annualized 6.7% decline in deposits in 1H25, the largest percentage decrease among peers. The loan-to-deposit ratio (LTD) increased to 82.4% at 2Q25 from 77.6% at YE24, roughly in line with its 2015-2019 average of 83.2%. Fitch expects that the bank's focus on lowering its total cost of funds will result in a LTD ratio moderately above pre-pandemic levels over the rating horizon.

Brokered deposits accounted for 7.31% of total deposits — well above the peer median — reflecting additional wholesale funding taken on to offset deposit runoff in 1H23, though this share has declined from a 3Q24 peak of 9.86%. Fitch believes brokered deposits will continue to decline over the rating horizon. ZION's Funding and Liquidity score of 'a-‌' is one notch below Category IV peers, in part reflecting the absence of liquidity coverage ratio requirements, which permits higher levels of short-term wholesale funding.

### Rating Sensitivities

### Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Negative Rating Action/Downgrade

-- Negative pressure could be placed on ZION's ratings should there be evidence of outsized deterioration in the level or volatility of earnings relative to peers. Sustained deterioration in the operating profitability to RWA ratio to below 0.5% over multiple quarters could result in negative ratings pressure. Likewise, if the bank's reliance on market-rate, wholesale funding begins to impact ZION's ability to achieve appropriate returns, it could result in negative rating action;

-- Significant deterioration in asset quality could drive downward rating action. A rapid increase in impaired loans to gross loans to above 2% or credit losses exceeding those of similarly rated peers would result in negative pressure;

-- The bank's rating would be at risk if its CET1 ratio were to approach or ultimately dip below 9% and remain there for multiple quarters absent a credible plan to build levels back above this threshold.

### Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Positive Rating Action/Upgrade

-- Positive rating momentum could develop if ZION were to demonstrate consistent and sustainable core earnings performance in line with higher-rated peers, including improved revenue diversity through maturation of its fee-based businesses, such as wealth management and capital markets. This would need to be accomplished while maintaining capital levels above peer medians, in line with management's stated target, and maintaining a prudent risk appetite;

-- Should ZION prove to be a positive outlier among its large regional peers on asset quality in the face of an adverse credit environment, validating the bank's de-risked credit management and matured risk function, it could also drive positive rating momentum.

### OTHER DEBT AND ISSUER RATINGS: KEY RATING DRIVERS

**Long- and Short-Term Deposit Ratings:**ZION's uninsured deposit ratings are rated one notch higher than the bank's IDR and senior unsecured debt because U.S. uninsured deposits benefit from depositor preference. U.S. depositor preference gives deposit liabilities superior recovery prospects in the event of default. The bank's long-term deposit rating is affirmed at 'A-‌'‌.

Short-term deposit ratings are linked to long-term deposit ratings using the Rating Correspondence Table in Fitch's "Bank Rating Criteria," published March 2025. Accordingly, Fitch affirmed the bank's short-term deposit rating at the lower 'F2' for short-term ratings associated with a long-term rating of 'A-‌'‌. This is supported by the bank's Funding and Liquidity factor score of 'a-‌'‌.

**Long- and Short-Term Senior Unsecured Debt**: Consistent with Fitch's baseline approach, ZION's long-term senior debt ratings are equalized with its Long-Term IDRs. ZION's short-term senior debt rating is affirmed at 'F2'. This is supported by the bank's Funding and Liquidity factor score of 'a-‌'‌.

**Subordinated Debt:**ZION's subordinated debt is notched one level below the bank's VR for loss severity. In accordance with Fitch's "Bank Rating Criteria," this reflects alternate notching to the base case of two notches due to our view of U.S. regulators' resolution alternatives for an entity like ZION, as well as early intervention options available to banking regulators under U.S. law.

**Government Support:**ZION's Government Support Ratings (GSRs) of 'ns' reflect Fitch's view that government support is unlikely.

### OTHER DEBT AND ISSUER RATINGS: RATING SENSITIVITIES

L**ong- and Short-Term Deposit Ratings:**The long- and short-term deposit ratings are sensitive to any change to ZION's Long- and Short-Term IDR. The short-term deposit rating is also sensitive to Fitch's assessment of ZION's funding and liquidity profile.

**Long- and Short-Term Senior Unsecured Debt:**ZION's long-term senior unsecured debt rating is sensitive to any change to respective it's IDRs. The short-term senior unsecured debt rating is also sensitive to Fitch's assessment of ZION's funding and liquidity profile.

**Subordinated Debt:**The ratings for ZION's subordinated debt are sensitive to any change to the VR. Ratings of subordinated debt would also be negatively sensitive to ZION and its operating companies becoming subject to a more formalized resolution process, as Fitch currently employs alternative notching for these instruments.

**Government Support:**ZION's GSR would be sensitive to any change in Fitch's view of U.S. sovereign support, which Fitch views as unlikely.

### VR ADJUSTMENTS

The VR has been assigned in line with the implied VR.

The Business Profile score of 'bbb+' has been assigned below the implied score of 'a' due to a negative adjustment for the business model.

Fitch Ratings affirmed the Long- and Short-Term Issuer Default Ratings (IDRs) of Zions Bancorporation N.A. (ZION) at 'BBB+' and 'F2', respectively, along with its Viability Rating (VR) at 'bbb+'. The Rating Outlook is Stable. The affirmation was announced on September 26, 2025, from Fitch's New York office.

KEY RATING DRIVERS:
- The affirmation reflects substantial headroom at the current rating, with Fitch expecting that an economic downturn's impact should be manageable.
- ZION has a solid franchise in the Western U.S., particularly in small-business lending, but limited fee-revenue diversity and higher reliance on spread-based income constrain its ratings.
- ZION has the highest CRE concentration among peers at 161% of risk-based capital as of 2Q25, and higher interest rate risk in its securities portfolio than Category IV peers, with lower use of cash flow hedges.
- Asset quality remains benign; impaired loan ratio was 1.29% at 2Q25 (up from 0.79% at 4Q24), with the lowest net charge-off rate among peers at 9 bps in 1H25 versus a peer median of 37 bps.
- Operating profit to risk-weighted assets rose to 1.61% in 1H25 from 1.49% in FY24; ZION remains the most spread-reliant bank among major regional peers.
- CET1 ratio was 10.97% as of 2Q25 (up from 10.6% a year earlier), with an AOCI-adjusted CET1 of approximately 7.83% — the lowest among peers. Fitch expects CET1 to accrete to 11.4% by 4Q25.
- Deposits declined an annualized 6.7% in 1H25 (largest among peers); loan-to-deposit ratio increased to 82.4% at 2Q25 from 77.6% at YE24. Brokered deposits accounted for 7.31% of total deposits (down from a 3Q24 peak of 9.86%). Funding and Liquidity score is 'a-' — one notch below Category IV peers.

RATING SENSITIVITIES:
Negative pressure could result from: sustained operating profitability to RWA below 0.5% over multiple quarters; impaired loans rising above 2% of gross loans; or CET1 dipping below 9% for multiple quarters. Positive momentum could develop if ZION demonstrates consistent core earnings, improved revenue diversity (e.g., wealth management and capital markets), and maintains capital above peer medians.

OTHER RATINGS AFFIRMED: Long-term deposits at 'A-', short-term deposits at 'F2', senior unsecured debt at 'BBB+' (LT) and 'F2' (ST), subordinated debt at 'BBB', and Government Support Rating at 'ns'.

VR ADJUSTMENTS: Business Profile scored 'bbb+' (below implied 'a' due to business model adjustment); Asset Quality scored 'a-' (below implied 'aa' due to loan concentration adjustment); Earnings and Profitability scored 'bbb+' (below implied 'a' due to revenue diversity adjustment); Capitalization scored 'bbb+' (below implied 'a' due to regulatory calculation adjustment).

The ratings were solicited by the rated entity. Endorsement status: EU Endorsed, UK Endorsed. Primary Rating Analyst is Patrick Yu (Director, New York).

args.summary:
This document is the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) Performance Evaluation for U.S. Bank National Association (USB), published January 18, 2022, by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). The bank received an overall rating of "Outstanding" for its performance in meeting the credit needs of its communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.

**Key Details:**
- USB is headquartered in Minneapolis, MN, and is a subsidiary of U.S. Bancorp, with $553.9 billion in assets as of December 31, 2020. It is the fifth largest commercial bank in the U.S. with approximately 2,500 banking offices in 27 states and 173 assessment areas (AAs), including 14 MMSAs.
- The evaluation period was January 1, 2016, through December 31, 2020, covering the Lending, Investment, and Service Tests.
- The bank received Outstanding ratings on the Lending and Investment Tests and High Satisfactory on the Service Test.
- The overall rating is based on a weighted average of 14 MMSAs and 27 state ratings, with nine rated areas (Minneapolis MMSA, California, Cincinnati MMSA, Colorado, Washington, Wisconsin, St. Louis MMSA, Portland MMSA, and Chicago MMSA) accounting for 73.3 percent of adjusted deposits.
- Lending: USB originated/purchased 66.1% of its total loans inside its AAs. The bank is a leader in Community Development (CD) loans, with CD lending having significantly positive impact in 15 rated areas. USB made significant use of innovative/flexible loan products in 25 of 41 rated areas.
- Investment: Investment performance was excellent in 30 of 41 rated areas.
- Service: Retail delivery systems were readily accessible in 32 of 47 full-scope areas, and the bank was a leader in CD services in 22 of 47 full-scope areas.
- During the evaluation period, USB closed 735 branches (606 during 2019-2020) as part of a branch consolidation project responding to changing customer banking preferences. The bank also expanded into North Carolina (Charlotte) in October 2019 and entered a strategic alliance with State Farm in 2020.
- In response to COVID-19, USB participated in the SBA Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), securing over $7.5 billion in funding for over 100,000 applicants in 2020. The USB Foundation directed $30 million to COVID-relief efforts, and the bank created a $15 million Rebuild and Transform Fund following the civil unrest of 2020.
- The bank's American Dream loan program targeted LMI borrowers, originating nearly 4,000 loans totaling $619 million during the evaluation period. USB facilitated over 13,000 SBA loans totaling $2.4 billion.

**Discriminatory/Illegal Practices Review:**
- In 2018, the OCC identified a Military Lending Act disclosure violation involving credit card accounts (no consumer harm identified).
- The bank self-identified a Servicemembers Civil Protection Act violation in 2018 involving untimely auto lease refunds.
- On July 28, 2022, the CFPB issued a consent order against the bank for issuing credit cards without consumer knowledge/consent and using consumer reports without permissible purpose, covering January 2010-December 2020, with a $37.5 million civil money penalty and a redress plan. The CRA rating was not lowered as a result of these findings.

**Chicago MMSA Detailed Evaluation (as an example of MMSA-level findings):**
- Rated Outstanding on Lending, Investment, and Service Tests.
- USB had 133 offices and 187 ATMs in the AA, $12.8 billion in deposits (4.4% of adjusted total), ranking ninth in deposit market share (2.6%) among 155 FDIC-insured institutions.
- Key community needs included affordable housing, small business credit access, economic development infrastructure, and job training. The AA had 23 certified CDFIs and numerous Opportunity Zones.
- Lending activity was excellent: USB ranked fourth in home mortgage market share (4.2%) and fifth in small business lending market share (5.5%).
args.key_excerpts: "The Lending Test rating is based on bank performance across all 41 rating areas... The bank's Outstanding Lending Test performance was driven by Outstanding ratings in 18 rated areas including six of the largest nine rated areas by deposit volume."

This is the Zions Bancorporation, National Association (Zions Bancorporation, N.A.) Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022. The company is incorporated in the United States with IRS Employer Identification Number 87-0189025 and principal executive offices at One South Main, Salt Lake City, Utah 84133-1109.

**Registered Securities:** Zions Bancorporation trades on The NASDAQ Stock Market LLC under the following symbols: Common Stock (ZION), Series A Floating-Rate Non-Cumulative Perpetual Preferred Stock depositary shares (ZIONP), Series G Fixed/Floating-Rate Non-Cumulative Perpetual Preferred Stock depositary shares (ZIONO), and 6.95% Fixed-to-Floating Rate Subordinated Notes due September 15, 2028 (ZIONL).

**Key Financial Highlights (FY2022):**
- Net income decreased 20% to $907 million (from $1,129 million in 2021), primarily due to an increase in the provision for credit losses
- Net earnings applicable to common shareholders decreased 20% to $878 million
- Diluted EPS decreased 15% to $5.79 (from $6.79)
- Net interest income increased 14% to $2,520 million
- Noninterest income decreased 10% to $632 million
- Total net revenue increased 8% to $3,152 million
- Noninterest expense increased 8% to $1,878 million
- Pre-provision net revenue increased 9% to $1,311 million
- Provision for credit losses was $122 million (vs. negative $276 million in 2021)

**Balance Sheet (Year-End 2022):**
- Total assets: $89,545 million (down 4%)
- Loans and leases, net: $55,653 million (up 9%)
- Deposits: $71,652 million (down 13%)
- Common equity: $4,453 million (down 37%)
- Tangible book value per share: $43.72 (up 9%)
- Market price at year-end: $49.16 (down 22%)

**Performance Ratios (2022):**
- Return on average assets: 1.01%
- Return on average common equity: 16.0%
- Return on average tangible common equity: 13.9%
- Net interest margin: 3.06% (up from 2.72%)
- Net charge-offs to average loans and leases (ex-PPP): 0.08%
- Efficiency ratio: 58.8% (improved from 60.8%)
- Dividends declared: $1.58 per share (up 10%)
- Common dividend payout ratio: 27.3%

**Capital Ratios (Year-End 2022):**
- Common Equity Tier 1 capital: 9.8% (minimum requirement 7.0% with buffer)
- Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets: 10.5%
- Total capital to risk-weighted assets: 12.2% (minimum 10.5% with buffer)
- Tier 1 leverage ratio: 7.7% (minimum 4.0%)
- Tangible common equity: 7.1%

**Net Interest Margin Details:** Net interest income increased 14% due to a 34 bps expansion in net interest margin (to 3.06%), driven largely by rate increases on interest-earning assets (yield increased 49 bps to 3.28%) while funding costs remained low (0.23% on total deposits and interest-bearing liabilities). Average interest-earning assets increased 2% to $83,638 million.

**Noninterest Income:** Customer-related noninterest income increased 7% to $614 million, driven by commercial account fees (+16% to $159M), capital markets and foreign exchange fees (+19% to $83M), and card fees (+9% to $104M). This was offset by securities losses of $15 million (vs. gains of $71 million in 2021) and lower dividends and other income.

**Noninterest Expense:** Total noninterest expense increased 8% to $1,878 million, led by higher salaries and employee benefits (+10% to $1,235 million) and deposit insurance/regulatory expense (+47% to $50 million), partially offset by lower professional and legal services (-21% to $57 million). Full-time equivalent employees increased 3% to 9,989.

**Share Repurchases:** In 2022, Zions repurchased 3,581,087 shares total at an average price of $56.19, of which 3,562,859 were part of publicly announced plans. Repurchases were concentrated in the first three quarters and November.

**Stock Performance:** Zions Bancorporation stock returned 104.0 (vs. 100.0 baseline in 2017), compared to the KRX Regional Bank Index at 118.7 and S&P 500 at 156.8, reflecting underperformance over the 2017-2022 period.

**Diversity Data (as of Dec 31, 2022):** Overall workforce composition: 59% women, 37% people of color, 12% disabled, 2% veterans. Management: 52% women, 28% people of color.

We demonstrated in spades this kind of focus on responding to community and client needs over the past two years during the pandemic, perhaps most especially through our performance with PPP. Through the two rounds of the program, we funded approximately 77,000 loans totaling $10.2 billion to small businesses across the western U.S. and were recognized as the nation’s 10th largest originator of these loans, which were critically important to the survival of so many local businesses. I occasionally tell our bankers of an experience I had years ago when I was a teenager. Toward the end of the evening, I happened to glance through the kitchen window, and what I saw remains etched in my memory: Mal Hill was there at the kitchen sink, with his shirtsleeves rolled up, washing dishes. He’d truly become “one of the family.” Mal Hill was our correspondent banker for years, and when we bought Nevada State Bank in 1985 and needed some bridge ﬁnancing to complete the purchase, I instinctively called Mal, who responded, “consider it done.” He was able to make that commitment because he’d developed the kind of deep understanding of our business that allowed him to commit quickly and conﬁdently. That’s the type of experience we aspire to have all our bankers able to deliver to their customers. One of my favorite recent examples of building this kind of relationship involves Chef Chris Williams, the owner of Lucille’s, a well-known and highly regarded restaurant in Houston’s Museum District. Lucille’s found itself in the national spotlight when then-candidate Joe Biden met with the family of George Floyd at the restaurant on the day of Floyd’s public viewing. But after connecting with Jevaughn Sterling, an executive vice president at Amegy Bank, through a mutual connection at the Greater Houston Black Chamber of Commerce, who analyzed the deal and explained its drawbacks. “I don’t have a ﬁnancial education, and Jevaughn walked me through these things so I could understand that I would have paid $1.5 million over the asking price, because I thought I had no other options,” Williams said. With Jevaughn Sterling’s help, Williams secured a loan from Amegy Bank, and he now owns the land on which his 1923 Museum District bungalow sits, making it possible for Williams to control his own destiny, and helping ensure that he’ll be serving his patrons some of the very best Southern cuisine in Houston for a very long time to come. This is the kind of experience that has led our customers, in surveys conducted by Greenwich Associates, a leading national market research ﬁrm that conducts over 24,000 interviews annually with small- and middle-market business owners, to rank us among the leading banks in the United States in serving the needs of these businesses, many of which are family owned. Zions was also one of only four banks in the country to win six of six possible awards in Small Business and Middle Market “Best Brands” categories, including “Bank You Can Trust,” “Values Long-term Relationships,” and “Ease of Doing Business.” I’m especially proud of the many bankers in our organization who provide such outstanding service to our customers.

We here at Kalb could not be happier with the service we have received over the years, and we hope to continue the relationship that has grown right along with the communities where both of our organizations began.” Steven C Kalb, CEO Kalb Industries 40 years, Nevada State Bank client ” | 11 | an opportunity for the bank to participate in a large, syndicated loan to a nationally recognized company. It’s how we uniquely create value, and it’s great fun to be a ﬁnancial partner to entrepreneurs working their tails off, pursuing their dreams.

Ten years ago, we embarked on the largest and most intensive project of its kind in the bank’s history, to replace our core loan and deposit systems with a modern, integrated core processing system that will allow us to integrate third-party products and deliver new and better experiences to customers, and to our own colleagues, with greater agility. Customer feedback has been exceptional, and we provide digital banking capabilities that equal or exceed those of most of our large competitors. A similar upgrade for our small business customers is currently underway. We launched our new Spark digital small business loan application, which has a more intuitive user experience and provides the ability for bankers to collaboratively complete a digital loan application with a borrower. We continue to upgrade the automation of our mortgage origination process with the result that over 95% of our mortgages are now originated using digital tools, allowing us to expedite underwriting and processing, and facilitating record production of over $4 billion in residential mortgages in 2021 — a 16% increase in a year when the Mortgage Bankers Association reported an overall 8% decline in production nationally.

This webpage is Zions Bancorporation's 2021 Annual Report, titled "A Legacy of Trust," featuring the Chairman's Message from Harris H. Simmons (Chairman & CEO, dated February 24, 2022). The report outlines the five characteristics that truly great banks have in common: (1) consistently producing strong risk-adjusted returns with strong capital, ample liquidity, and exceptional credit quality; (2) investing in communities using financial and human resources; (3) building enduring, reliable relationships based on deep customer understanding and unwavering commitment to ethics and integrity; (4) investing in the future; and (5) investing in people and strengthening their team.

KEY FINANCIAL HIGHLIGHTS (2021): Net income applicable to common shareholders reached $1.1 billion, or $6.79 per fully diluted share, up 118% and 125% respectively over 2020. Return on average assets was 1.29%, return on average tangible common equity was 17.3%, and return on average common equity was 14.9%. Net interest margin declined to 2.72% from 3.15% in 2020. Average loans totaled $52.0 billion (down $1.0 billion), average deposits grew 20% to $76.3 billion, and total assets reached $93.2 billion at year-end. Net charged-off loans were a mere 0.01% of average loans. Common Equity Tier 1 capital ratio was 10.2% at year-end. Total net revenue was $2.911 billion. The efficiency ratio was 60.8%. Adjusted PPNR less net charged-off loans totaled $1,115 million, up 7% from 2020. PPP loan revenue totaled $235 million. The quarterly dividend was increased 12% mid-2021 to $0.38 per share, and $800 million of common stock was repurchased. Customer-related fees increased 5% to $575 million, with card fees up 16% and wealth management fees up 14%. Assets under management grew 26% to $11 billion.

BUSINESS/OPERATIONAL HIGHLIGHTS: Zions funded approximately 77,000 PPP loans totaling $10.2 billion, ranking as the nation's 10th largest originator. The Small Business Diversity Banking Program (launched May 2021 under OCC's "Project REACh") approved 502 loans totaling $155 million to minority, women, and veteran-owned businesses. The bank received an "Outstanding" Community Reinvestment Act rating. Greenwich Associates ranked Zions second among all U.S. banks in "Excellence" awards (27 awards), and it was one of only four banks to win six of six "Best Brands" categories including "Bank You Can Trust." A $4 billion mortgage production (up 16% despite an 8% national decline) was achieved with over 95% of mortgages originated digitally. Zions is completing a decade-long core processing system replacement by mid-2023. Process automation saved nearly 300,000 hours of manual labor in 2021 with a goal of 1 million hours by 2025. The bank launched a new digital consumer banking platform and "Spark" digital small business loan application. Cybersecurity spending has grown at double-digit rates. A new 400,000 square foot technology campus in Midvale, Utah (Platinum LEED standard) will house ~2,000 employees. Over 900 training experiences were hosted in 2021. Over 10,000 bankers work at Zions Bancorporation across affiliates including Zions Bank, Amegy Bank, California Bank & Trust, Nevada State Bank, Vectra Bank Colorado, The Commerce Bank of Washington/Oregon, and National Bank of Arizona.

The report also includes affiliate footprint data (Salt Lake City, Las Vegas, Houston, Denver, San Diego, Seattle, Phoenix), financial highlights tables for 2017-2021, a GAAP to Non-GAAP reconciliation, board of directors and corporate officers listings, and corporate information. Board changes included the retirement of J. David Heaney and the addition of Maria Contreras-Sweet (former U.S. SBA administrator). Zions Bancorporation is approaching its 150th anniversary (founded 1873 as Zion's Savings Bank & Trust Company).

# NCRC’s Full Public Comment Letter On Community Reinvestment Act Interagency Rulemaking

By   [NCRC](https://ncrc.org/author/ncrc-editor/ "View all posts by NCRC")   /  August 4, 2022  / [Testimony & Regulatory Comments](https://ncrc.org/category/testimony/) / 266 minutes of reading

Chief Counsel’s Office  
 Office of the Comptroller of the Currency  
 400 7th Street SW, Suite 3E-218  
 Washington, DC 20219

Ann E. Misback  
 Secretary  
 Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System  
 20th Street and Constitution Avenue NW  
 Washington, DC 20551

James P. Sheesley  
 Assistant Executive Secretary  
 Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation  
 550 17th Street NW  
 Washington, DC 20429

August 3, 2022

RE: **Community Reinvestment Act Proposed Rulemaking [87 FR 33884]**

OCC: 12 CFR Part 25; Docket ID OCC-2022-0002; RIN 1557-AF15

Federal Reserve: 12 CFR Part 228; Regulation BB Docket No. R-1769; RIN 7100-AG29

FDIC: 12 CFR Part 345; RIN 3064-AF81

To Whom it May Concern:

The National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPR) regarding updating the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). This NPR represents the most significant changes to the CRA regulation and exams in 27 years. Nevertheless, it should be strengthened further to realize the statute’s full potential to increase loans, investments and services in traditionally underserved communities. NCRC and our 600 member organizations use CRA daily to increase lending, investment and services in traditionally underserved communities. A robust CRA is key to our efforts.

CRA has successfully leveraged loans, investments and services. Between 2009 and 2020, banks have made more than $2.58 trillion in home loans to low- and moderate-income (LMI) borrowers or in LMI census tracts. They made $856 billion in loans to small businesses with revenues under $1 million.[[1]](#_ftn1) Despite the progress, persistent lending disparities remain. A recent national level analysis showed continuing disparities in loan denials by race and when people of color received home loans, their equity accumulation was less.[[2]](#_ftn2) In addition, people of color are more likely to be unbanked and underbanked than their white counterparts. A major contributing factor to this disparity is fewer branches in communities of color and less competition among banks in those communities, which reduces choices for affordable bank products.[[3]](#_ftn3)

CRA will be more effective in bolstering bank reinvestment activity in underserved communities, the more rigorous CRA exams and ratings are. The agencies proposed important improvements in the CRA regulation including increasing the rigor of the subtests on the CRA exams, expanding geographical areas on CRA exams and collecting more data to scrutinize bank performance. However, they did not sufficiently address pressing and persistent racial inequities. The agencies also proposed reducing community development finance and service responsibilities for about 20% of all banks. In addition, the agencies’ proposal is uneven regarding increasing rigor across all parts of the CRA exam. Further, the CRA regulation must ensure that its designations of eligible activities are clear, accurate, and effective in serving community needs (such as affordable housing, climate remediation, and other important measures).

This comment first summarizes our position on major issues including:

* CRA exams must explicitly consider banks’ records in serving people of color and communities of color.
* Public input mechanisms in CRA exams and merger reviews must be robust and include consideration of community benefit agreements. The agencies and banks must proactively reach out to community organizations and members of the public.
* Improvements to exam rigor and more objectivity in performance measures are needed to reduce ratings inflation and loopholes such as not examining major loan products must be closed.
* Enhancements to community development definitions are needed to more effectively target activities to communities in need.
* Data improvements must provide more insight into banks’ records of meeting credit and community needs.
* Anti-discrimination and fair lending reviews must be more transparent. CRA exams must examine affordability and sustainability of lending in order to prevent abusive lending.
* Assessment area changes must sufficiently capture online lending and deposit taking activity.
* The proposed asset threshold and bank classification changes would reduce community development financing and branching.

After the summary, this comment letter will next answer the questions posed by the NPR but before doing so we will expand upon our position regarding CRA and race.

### **Summary of Major Positions**

**CRA must explicitly consider bank activity by race and ethnicity**

Although the CRA statute does not explicitly mention race, it was passed as a measure to remedy and prevent racial discrimination. It required banks to serve all communities, which provides room for the federal bank agencies to incorporate race in CRA exams in order to ensure this end is met. The government should take these measures to rectify ongoing discrimination as well as decades of redlining. The federal government instituted redlining practices in New Deal housing programs and which was later adopted on a widespread basis by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and the private sector. Persistent racial disparities in lending must compel the agencies to incorporate race and ethnicity in CRA exams.

The agencies proposed to use the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) data to produce exam tables describing lending by race, but not to use the results of these analyses to influence a bank’s rating.[[4]](#_ftn4) NCRC had asserted in a paper co-authored by Relman Colfax PLLC that changes to CRA would comply with legal standards (as well as advance its statutory purpose) if CRA examined lending by race and ethnicity in geographical areas experiencing ongoing discrimination or exhibiting significant racial disparities in lending.[[5]](#_ftn5) NCRC had also proposed including analyses of bank CRA performance in underserved neighborhoods with low levels of lending, which are disproportionately communities of color.[[6]](#_ftn6)

In addition to examining banks’ records of lending by race, the agencies should also bolster fair lending reviews accompanying CRA exams for banks that perform poorly in the HMDA data analysis of lending by race. Furthermore, the agencies proposed using Section 1071 data on small business lending by race and gender of the business owner[[7]](#_ftn7), and this data should be used as a screen for fair lending reviews. By including race and ethnicity, CRA can identify and address persistent racial disparities that have direct impacts on economic inclusion, quality of life and health outcomes.

**Public input mechanisms: agencies propose improvements that must be codified**

Since CRA requires banks to meet the needs of communities, the agencies must elevate the importance of public comments regarding the extent to which banks meet local needs. The agencies proposed to continue the recent practice of publishing 60 days in advance of each calendar quarter the schedule of CRA exams for the next two quarters,[[8]](#_ftn8) which will help provide ample opportunities for the public to comment on exams. The agencies proposed to continue the current practice of sending any comments on CRA performance to banks and are also considering publishing comments received on agency websites.[[9]](#_ftn9)

Posting comments on agency websites will establish accountability on the part of examiners to consider them. In addition, these comments can be referenced during future merger applications to determine if the banks addressed significant concerns of the public. Also, the agencies should establish a public registry that community organizations can use to sign up if they want to be contacted about community needs and bank CRA performance. Furthermore, we request that the agencies publish which organizations they consult with to understand local community needs, commit to collecting input from a diverse range of organizations that includes organizations led by people of color and women, follow up on needs identified, and detail how community input was factored into the results of CRA performance evaluations.

We also agree with Acting Comptroller Hsu that the agencies must hold frequent public hearings on large bank mergers.[[10]](#_ftn10) CRA exams, if they are made more rigorous by a final rule, will help hold merging banks accountable. However, merging banks must also submit a community benefits plan as part of their merger applications, which could include community benefits agreements negotiated with community organizations. As further described in our recent comments to the FDIC on bank mergers, an Outstanding CRA rating must not be considered evidence that merging banks have satisfied the public benefits legal requirement.[[11]](#_ftn11)

Furthermore, CRA exams following merger approvals must review compliance with community benefit agreements or conditional merger approvals.

**Reducing CRA ratings inflation: progress on the lending test of the large bank exam, but not as much on the other subtests**

Currently, about 98% of banks pass their CRA exams on an annual basis with just less than 10% receiving an Outstanding rating and almost 90% of them receiving a rating of Satisfactory.[[12]](#_ftn12) CRA has successfully leveraged more loans, investments and services for LMI communities, but it would be more effective in doing so if the ratings system more accurately revealed distinctions in performance.[[13]](#_ftn13)

More banks would be identified as significantly lagging their peers, which would motivate them to improve their ratings and increase their reinvestment activity.

The agencies bolstered the rigor on the large bank retail lending test by introducing performance ranges for comparisons among a bank’s lending and demographic and market benchmarks.[[14]](#_ftn14) This quantitative approach would decrease ratings inflation and result in more failing and low satisfactory ratings on the lending test. As a result of this proposed reform, several banks would likely respond by boosting their retail lending to underserved communities.

The agencies proposed improvements to the other subtests of the large bank exam but did not establish as many guidelines for the performance measures, which could contribute to inflation on the subtests. The community development finance test, for example, will consist of a quantitative measure of a bank’s ratio of community development finance divided by deposits. The bank’s ratio will be compared to a local and national ratio.[[15]](#_ftn15) The agencies, however, did not provide enough guidelines to examiners for comparing the bank’s ratio to either the local or national ratio, making it possible for an examiner to inflate a rating by choosing the lowest comparator ratio. In addition, the impact review, the qualitative part of the test, must be more fully developed and contribute in a significant way to the score on the community development test.

The possibilities of misplaced examiner discretion can also occur on the retail services test and the community development services test. The retail services test contains quantitative measures comparing a bank’s branch distribution to market and demographic benchmarks but does not provide enough instructions to examiners about how to weigh these benchmarks. Furthermore, the proposal would allow examiners to use their discretion regarding how to weight the component tests of the retail services test, which would create inconsistent exams and could contribute to another round of ratings inflation.[[16]](#_ftn16) Below, we ask the agencies to develop weights for the components of the service test and develop more guidelines to examiners about how to use performance measures.

**Enhancements to community development definitions will increase responsiveness of banks to community needs**

The agencies proposed refinements to the definitions of affordable housing, economic development, climate resiliency and remediation, community facilities and infrastructure that we believe would more effectively target revitalization activities to communities such as persistent poverty counties and Native American communities.

The agencies have clarified that revitalization activities must not displace LMI populations.[[17]](#_ftn17) The anti-displacement provision must be applied to all community development (CD) activities including affordable housing. A final CRA rule that does not adequately protect against displacement would not be upholding CRA’s requirement that banks serve the needs of LMI populations and communities. For example, multifamily housing that may initially be affordable but then involves rapid rent increases that pushes out LMI tenants is not serving the needs for housing. Further, needs are not met if housing is kept in poor condition and tenants face harassment. In addition, it will be important that the rule ensure sufficient income targeting, promote access to opportunity and promote fair housing and tenants’ rights.

Harmful projects like landfills or fossil fuel facilities that are disproportionately placed in LMI neighborhoods and communities of color must not receive CRA credit under the new definition of CD. Instead, they must be penalized by lowering scores on the CD finance test. The proposed addition of climate adaptation and resiliency measures for CRA credit is an important and positive step forward, reflecting the increasing harms of climate change for vulnerable communities and the ways in which climate resilience is a critical foundation for community health and economic stability and growth.

The NPR clarified that financing health services qualifies under the definition of community support services. Essential community facilities now include hospitals and health centers without current documentation requirements, applied inconsistently, that the financing attract and retain residents to the community.[[18]](#_ftn18) This streamlining would boost financing of critical community infrastructure.

The community development finance test will include an impact review[[19]](#_ftn19) which must be further developed and include points and ratings like the other subtests so that the test can be more effective in stimulating responsive community development activities. We ask the agencies to reconsider their proposal to expand CRA consideration for financial literacy with no income limits[[20]](#_ftn20); scarce counseling resources need to be targeted to LMI and other underserved populations.

Finally, we ask the agencies to carefully develop their proposed list of illustrative activities that qualify for CRA to avoid the impression that this list is an exclusive list of approved activities. Novel and responsive activities like financing minority-owned media outlets, childcare centers and workforce development for people with disabilities should be highlighted.

**Data improvements will help hold banks accountable but all new data should be publicly available**

The agencies correctly proposed to include new data collecting requirements for deposits, community development activities and automobile lending. Some of this data such as deposit and automobile lending would not be publicly available[[21]](#_ftn21), which limits the extent to which the public can hold banks accountable for reaching underserved communities. We ask the agencies to reconsider this decision and also to expand data collection to all large banks instead of just banks with assets of more than $10 billion in the case of deposits and automobile lending.[[22]](#_ftn22) Finally, CRA exams should not only analyze access to deposits accounts for LMI communities but also affordability by comparing and refining, if necessary, fee information collected in call report data.

**Accountability for discrimination will increase but the agencies need to bolster their reviews concerning the quality of lending**

The agencies proposed to include all activities and products such as deposit accounts in addition to credit in anti-discrimination and consumer protection legal reviews.[[23]](#_ftn23) This is an important advance but we urge the agencies to expand their reviews to include the quality of lending. Massachusetts CRA exams include analysis of delinquency and defaults rates in home lending.[[24]](#_ftn24) Federal CRA exams should do likewise in all major product lines including single family, multifamily, small business and consumer lending. Moreover, reviews of lending must include an affordability analysis and impose penalties when banks offer on their own or in partnerships with non-banks abusive, high-cost loans that exceed state usury caps and that exceed borrowers’ abilities to repay. Finally, we are pleased that the agencies added the Military Lending Act[[25]](#_ftn25) to the list of laws to be included in the fair lending review but we urge them to also add the Americans with Disability Act.

**Assessment areas are expanded to include online lending but performance in smaller areas needs to be considered more carefully**

For several years, advocates have urged the agencies to examine lending that occurs online. The agencies proposed to create retail assessment areas where a large bank does not have branches when a bank has issued 100 home loans or 250 small business loans.[[26]](#_ftn26) This proposal would result in the great majority of total lending being incorporated on exams and would therefore hold non-traditional banks more accountable for serving LMI communities.

We ask the agencies to expand upon their proposal to include partnerships with banks and non-banks for retail lending. When a bank partners with more than one non-bank, the lending of all the non-banks needs to be totaled together for calculating if the threshold is exceeded for purposes of creating assessment areas.

In order to ensure that banks serve smaller metropolitan areas and rural counties, the agencies proposed requiring that banks with 10 or more assessment areas must receive at least a Low Satisfactory rating in 60% of the assessment areas in order to pass overall.[[27]](#_ftn27) This still may not be an adequate solution since the smaller areas could represent a minority of areas, allowing a bank to pass the 60% threshold by focusing on the larger areas. One possible fix is to require banks to achieve at least a Low Satisfactory rating of 60% in each of its large metropolitan, small metropolitan and rural assessment areas. The overall passage rate for all assessment areas should be increased to 70% or higher to ensure banks are responding to community needs across their geographical footprint.

**Reclassifying banks as small and intermediate small banks (ISB) would reduce community reinvestment activity**

By adjusting asset thresholds for qualifying for various CRA exams, the agencies proposed to reclassify about 779 ISB banks as small banks, which would involve no longer holding these banks accountable for community development finance. In addition, the agencies proposed to reclassify 217 large banks as ISB banks, eliminating their service test and accountability for placing branches in LMI communities.[[28]](#_ftn28) These changes lack justification since these banks have been successfully performing these activities for several years. We urge the agencies to eliminate this aspect of the NPR since it would reduce reinvestment activity.

**The question the agencies did not ask in the NPR: how to incorporate race in CRA exams**

The agencies assert that the increased granularity of their proposed CRA exams would address racial disparities. For example, they have stated that the proposed lending test would explicitly scrutinize lending to the smallest businesses with revenues under $250,000. Since these businesses are disproportionately owned by people of color and women, the bolstered scrutiny of lending to these business would help address disparities in access to credit. The agencies’ proposal likewise provided more incentives for banks to finance minority-depository institutions, women-owned depository institutions and community development financial institutions (CDFIs). All of these institutions engage in lending focused on traditionally underserved communities including communities of color. However, their reach remains relatively small compared to their larger counterparts.

As important as these proposed changes are, they fall far short of the measures needed to remedy the persisting legacy of discrimination in the areas covered by the CRA. Ongoing disparities and patterns of discrimination continue, against a backdrop of systemic racism that has plagued our nation for centuries. Systematic racism against African Americans started in 1619 when the first slave ships landed on the east coast. Slavery established debilitating disadvantages that were not sufficiently redressed in the short time period known as Reconstruction. Not long thereafter, private and public sector entities embarked on segregation, designed to separate the races and place African Americans and other people of color in crippling disadvantages.

In the midst of a Great Depression and in a genuine effort to uplift the dispossessed through the New Deal and a program to rescue families from foreclosure, the Roosevelt administration nevertheless invented redlining and exacerbated segregation. Within the administration, there were civil rights figures including Eleanor Roosevelt but the overwhelming racism within society guided the Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC).

HOLC sponsored the creation of maps that classified city neighborhoods by risk they posed to lending institutions. Neighborhoods were color coded – green for the most desirable neighborhoods while red classified the most hazardous ones. The classifications were guided by some objective criteria such as the quality of the housing stock but a heavily weighted factor, if not the predominant factor, was the racial composition of the neighborhoods.[[29]](#_ftn29)

A significant presence of African Americans or an in-migration of African Americans usually resulted in a classification of “hazardous.” A presence of other “undesirables” such as Jews or other recent Eastern or Southern European immigrants often propelled a neighborhood into the red category.

These classifications later influenced the maps created by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA). The maps and their racist assumptions subsequently guided public and private sector lending across neighborhoods. In the post-World War II years, FHA-guaranteed lending dominated and contributed to segregated white suburbs and established a white middle class of homeowners. African Americans were systematically excluded – only 1% of mortgage loans from 1930 to 1960 went to African Americans.[[30]](#_ftn30) The institutionalized racism in the public sector and in the lending industry was aided and abetted by the KKK and white supremacist violence.

NCRC studied the impact of the HOLC maps on the fate of the urban neighborhoods classified into the various risk categories.

* We found that nationally, 91% of the areas classified as “best” are middle and upper income today, while 74% of the areas classified as “hazardous” are low- and moderate-income today.
* By race, 85% of the “best” areas are predominantly white today while 63% of the “hazardous” areas are majority-minority.[[31]](#_ftn31)
* The average poverty rate increased from 14.3% in tracts in the lowest quartile of historic redlining score to 28.1% in tracts in the highest quartile of historic redlining score.[[32]](#_ftn32)
* In 2019, Black homeownership was lower than it was when segregation was legal.[[33]](#_ftn33)

NCRC also found statistically significant associations between greater redlining and pre-existing conditions for heightened risk of serious health conditions like asthma, COPD, diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, kidney disease, obesity and stroke. All of these conditions made the “hazardous HOLC communities” more susceptible to COVID during the pandemic.

On average, life expectancy was lower by 3.6 years in redlined communities, when compared to the communities that existed at the same time, but were high-graded by the HOLC.[[34]](#_ftn34) In addition to health risk factors, the Center for American Progress found that underserved tracts with high percentages of people of color were also more likely to confront environmental hazards.[[35]](#_ftn35)

NCRC partnered with the University of Richmond to create digital and historical maps of the redlined neighborhoods. One of the centers of the civil rights struggle was the City of Birmingham, Alabama. Yet, predominantly African American communities did not escape the disadvantages created by the HOLC maps. An example is a community called Smithfield Court.

Here is what the appraiser creating the HOLC map said about that community:[[36]](#_ftn36)
